title: Russian drone factory director seriously injured in car explosion
summary: Vladimir Tkachuk has been pictured showcasing his drones to President Vladimir Putin.
story: The director of a factory supplying drones to the Russian military was badly wounded when his car exploded, news reports said Wednesday, marking the second attack in a week on Russian drone makers.

The state Tass and RIA Novosti agencies said that Vladimir Tkachuk was hospitalized in grave condition following the explosion late Tuesday in Bolshoy Istok just outside Yekaterinburg, about 870 miles east of Moscow. The driver of the car was killed in the explosion, the Reuters news agency reported.
Images published on Russian social media channels purported to show the burned out chassis of Tkachuk's Mercedes, surrounded by charred debris.
Tass and RIA Novosti didn't immediately give details of the explosion or say who could be responsible. There was no immediate comment from the authorities.

Tkachuk headed the Uraldronzavod factory that manufactures Upyr (Russian for "Ghoul") drones. Tkachuk, a small-scale entrepreneur, set up a team of engineers that developed the Upyr and organized its production near Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city, and a key industrial hub in the Ural Mountains
The Upyr, a cheap and simple first-person view drone, was hailed by troops for the protection it offers against jamming.
Tkachuk, who founded the firm in 2023, has been pictured showcasing his drones to President Vladimir Putin.
Last week, the director and founder of a different Russian drone manufacturer was wounded in a shooting, in what prosecutors described as an "attempted murder."
Ukraine made no immediate comment on this latest attack.

The car explosion was reported one day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared a video purporting to show a civilian being chased and attacked by a Russian drone in the city of Kherson. In a social media post on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the world "must see" the footage that he said shows Russia's soldiers "take pleasure in killing and abusing civilians."
Moscow blames Kyiv for targeted attacks
Russian authorities have blamed Kyiv for a series of bombings and other attacks against senior military officials after Moscow sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022.

The explosion followed Saturday's deadly bombing at an upscale Moscow restaurant, which the Russian Embassy in Rome blamed on Ukraine, describing it as an attempt to intimidate the Italian community in Russia. It said in a statement Monday that the attack on the Balzi Rossi restaurant killed five and injured 19.

The Russian Foreign Ministry reposted the embassy statement without comment, and Russia's security agencies haven't named the suspected culprits. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin has described the bombing as a "brutal terrorist act," but did not say who was responsible.

Several Russian media outlets claimed the bombing targeted a Russian general who was celebrating his birthday at the restaurant. Some claimed that the general was Col.-Gen. Alexander Chaiko, who led the troops that made a botched attempt to storm the Ukrainian capital in 2022 and recently was appointed the chief of Russia's aerospace forces. The claims could not be independently verified.

title: $25 million reward offered for U.S.-born leader of powerful cartel
summary: Juan Carlos González is the stepson of "El Mencho," who was killed by the Mexican military.
story: The State Department on Wednesday offered a $25 million reward for information leading to the capture of Juan Carlos González, or "Pelón," scaling up pressure on a U.S. citizen who has emerged as the figurehead of Mexico's most powerful cartel.

The reward was bumped up from $5 million. The Trump administration offered a total of $102 million in rewards for various leaders of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG, and restricted the visas of family members and business associates of cartel members.

The State Department said it was aimed at "crippling the organization's leadership" while President Trump has ramped up pressure on Mexico and other Latin American nations to carry out his security agenda.

CJNG is among eight Mexican cartels designated as foreign terrorist organizations. The group was dealt a blow in February when leader Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, or "El Mencho," was killed by the Mexican military. The U.S. provided intelligence for the operation, which resulted in a burst in violence in the state of Jalisco.

González, Oseguera Cervantes' stepson and a dual Mexican and U.S. citizen, is reported to have taken control of the cartel, which is involved in everything from avocado production to drug smuggling. According to the State Department, González was born in Santa Ana, California, on Sept. 12, 1984.

The reward offers also include up to $15 million for Audias Flores Silva, a.k.a. "El Jardinero" ("The Gardener"); up to $15 million each for Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, a.k.a. "Sapo," and Oseguera Cervantes' son-in-law, Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez, a.k.a. "Chorro"; up to $10 million each for Ricardo Ruiz Velasco, a.k.a. "Tripa," Julio César Montero Pinzón, a.k.a. "El Tarjetas," and Carlos Andrés Rivera Varela, a.k.a. "La Firma"; and up to $2 million for Griselda Margarita Arredondo Pinzón.

Wednesday's move comes a few weeks after the Trump administration slapped sanctions on 50 people and companies linked with the cartel, including González. The sanctions froze assets and blocked U.S. financial transactions with those cited.
The cartel is considered the largest in Mexico, with a presence in 21 of its 32 states. Its operations have extended to several countries, including the U.S.
"The United States is hunting down, dismantling, and destroying Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement Wednesday.
The Trump administration has ramped up pressure on the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down more heavily on cartels, even threatening military action against the groups.

In June, the U.S. Treasury announced a new bank alert targeting the cartel. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control imposed sanctions on two men and nine companies involved in transportation, financial services and real estate, accused of being tied to a cartel-linked fuel theft ring intended to evade Mexican taxes while generating tens of millions of dollars annually for the cartel.

title: Baby "cocaine hippo" linked to infamous drug lord is rescued in Colombia
summary: Colombia has around 200 so-called "cocaine hippos" living in the wild, all of which descended from a colony brought to South America by slain cocaine kingpin Pablo Escobar.
story: Authorities in northwestern Colombia said they rescued a newborn hippopotamus found alone by fishermen on the banks of a river and showing signs of malnutrition.

Colombia has around 200 so-called "cocaine hippos" living in the wild, according to the Environment Ministry, all of which descended from a colony brought to South America by slain cocaine kingpin Pablo Escobar.

Fishermen found the small hippo separated from its mother and hidden in the bushes along the riverbank in a rural area of the Puerto Nare municipality in Antioquia, said Javier Valencia, director of the regional environmental authority, in a statement on Tuesday.
Veterinarians treated it for "advanced dehydration and malnutrition," according to a statement.
After being stabilized, the animal was transferred to a hippo sanctuary at Hacienda Napoles, the estate previously owned by Escobar and which is now a theme park.
Escobar imported four hippos in the 1980s for his private zoo at the hacienda.
After the Medellin cartel leader's death in 1993, the animals escaped and settled along the banks of the Magdalena River, where they have disrupted the ecosystem and even attacked local residents.

Independent journalist Audrey Huse, who has lived in Colombia for years, previously told CBS News that because the hippos roam freely, they end up killing fish and threatening endemic species like manatees, otters and turtles.

"Because they have no natural predators here, as they would in Africa, the population is booming and it's affecting the local ecosystem," Huse said. "Because they are such large animals, they consume considerable amounts of grassland and produce significant waste, which then poisons the rivers."

They are now considered an invasive species and are destabilizing native ecosystems, prompting the government this year to approve a plan to cull around 80 of them after attempts to curb their reproduction through sterilization failed.
The government previously arranged for the possible transfer of hippos to overseas sanctuaries. But the cost of deporting the hippos is also expensive — an estimated $3.5 million.
It is the largest hippo colony outside Africa.

title: Record-low Danube River levels threaten shutdown of Hungary's nuclear plant
summary: Three of four units of Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant were not in operation and the fourth was operating at about 50%, as of Wednesday morning.
story: As the Danube River breaks new record lows across much of its nearly 1,800-mile stretch through eastern Europe, curiosities of the past — including woolly mammoth bones in Bulgaria, sunken Nazi warships in Serbia and unexploded WWII artillery in Hungary's capital — are emerging. But there's also an energy crisis unfolding for Hungary's nearly 10 million people.

The country's only nuclear power plant, known as Paks, is on the brink of completely shutting down. As of Wednesday morning, three of the plant's four reactors are not in operation, while one continues to operate at approximately 50% power.
On normal days, the 44-year-old Soviet-designed facility, which sits on the Danube about 60 miles south of Budapest, generates roughly 50% of the country's electricity.
But with a drought across southeast Europe now more than three months in, these are not normal days.

Unlike nuclear plants in the U.S., U.K., Germany and France — many of which sit on smaller rivers and rely on giant hourglass-shaped cooling towers to recirculate water — Paks was built to suck water in directly from the Danube, a river long assumed too mighty to run dry. Approaching the plant, there are no telltale dumb-bell silhouettes on the horizon signaling its presence.

"Several factors will determine whether Hungary's most important power plant can avoid a complete shutdown in the coming days," said Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, visiting the site Tuesday, attempting to balance reality while projecting optimism.
Just three months into office after his Tisza party ended Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule in a landslide election this spring, Magyar has called on all Hungarians to unite to conserve power.
Hardly any precipitation is forecast for at least the next 10 days and the Danube's water levels are expected to slip even lower.

"There are a few critical days left. Today and tomorrow are certainly that," Magyar said. "I ask everyone to continue the national unity that has developed in the country. Let's do what our country demands."

Magyar noted there is "light at the end of the tunnel," as forecasters predict a cold front moving in on Friday. The temperature in Budapest Wednesday and Thursday was expected to be above 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
The anxiety over Paks, Hungary's most critical piece of infrastructure, is the first real test of Magyar's young government.

This week, more than 300 government-linked buildings in Budapest have been ordered to turn off their lights, with the romantic spotlights on popular tourist hotspots like Buda Castle and the Chain Bridge staying dark after the late-summer sunsets.

To offset the loss of power generation, Hungary has nearly doubled its electricity imports from neighboring countries via the region's power grid, news site Euractiv reported. Hungary's electricity network is among Europe's most interconnected, letting the country easily buy power from its neighbors. Costs have not hit consumers yet as the new government absorbs the difference for now.

"The electricity market is stable, and supply is problem-free," the government said, while urging households to avoid running washing machines and tumble dryers between 5 and 10 p.m. to ease pressure on the grid.
Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, warming more than twice as fast as the global average, according to Copernicus, the European Union's Earth observation and climate monitoring group.
The continent has warmed by around 4.5 degrees Fahrenheit compared to pre-industrial levels, with the fastest warming areas in eastern and parts of central Europe, as well as the European Arctic.

title: Nazi warships, mammoth bones emerge as Danube River dries up
summary: Water levels on the Danube River have dropped so low that dozens of World War II German battleships – and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth — are emerging into view.
story: Water levels on the Danube River, the second longest in Europe, have dropped so low because of drought that the hulks of dozens of World War II German battleships — and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth — are emerging into view.

They are a curious distraction from the summer heat crisis. The Danube's record-low water levels have also forced power plants to the brink of shutting down, and governments across Central and Eastern Europe are taking steps to conserve electricity.
In the middle of the river separating Serbia and Romania, near the Serbian port of Prahovo, a rusty hull is now visible, along with a broken mast where the Nazi flag once flew.

The ships, some still laden with weapons, belonged to Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet that the Germans deliberately sank as they retreated from Romania and as Soviet forces advanced deeper into Europe near the end of the war.
At least 20 World War II wrecks of various sizes are now visible to the naked eye from the banks of Prahovo.

Ivica Gavrilovic, who has spent his whole life living beside the Danube, said the interest in the wrecks was high but access remained difficult. "People still don't know how to access the ships themselves," he said, while taking a family of three out on his small boat.

Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in September 1944 near Prahovo in the Danube gorge as they came under Soviet fire. The idea behind the deliberate sinking was to slow down the Soviet advance in the Balkans. But Nazi Germany surrendered months later, in May 1945.

The sight of the old warships is a reminder that the Serbian government, with European Union financial support, has long been trying to do something about them. Some were removed from the river by Communist Yugoslav authorities, but most have remained because of the explosives they carried.

Now, however, authorities are trying to keep traffic flowing on the Danube, which flows through 10 nations, as the dropping water levels create dangerous conditions. Experts have linked the unusually hot weather to global warming and other factors.
Krsta Brandic, a Prahovo resident, said the low water levels have almost stopped ship traffic: "As you can see, the (big) ships can't pass anymore."

The old vessels have emerged before. In 2024, a trove of sunken Nazi ships, still decked out with explosives, emerged in the Danube following a blistering summer drought. Dozens of scattered ships operated by Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet also appeared in 2022 near Prahovo after water levels reached record lows.
Mammoth bones found on parched riverbed
Meanwhile, falling water levels in the Danube unveiled bones of a mammoth in Bulgaria, a local museum director told AFP.
The bone fragments found near the northeastern city of Ruse "very likely" belonged to a woolly mammoth that lived during the Ice Age, said Nikolay Nenov, director of the Regional Historical Museum.
Specialists have so far identified a jawbone, fragments of tusks, part of a shoulder blade, and a femur with its articular head among the stash, Nenov said.
The animal is thought to have been young and the dark color of the bones may indicate that it spent a lot of time in a marshy environment, he added.

The bones are an important discovery because they are well preserved and "unlike many previous discoveries ... were concentrated in the same place," indicating that they all belonged to the same animal, Nenov said.
Woolly mammoths coexisted with early humans who hunted the cold-resistant herbivores for food and used their tusks and bones as tools.
The animals died out about 4,000 years ago. For decades, scientists have been recovering bits and pieces of mammoth tusks, bones, teeth and hair.

title: Martha Stewart questions Meghan Markle’s homemaking credentials with blunt career assessment
summary: Martha Stewart questioned Meghan Markle's transition from actress to princess to homemaking guru, saying the career path "doesn't sort of follow."
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Martha Stewart is not entirely convinced Meghan Markle’s path into the lifestyle world adds up.

The 85-year-old homemaking icon offered a pointed assessment of the Duchess of Sussex’s transition from actress to royal to television host while discussing Markle’s Netflix series, "With Love, Meghan."
When asked about Markle stepping into her space with a cooking and lifestyle show, Stewart questioned whether the career transition made sense.
MEGHAN MARKLE RETURNS TO BRITAIN WITH PRINCE ARCHIE AND PRINCESS LILIBET FOR FIRST TIME IN YEARS
Martha Stewart questioned Meghan Markle's transition into the lifestyle television space during a recent interview. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images;Jonathan Brady / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

"If you’re an actress, it’s hard to then transition to a princess and then from a princess into a homemaking guru on a television show," Stewart told People. "It doesn’t sort of follow. So go from there."
Stewart also revealed that she recently crossed paths with Markle at a dinner party in California shortly after the duchess returned from a family trip to the United Kingdom.
"I had dinner with Meghan Markle the other night," she said. "We were both guests at a dinner party in California. And she had just gotten back from the palace."
Stewart said their interaction was brief.
"I didn’t talk to her really more than to say a couple words, but I know she was talking about it," she added.
Last month, Markle traveled to Britain with Prince Harry and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, marking the family’s first visit to England in four years.
King Charles and Queen Camilla hosted the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their children for a private family meeting at Highgrove House in July.

The Sussexes moved to California in 2020 after stepping back as senior working members of the royal family. Markle later returned to the entertainment industry while expanding into media, business and lifestyle ventures.
MEGHAN MARKLE AND NETFLIX END LIFESTYLE BRAND PARTNERSHIP AS CRITICS SAY THEY 'GOT MARKLED ENOUGH'
Meghan Markle and Prince Harry married in 2018. (Chris Jackson)
"With Love, Meghan" premiered on Netflix in March 2025 and featured Markle sharing cooking, gardening, hosting and entertaining ideas with celebrity guests.
The series launched alongside her lifestyle brand, As Ever, which has sold products including fruit spreads, honey, tea, wine, candles and chocolate.
Stewart’s latest remarks echo comments she made in July 2025, when she was asked by Yahoo Lifestyle about Markle’s attempt to establish herself as a lifestyle authority.
"Meghan, I don’t really know very well, and I hope she knows what she’s talking about," Stewart told the outlet.
The cookbook author emphasized that credibility and experience are essential when building a connection with an audience.
"Authenticity, to me, is everything, and to be authentic and knowledgeable about your subject matter is extremely important," she said.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Martha Stewart has built one of the world's most recognizable lifestyle brands. (Getty Images for Friends of Hudson River Park)
Stewart added that she did not object to other celebrities entering the lifestyle industry, offering a brief message to those following in her footsteps.
"I don’t mind. Good luck."
Stewart built her own homemaking empire after launching a catering business and publishing her first cookbook, "Entertaining," in 1982.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Her brand later expanded into magazines, television programs, books, retail partnerships and home products. She became the first self-made female billionaire in the United States in 1999.
The Netflix series ran for two seasons and was followed by a holiday special.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, relocated to California in 2020. (Karwai Tang)
In March 2026, Netflix and Markle announced they were ending their partnership involving As Ever, with the duchess continuing to operate the lifestyle brand independently.

"Meghan’s passion for elevating everyday moments in beautiful yet simple ways inspired the creation of the As Ever brand, and we are glad to have played a role in bringing that vision to life," a Netflix spokesperson told Fox News Digital at the time.

"As it was always intended, Meghan will continue growing the brand and take it into its next chapter independently, and we look forward to celebrating how she continues to bring joy to households around the world."
In its own statement to People, As Ever said it was "grateful for Netflix’s partnership through launch and our first year."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We have experienced meaningful and rapid growth, and As Ever is now ready to stand on its own," the statement continued. "We have an exciting year ahead and can’t wait to share more."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Archewell for comment regarding Stewart’s remarks.
Danielle Minnetian is an Entertainment Production Assistant for Fox News Digital covering celebrity news, entertainment trends and pop culture.

title: 'Melrose Place' star Andrew Shue says 70% believe the American Dream is 'dead or dying'
summary: Andrew Shue claims 70% of Americans believe the American dream is dead or dying, driving him to launch The Forum bipartisan civic initiative.
story: Melrose Place" alum Andrew Shue told Fox News Digital that economic strain, political dysfunction and anxiety about the future have left Americans feeling like the country’s "engine is broken."
Former "Melrose Place" star Andrew Shue believes that the majority of Americans have lost faith in the promise that once defined the country.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 59-year-old actor, who founded the new bipartisan initiative The Forum, shared his grim assessment of the current mood of citizens in the United States, arguing that people across the economic and political spectrum are struggling.
JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

"There's nobody in this country right now that thinks we're in a good place," Shue said. "You look around and you say, how do we feel about our kids? How do we fill it feel about our kid's future? What kind of anxiety level do we all have? You're seeing 70% believe the American dream is dead or dying."
Andrew Shue became a household name on ‘Melrose Place’ (Getty Images for ADAPT Leadership Awards)
"So we're all in this boat together," he continued. "There's nobody who's jumping out, whether you're a billionaire, a bartender, everybody in between, we are all in this together."
Shue said that Americans' growing pessimism is not being driven by a single election or political figure, but by systemic problems he believes have accumulated over decades.

"We're realizing that the engine is broken and the main systems that drive that engine are our political system and our economic system," Shue explained. "The political system only rewards people in power — there happen to be a lot of old people — and performative conflict. The economic system is really just rewarding people at the top. Ninety percent feel like they're treading water or underwater, and have been for decades. The other thing I'll say is all of these problems existed long before [current U.S. President] Donald Trump came to the scene."
WATCH HERE: ‘MELROSE PLACE’ ALUM ANDREW SHUE SAYS 70% BELIEVE THE AMERICAN DREAM IS ‘DEAD OR DYING’
WORLD SERIES CHAMPION JOE GIRARDI REVEALS WHAT HE FINDS MOST 'DISTURBING' ABOUT POLITICS TODAY

"And so, as we look around, and we're fighting each other, and we try to figure out, what are we gonna do? Who's coming to save us? The answer is right in front of us," he continued. "It's us. It's the American people. The question is, ‘Oh, that seems kind of obvious. Yeah, the consent of the governed.’ We are the ones who are supposed to be the ultimate authority."

To help address what he sees as the country's growing divide, Shue founded The Forum, a nonpartisan civic initiative that brings together politically diverse Americans to identify areas of agreement and develop policy proposals. The initiative has already been implemented in three early primary states, including South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada.

"We have launched the Forum that I've been working on for the last eight years with an incredible team," he said. "It's the place and the process for the American people to co-create that renewal agenda. Over 300,000 people have participated so far. Perfectly politically balanced — conservatives showing up, liberals showing up, people on the far left, far right — everybody's showing up, and we have credibility and legitimacy."
Shue spent eight years founding the new bipartisan initiative The Forum to help bridge the political divide.  (Gary Gershoff/Getty Images)

"Elected leaders from both sides who put down their arms are actually leading the efforts in each state," he added. "So this is the way forward. The question is, will the legislators, the elected leaders, follow? The American people are ready to lead."
SEN CHUCK SCHUMER UNVEILS ANTI-CORRUPTION AGENCY AIMED AT TRUMP AND FUTURE PRESIDENTS
As the initiative has expanded across three states, Shue told Fox News Digital that he has been struck by how quickly participants find common ground despite their political differences.

"I think that the thing that surprised me the most was that when you give people this assignment, you say, 'It's now on you, you are going to be the hero of the story. All you have to do is work together, listen to each other, listen to your lived experiences, and come up with something that you can agree on,'" Shue said.
WATCH HERE: ‘MELROSE PLACE’ ALUM ANDREW SHUE LAUNCHES NEW BIPARTISAN INITIATIVE THE FORUM TO BREAK AMERICA'S POLITICAL GRIDLOCK

"And 70% have to agree — that's the supermajority number, 70% or higher — and then it can go forward as draft legislation," he continued. "And the thing that's beautiful is when you get these people in the rooms with people who are different, they can't figure out who the Democrat or the Republican is. They see all the common values. They see the common goal."

"Once you start listening to each other, once you start feeling like you're on the same team, and you have the same goal, anything's possible," Shue added. "And people are desperate. That's the thing. People are desperate. They're really ready for something new."
AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US
The Delaware native also reflected on what has restored his optimism about Americans and what they can achieve when they are united.
Shue said that he remains optimistic that Americans can come together to fix the system that he described as "broken." (Scott Gries/Getty Images)

"That we know what makes America, America," he said. "It's about that confidence, that belief in what's possible. You know, I think [U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it best, 'Anyone from anywhere can become anything.' And people believe that and they live that."

"America is a place — obviously we talk about opportunity — it's a place that gives everybody a shot," Shue continued. "And this is the moment where, again, we talk about the hero. This is the moment for the American people to be the heroes."
While Shue has largely stepped away from Hollywood, he said his "Melrose Place" fame has helped shine a spotlight on The Forum.
"It certainly hasn't hurt," he said. "People are a little bit confused. And then I tell them what I've been doing for the last eight years and how committed I've been to this project."

"This provides not just the pathway to create that renewal agenda, not just a pathway to create this new power source that's going to kind of break through this partisan gridlock that we have, but it's the opportunity for everybody to be part of something," Shue explained.
WATCH HERE: ANDREW SHUE CALLS ‘MELROSE’ PLACE THE ‘ULTIMATE EXAMPLE OF THE AMERICAN DREAM’

"If you think about even MAGA and you say, why was MAGA so strong? It's because they belonged to something," he added. "But we need to belong to something that's not about beating the other side. We've got to belong to something that's about going somewhere together. We want to be on the same team. We are so exhausted with our politics."

"The American people can do this, create that renewal agenda, and then we create the power base to enforce it. And like I said, the elected leaders are going to have to go along with it because this is the only way we can do it."
Reflecting on the personal challenges he has faced in recent years, Shue said difficult experiences have changed the way he approaches relationships and community.
Shue said that he believes Americans "want to be on the same team." (Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Do Something)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"It definitely makes you try to put yourself in other people's shoes," he said. "To walk in other people's shoes is such an important part of building any kind of community, building any kind of understanding. We are all flawed. We are trying to be better people. We make decisions sometimes that don't work out for us or for our kids."
"And those experiences, when you really struggle, and you go through something painful, it teaches you what you're all about," Shue added.

As Shue now spends his time trying to help others rediscover faith in the American Dream, he said that he feels he experienced it firsthand during his own acting career when he landed his starring role on "Melrose Place."
MICRON'S $250 MILLION BET ON KIDS IS A BLUEPRINT FOR AMERICA'S FUTURE
Shue said that starring in "Melrose Place" was the "ultimate example of the American Dream." ( Fotos International/Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"It just gave me a ton of confidence," he said. "It gave me doors that were opened and it gave me a platform. And it came at a time in my life where I was a little bit trying to figure out my direction and what I was capable of. But it did give me possibility. I mean, it was the ultimate example of the American dream."

"It was a real boost to my confidence and a boost to my thought process about what could be possible."
Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: Prince Harry's most controversial royal plan could still become reality, author says
summary: Royal author Simon Vigar says Prince Harry's rejected "half-in half-out" proposal is inevitable, but experts warn trust issues make his return unlikely.
story: Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," explains why Prince Harry expected a half-in, half-out role and what led to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit from royal duties.
One royal author believes Prince Harry's controversial "half-in, half-out" proposal may still have a future within the monarchy.
Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," told Fox News Digital that while Buckingham Palace quickly rejected the proposal in 2020, he believes a similar model is ultimately inevitable.

"Harry did think that there was a hybrid version that they could do," said Vigar. "And I think in years to come, there will be a hybrid version. I think he's right. There has to be a hybrid version of this where people don't get accused of cashing in but can support their cousins or their brother or whatever."
PRINCE HARRY LONGS FOR HIS OLD ROYAL LIFE AS AMERICA ISN'T WHAT HE EXPECTED, EXPERTS SAY

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were on a four-day visit to Australia, with engagements across Melbourne, Canberra and Sydney. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

"[The Sussexes] thought they could have a hybrid role of having a business life and a private life, while also spending a few months in the U.K. supporting the queen," he shared. "Harry believed that was an option, which was whipped away from him."
In 2020, Harry attended the Sandringham Summit at Queen Elizabeth II's Norfolk estate, where senior royals decided the terms of his and Meghan's departure from royal life.
A view of Sandringham House, Queen Elizabeth II's Sandringham estate, in Norfolk, England. (Radcliffe/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

According to People magazine, it was there that the late queen drew a firm line. After intense discussions, the answer was made clear to Harry: There would be no "half-in, half-out" role for the Sussexes. They couldn't be working royals while also pursuing independent, income-generating ventures.
WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A ‘HYBRID’ ROLE: AUTHOR
That year, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals, citing intrusive coverage by the British press and a lack of support from the palace.
In the couple's Netflix series, "Harry & Meghan," the prince said the decision to step down was his.
Simon Vigar's "The Four Wives of Windsor" is available now. Vigar is one of British television's longest-serving royal correspondents. (Penguin)
"In fact, it was my decision," he said. "She never asked to leave. I was the one that had to see it for myself. But it's misogyny at its best."
Office workers in London watch the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's "Harry & Meghan" docuseries on Netflix on Dec. 8, 2022. (Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images)

In a statement, the queen publicly confirmed the decision, making it clear that it was "not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service." The Sussexes responded with a statement of their own: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."
In the Netflix docuseries, Harry claimed that William "screamed and shouted" at him during the "Sandringham Summit."

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father King Charles III at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"It was terrifying to have my brother scream and shout at me, and my father say things that just simply weren't true, and my grandmother quietly sit there and sort of take it all in," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the last time the brothers spoke was in 2022 during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

In "Spare," Harry wrote that he arrived at Sandringham with the impression that the family would consider five options for the Sussexes. "Option Five" was a full departure. After an hour, the queen's private secretary, nicknamed by Harry "The Bee," distributed drafts of a statement announcing "Option Five." Harry said he was stunned.
"Wait. I'm confused," he wrote. "You've already drafted a statement? Before any discussion? Announcing Option Five? In other words, the fix was in this whole time? This summit was just for show?"

Britain's Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, looks on as Britain's King Charles III leaves Westminster Abbey after the coronation ceremonies in central London on May 6, 2023. He was sitting a few rows away from his family. (Ben Stansall/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the palace made a mistake by not considering the option.

Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry watch a flypast marking the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London, England, on July 10, 2018. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"The half-in, half-out approach advocated by Harry and Meghan is the modern-day method of how royal families should operate," he said. "The late queen was extremely badly advised not to accept the formula laid out by Harry as he attempted to protect Meghan from the ravages of sustained attacks."

But not everyone agrees. Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that while Harry may eventually have a better personal relationship with his family, a return as a working royal — especially under a "half-in, half-out" model — is highly unlikely.
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex depart Canada House in London, on Jan. 7, 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"There's always room for Harry to support his family privately as a son and brother," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "That's very different from supporting the monarchy publicly as a working royal. The monarchy has successfully adapted to a smaller working team."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Prince William, Prince of Wales, known as the Duke of Rothesay and Catherine, Princess of Wales, known as the Duchess of Rothesay when in Scotland, smile to well-wishers as they arrive for a visit to Aros Hall, a local community hub on April 29, 2025, in Tobermory, Scotland. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"We continue to see King Charles, Queen Camilla, the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Princess Royal, the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh and the Duke of Gloucester carrying out official duties," she pointed out. "While it's a leaner operation, it has demonstrated that it can function without reopening the constitutional questions raised in 2020."

After moving to California, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex publicly aired their grievances in interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further strained his relationship with his family.
Prince Harry's book "Spare" is displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)

On July 10, Charles hosted Harry and met with his family for the first time in years as they attempted to repair their rift. At Highgrove House, Charles' country estate, Harry and Meghan, along with their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, reunited with the king and Queen Camilla.
A photo of Highgrove House, King Charles III's country estate. (Neil Bennett/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)

Harry had arrived in the U.K. for several charity events that were overshadowed by speculation about whether he would meet with his father. The 41-year-old prince has said he wants to reconcile with the monarch, 77, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer.
Father and son met briefly for tea in September 2025, marking the first time they had seen each other in well over a year.
King Charles III is seen arriving at Clarence House on Sept. 10, 2025, in London, England. The monarch had a private tea with his son, Prince Harry. (Belinda Jiao/Getty Images)

The Duke of Sussex is expected to visit the U.K. in September of this year. The Sun reported that the king will offer his younger son a room at Buckingham Palace during his stay. Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Archewell, which oversees the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, for comment.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, poses for a selfie with well-wishers as he attends Scotty's Summer Festival at Maxstoke Castle in Birmingham, England. (Heathcliff O'Malley-Pool/Getty Images)

"Harry's issue isn't that he left," said Schofield. "It's what he did after he left. Between the Oprah interview, the Netflix series, ‘Spare,’ and years of public criticism, he established a pattern of taking private family matters and turning them into commercial products. That's exactly the type of risk the late queen was trying to avoid."

"If anything, Harry's conduct since 2020 has validated her decision rather than undermined it," she argued. "In any professional organization, that wouldn't strengthen your case for rejoining the leadership team. It would be cited as evidence that you cannot be trusted with confidential information or institutional responsibilities."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle meet well-wishers during a visit to Reprezent 107.3FM in London on Jan. 9, 2018. The "Suits" alum became the Duchess of Sussex when she married the British prince later that year. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

"The monarchy runs on trust," Schofield continued. "Harry has spent the last several years demonstrating a pattern of monetizing privileged access to the royal family. The palace would have to ask itself whether Harry could be trusted to represent the institution. I think the answer to that question is no."
Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, departs after attending a bingo night at The Royal Hospital Chelsea in London on April 29, 2025. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Schofield pointed to Sophie, now the Duchess of Edinburgh, as a cautionary tale. In 2001, she gave up her public relations career after an undercover reporter posing as a prospective client secretly recorded her discussing her royal connections. The controversy reinforced the palace's view that commercial work and official royal duties could create conflicts, and Sophie went on to become a full-time working royal.
Today, she is widely regarded as one of the monarchy's most valuable assets.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting Queen Elizabeth II's coffin to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Royal experts told Fox News Digital that William and Harry haven't spoken since 2022, when their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, died.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that, at most, she expects Harry to be offered "informal, limited and tightly controlled opportunities" while in the U.K. as he continues reconciliation efforts with his family. She said he will continue to participate in events supporting his charitable causes in his home country. However, a functional hybrid role isn't in the cards, she insisted.
KING CHARLES MAKES RISKY MOVE TOWARD PRINCE HARRY AS PRINCE WILLIAM 'REMAINS WARY': EXPERTS
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, take part in a Scar Tree Walk in Melbourne, Australia, on April 16, 2026. (Asanka Ratnayake/Getty Images)

"Prince William has been consistent in his opposition," said Fordwich, referring to the king's heir. "Princess Catherine is by his side on this, as are the courtiers and those whose role it is to protect the monarchy."

The Sussexes continue to raise their children in the wealthy, coastal city of Montecito. As Harry continues to rebuild his relationship with his father, Schofield doesn't believe a "half-in, half-out" role would ever be reconsidered.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, are seen here waving from the balcony of the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, Fiji, on Oct. 23, 2018. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were on their official 16-day autumn tour visiting cities in Australia, Fiji, Tonga and New Zealand. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"The late queen's decision wasn't a personal preference," she said. "It was an institutional decision designed to protect the Crown's impartiality and integrity. I don't see King Charles reversing it.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex departs from The Invictus Games Foundation Conversation: From Policy to Practice at Chatham House on July 7, 2026, in London. Multiple royal experts told Fox News Digital that there's no doubt King Charles' younger son misses his life in the U.K. (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)

"The strongest opposition would likely come from those responsible for protecting the monarchy's long-term stability, including Prince William and senior officials who understand the reputational risks. Once you allow one royal to commercially monetize royal status while carrying out official duties, it becomes incredibly difficult to explain why others cannot do the same."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Primetime' star Robert Pattinson shocks fans with Chris Hansen transformation in 'unsettling' trailer
summary: The trailer for A24's "Primetime" reveals Robert Pattinson's uncanny Chris Hansen transformation, sparking Oscar buzz and true crime debate.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Robert Pattinson left fans doing a double take after debuting his eerie Chris Hansen transformation in A24's "Primetime" trailer.

A24 released the first trailer for "Primetime," the upcoming thriller starring Pattinson as the "To Catch a Predator" host, on Thursday. The film, directed by Lance Oppenheim, follows Hansen as he sets out to make television history in the 2000s.

"To Catch a Predator" was a popular Dateline NBC series hosted by Hansen that used undercover sting operations to confront adults accused of attempting to meet minors for sex before they were arrested by police. Pattinson did truly morph into Hansen for the film in the trailer.
'THE SOCIAL RECKONING' TRAILER DROPS WITH JEREMY STRONG AS ZUCKERBERG IN AARON SORKIN'S FACEBOOK SEQUEL
Robert Pattinson transforms into "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hansen in A24's upcoming thriller "Primetime." (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)

"What would have happened if I wasn't here," the actor said in the trailer, using some of Hansen's most iconic lines. "You see how this looks, right? At the end of the day, a man must be held accountable for the decisions that he makes. Would you agree? Do you watch television? Well, there is something you should know. I'm Chris Hansen, with Dateline NBC, and you're about to be a part of television history."
It didn't take long for the trailer to set social media ablaze. Fans praised Pattinson's performance, predicted Oscar buzz and declared A24 had another hit on its hands.
"Pattinson is about to get an Oscar nomination for this," one user wrote. "The man cannot miss."
"If there's one thing Pattinson is going to bring to the table, it's a crazy little voice," another user added. "He's had an incredible year; I can't wait for this one."
JESSICA CHASTAIN'S NEW HORROR MOVIE 'OTHER MOMMY' DROPS A TERRIFYING FIRST TRAILER FOR FANS
Chris Hansen hosted NBC's "To Catch a Predator," a hidden-camera series that confronted adults accused of attempting to meet minors for sex. (Lisa Berg/NBCUniversal)
"This is gonna be so PEAK I cannot wait," one fan wrote.
"A24 somehow took one of the most memeable true-crime shows of all time and turned it into something that feels genuinely unsettling," another said. "September 25th is going to be a problem."
But not everyone was focused on Pattinson's performance. Some viewers were left wondering whether the film would tackle the real-life controversy that brought "To Catch a Predator" to an abrupt end.
"Ok, but why does this trailer make it seem like Hansen is the bad guy?" one user questioned.
"Is the story of why they stopped filming the show in there like about the guy who killed himself when caught," another asked.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"To Catch a Predator" became a cultural phenomenon before ending after its final investigation aired in 2007 following a controversial Texas sting operation. (Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images)

"To Catch A Predator" quickly ended after a highly controversial 2006 sting in Texas involving Assistant District Attorney Bill Conradt. Conradt had allegedly communicated online with a decoy posing as a 13-year-old boy but never arrived at the sting house. Instead, police, accompanied by Dateline NBC cameras, went to his home to serve a search warrant. As officers entered the house, Conradt died by suicide.
Although Hansen has maintained that the series simply ran its course after three years, the Conradt case is widely viewed as the event that led to the show's cancellation in 2008.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Robert Pattinson has earned early Oscar buzz after the first trailer for "Primetime" showcased his uncanny performance as Chris Hansen. (Stephane Cardinale/Corbis)

Pattinson has balanced major studio films with acclaimed auteur projects in recent years. He's appeared in "The Batman," "The Boy and the Heron," "Mickey 17," "Die My Love," "The Drama" and Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
He also has several high-profile projects in the pipeline, including "Dune: Part Three," "Here Comes the Flood" and "The Batman: Part II."
"Primetime" is scheduled to open in theaters Sept. 25.

title: Country star Hannah Dasher says famous, married celebrity once slid into her DMs
summary: Country star Hannah Dasher says a famous, married celebrity once slid into her DMs. She explained that her Christian faith kept her from taking shortcuts in country music.
story: Rapid Fire with country music stars at the ACMS

Country singer Hannah Dasher revealed that a famous, married celebrity once slid into her direct messages on social media, but explained her Christian faith has kept her from taking shortcuts in the music industry.
During a recent appearance on the "Like a Farmer" podcast, the 40-year-old musician was asked about the "weirdest" DM that she has ever received.
"Well, I don't know that I could share it because they're famous and married," Dasher said, without naming the individual. "So let me think of another one."
Country star Hannah Dasher revealed that a famous, married celebrity once slid into her DMs. (Getty Images for CMT)
ELLA LANGLEY GOES VIRAL WITH PASSIONATE COMMENTS ABOUT HER CHRISTIAN FAITH, GOD, LOVE AND RELIGION
"I could have gone on some pretty big tours, you know, if I wasn't a Christian," she added with a smile. "Golly, the weirdest DM that I've gotten. I guess that would be it, right? I don't know."
"Oh, I think about that one."

Raised near Savannah, Georgia, Dasher has previously said that she grew up on '90s country music. After graduating from college, she moved to Nashville, Tennessee to pursue a career in country music. Dasher has previously said that she worked selling boats and outboard motors at Bass Pro Shops to support herself before being fired for writing songs while on the job.

In 2013, she landed her first publishing deal with BMG Chrysalis and later signed with Sony/ATV Music Publishing in partnership with Jaren Johnston of The Cadillac Three. Dasher's first major break as a songwriter came in 2017, when Brad Paisley recorded her co-written song "Go to Bed Early" for his "Love and War" album, marking her first cut for a major label.
The singer did not name the individual who messaged her.  (Catherine Powell/NBC via Getty Images)
LAINEY WILSON SAYS CITY PEOPLE HAVE WRONG VIEW OF COUNTRY TOWNS AS SHE DEFENDS HER 'BLUE COLLAR' ROOTS

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dasher launched her viral TikTok cooking series, "Stand By Your Pan," where she mixes Southern recipes with country music and comedy. The series quickly attracted more than a million followers and helped introduce her to audiences beyond traditional country music fans.
Dasher signed a recording deal with Sony Music Nashville in 2021 and released her debut EP, "The Half Record," which featured songs including "Leave This Bar" and "Girls Call the Shots."
That same year, she was named one of CMT's Next Women of Country and made multiple appearances performing at the Grand Ole Opry.
She has since said that Sony "pulled the plug" on her recording deal shortly after the EP's release, leaving her to continue her career independently.
SHANIA TWAIN SAYS SHE'S FINALLY 'GETTING IT RIGHT' IN HER 60S AFTER STARTING LIFE ‘ON THE TOUGH SIDE’
Dasher said her Christian faith kept her from going on "some pretty big tours." (Michael Simon/Getty Images)
While speaking on the "Like a Farmer" podcast, Dasher candidly reflected on her career setback.

"I think losing my record deal was a huge humbling that needed to occur in me and it was the last thing that I thought was ever going to happen," she said. "But the devil will steal your confidence when moments like that happen."
ELLA LANGLEY'S FAITH AND AUTHENTICITY FUEL RECORD-BREAKING RISE, EXPERTS SAY

"And so I just had to remind myself that I didn't move to this town for anybody but me," she continued. "And you know that I have people that love me and depended on me and I just knew that I needed to um to get out of that lull and to start writing songs again."

Dasher explained that taking some time off from songwriting to pen her cookbook "Stand By Your Pan: 100 Easy and Affordable Comfort Food Recipes So Good They'll Hurt People's Feelin's," which was published in March was a "great way to kind of get those wheels turning again."
SINGER ZACH TOP SLAMS MODERN COUNTRY MUSIC, SAYS IT LACKS 'SOUL'
Dasher also opened up about losing her recording deal with Sony.  (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)

"And so I've kind of been out of the songwriting thing for a couple of years because of this, and now I'm back into it and I caught the fever again, if you will," she said. "I'm so excited to be working on new music and just to be growing this thing."

"And this time it's just so much more free," Dasher continued. "I don't have any rules over me that I feel like I'm having to write for, or that I can't do this or I can't say this. I'm just making this as authentically Hannah as it can be. Just real."
Dasher explained how she is embracing the freedom of working as an independent artist.  (Tammie Arroyo/Variety via Getty Images)
Dasher also shared her thoughts on the current state of country music, which has recently experienced a massive surge in popularity.
"I think country is always trending," she said. "I knew this '90s thing would come back around."

title: 'Boyhood' child actor lives 'in the middle of nowhere' after leaving Hollywood behind
summary: Ellar Coltrane, now 31, says he lives in the middle of nowhere doing manual labor and firefighting, but misses collaborating on independent films.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
"Boyhood" actor Ellar Coltrane, who starred in Richard Linklater's Academy Award-nominated flick, moved on from Hollywood.
Coltrane, now 31, portrayed Mason Evans Jr. in the epic about a boy growing up in Texas, which was filmed over a 12-year span from 2002-14. He was 18 when the movie ultimately debuted.
The film earned high praise from critics for compelling storytelling and performances, however Coltrane admitted he's now mostly "pretty far away from film" now and lives "in the middle of nowhere."
'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER'
Ellar Coltrane "moved on" from Hollywood after "Boyhood" stardom. (Rick Crane)
"I’ve acted in a couple of short films," Coltrane told Variety. "One called 'El Fantasma,' which we filmed in Mexico City, where I play Lee Harvey Oswald, that’s really cool.

"And then I did a film in El Paso two years ago, a short film called 'So, Who Was It This Time?' I’ve become kind of integrated with the independent film community in El Paso, which is really wonderful."
BROOKE SHIELDS REFLECTS ON BEING MADE A 'SEX SYMBOL' AT A YOUNG AGE AND HOW SHE TURNED THE PAGE ON FAME
He added, "I'm really inspired by the energy there and what my friends are up to. It reminds me of Austin 20 years ago."
While he appeared in the indie "Shoplifters of the World Unite," Coltrane admitted that he's no longer moved by the entertainment industry.
The "Boyhood" cast appeared during the "Boyhood" 12-Year Reunion Q&A at Austin Film Society's AFS Cinema in July. (Rick Kern)

"Really, in my life I’ve moved on," he said. "I do manual labor, and I’m a volunteer firefighter, and I’m working on my EMT license right now. But being back in Austin at the AFS event, interacting with film people again, I am missing being on set, missing collaborating."
DANNY MCBRIDE SAYS DITCHING LA WAS THE BEST MOVE FOR HIS CAREER AND FAMILY

He continued, "I do very well collaborating with a director who has a passion project. When I can get into that headspace with an artist and work closely with them to figure out how I can express what they’re trying to express, I think I can do really good work."

Coltrane, who was six when he was cast to portray the son of divorced parents played by Patricia Arquette and Ethan Hawke, admitted that while he enjoys acting, he's not equipped to show up "on a big set with a million producers as an actor."
Richard Linklater's "Boyhood" received a slew of awards and was nominated for Best Picture at the 87th annual Academy Awards. (Jeff Kravitz)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I don’t know how to do that," he said. "I was never really trained as an actor. I was trained by Richard and Ethan as a collaborator and part of the machine of the film. So I’m hoping for more small, independent passion projects that I can be a part of, because I have a lot to offer."
When it comes to life after child stardom, Coltrane thinks he "did pretty well in terms of navigating that and coming out the other side not too damaged, but it’s a lot."

"Being a child actor is always a strange thing," he said. "A big saving grace for me, in that context of being a child actor, and later interacting with the 'Harry Potter' kids and other people who starred in a long-term project or started a career around the same time, for them there was something released to the world also in childhood.
Patricia Arquette won the Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her role in "Boyhood" as divorced mother Olivia Evans. (Jason Merritt)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I didn’t have to experience that, and I am grateful for that, because when I did experience celebrity, it was a lot. It allowed me to have the experience of acting and learning to do all these things and being on set."

He added, "It allowed me to avoid being a child star, which is really difficult for a lot of people. I have a lot of compassion for people who really struggle with fame early in life."

title: Jeff Bridges nearly played John Dutton before Kevin Costner landed 'Yellowstone' role
summary: Taylor Sheridan originally wanted Jeff Bridges as John Dutton, but a Paramount executive pushed for Kevin Costner based on marketing appeal.
story: The Academy Award winner spoke with Fox News Digital about his new film, "Horizon: An American Saga" during the premiere at the TCL Chinese Theatre.
Jeff Bridges came close to ruling the Dutton ranch.
"Yellowstone" creator Taylor Sheridan originally envisioned the Oscar winner as John Dutton before executives pushed for Kevin Costner.

"Because he had worked with Jeff on 'Hell or High Water' and he really liked him, and he thought he would be great," Kevin Kay, former top Paramount executive, explained during an appearance on "The Joint Venture Show."
But the conversation quickly shifted to another Hollywood heavyweight.
TAYLOR SHERIDAN SAYS HOLLYWOOD DIDN'T BELIEVE IN ‘YELLOWSTONE,’ NOT IT'S A TV EMPIRE
Jeff Bridges and Kevin Costner were both considered for the lead role in "Yellowstone." (Getty Images)

"And I was kind of like, 'Listen, he's a great actor, but I'm thinking about the marketing, and I'm thinking about the poster, and I'm thinking about who is going to be on a horse with a cowboy hat, and I'm not seeing Jeff Bridges," Kay admitted.
"Like, I could see Jeff Bridges, but then suddenly I was like, 'What about Costner? Can we get Costner?'" he recalled. "And we did get him."
Landing Costner, however, wasn't easy.
"It was painful because Kevin Costner doesn't like to do TV apparently," Kay said. "He's a movie actor."
"And he had done the 'Hatfields & McCoys' and he had a really bad experience," the TV executive claimed. "It was on A&E."
Jeff Bridges was considered as an option to portray John Dutton in "Yellowstone." (Getty Images)
There was a reason Costner had reservations about returning to the small screen.

"I think it was a low-budget thing, and he didn't have a great time, and he really did not want to do TV again," Kay said. "But I think he read the script and something about it appealed to him. And he said yes."

Minnie Driver is "grateful to be alive" after surviving a serious car accident in France. (Minnie Driver/Instagram)

title: Tim McGraw and Faith Hill's daughter says weight-loss drugs led to the return of her eating disorder
summary: Gracie McGraw reveals how Ozempic brought back her eating disorder after being prescribed the weight loss drug for her PCOS diagnosis in 2022.
story: Dr. Rocio Salas-Whalen shares how rapid GLP-1–driven weight reductions leave many individuals confronting psychological challenges that complicate relationships and social routines.
Gracie McGraw, the eldest daughter of Tim McGraw and Faith Hill, is opening up about her experience with weight-loss drugs, saying the Ozempic craze contributed to the return of her eating disorder.

In a series of Instagram Stories shared on Monday, the 29-year-old actress and singer reflected on using the medication after being diagnosed with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), in 2022.

"Yes, it worked and made my PCOS symptoms easier to control," McGraw wrote on her Instagram Stories, according to People. But she said the medication also "brought back" her eating disorder and negative body image issues.
'REMEMBER THE TITANS' STAR ETHAN SUPLEE ISSUES WARNING ABOUT WEIGHT LOSS DRUG CRAZE
Tim McGraw and Faith Hill's daughter, Gracie McGraw, says she caved into "skinny culture" by taking Ozempic in 2022. (Getty Images)

"At that time I thought it was the best decision I ever made because I finally lost weight and got skinny," she said. "As soon as I started shedding a few pounds I noticed how people looked at me differently on the streets, in my friend groups and family, and in my own job. I got more opportunities when I lost weight than I ever have had in my life."

"I’ve been called fat and ugly my entire life, whether that had been from magazines or the internet, constantly saying I must have different genes than my sisters and parents because I was the ‘fat’ one and didn’t have the looks that my family has," she continued.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
McGraw said she quickly realized she had become "too skinny."

"All of a sudden skinny culture is back and I realized holy crap I have been feeding into my eating disorder this whole time under the guise of this miracle shot," she said. "I think it was probably one of the worst things I’ve ever done for myself, looking back. Because now as everyone is getting smaller and smaller, I am gaining my weight back and seeing how much losing all of that weight actually affected me and my views of myself."
Gracie McGraw has been open about her use of GLP-1s to treat her symptoms. (Gracie McGraw/Instagram)

"My internal system is forever changed since taking the meds," she continued. "Yes, it f---ing worked and made my pcos symptoms easier to control, but it also brought back my ED and negative views on my body."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Telling people to not speak on this is incredibly wrong and damaging," she added. "It’s promoting created thinness as [a] goal not as danger. We are at a time when we need to be taking care of ourselves and our people. If you know someone who is struggling or if you are, please never feel embarrassed to reach out to anyone. We are here for each other."
Gracie McGraw said a medical condition led her to start using Ozempic in 2022. (Joe Maher/Manny Carabel)
These days, McGraw reassured followers she is "doing so good now" despite "slip ups from time to time" when it comes to body image.
In 2022, McGraw shared her PCOS with the world, detailing the challenges of the diagnosis.

"I just wanted to share really quick that I have recently been diagnosed with PCOS (polycystic ovarian syndrome). To get the correct diagnosis you would need 2 out of the 5 characteristics of PCOS and I had 4. During my appointment with my endocrinologist I realized that may had been a factor in my issues with weight, so we decided to try a medicine to regulate my body more normally and create the tools to continue to keep my body and myself healthy as I get older," she wrote to her Instagram followers.

"I’m learning to navigate the new blemishes but I don’t think that I would have ever allowed myself to go to a doctors appointment like this unless I had taken the correct steps toward my mental health, because as much as physical health is important, mental goes hand and hand. Sending love to those who are struggling with something similar or literally anything at all. Mental health is freaking hard !! It’s a long road but we can get through it. I share my experience to hope my situation has reached someone who can relate," she explained.

title: Thomas Rhett reveals why he and wife Lauren reject celebrity perks for country life
summary: The country singer says wife, Lauren Akins, craves simplicity and normalcy, admitting the rush of performing for thousands made him struggle at home.
story: The country music singer told Fox News Digital that is the one piece of marriage advice she's received that has actually worked.
Thomas Rhett admitted this week that his wife didn’t think he was going to become a famous country singer.

"We've definitely had our fair share of ups and downs, ‘cause I think that Lauren really… she craves simplicity, at all costs, simplicity," the country singer said on the "Girls In Low Places" podcast on Sunday, clarifying that she believed he was talented, but knew that stardom was rare.

"She grew up, you know, real country, and her and her daddy would lay in the street at night and look at the stars," noting that "he would just call out different constellations and stuff like, ‘That's a satellite and that's this.’"
He explained that was how she saw her life, calling it "a real suburban neighborhood thing."
Rhett said he and Lauren Akins have known each other since they were in first grade, and they briefly dated in high school before reconnecting after she graduated from college.
MARCUS MUMFORD SAYS BIBLE CAMP SPARKED DECADES-LONG LOVE STORY WITH WIFE CAREY MULLIGAN
Thomas Rhett said his wife, Lauren Akins, has always wanted a simple life. (Getty Images for CMA)
"So, we got married at 22."
Admitting "there’s nothing normal" about fame, they noted that it affects everyone.
"There's just so many crazy things that come with being famous," he said, giving the example of getting to cut lines, which he said he refuses to do.

"I think that's why so many people try to just live their life in search of such normalcy and I think my wife obviously has wanted that her whole life, and we do live very simply," the "Die a Happy Man" singer said. "But it took me a minute."
HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE
He said his career "really started to pop" around 2017 to 2019.
"I don't think I let it get to my head, but I do think I got really used to it," the 36-year-old admitted. "In probably not the best way."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Rhett admitted he has to actively focus on not letting fame get him, because "when you walk on stage in front of, you know, 10,000 people, that's like a rush that you can't like go replicate. You know what I'm saying? Like you can't just go like play flag football with your friends and think that's going to entice the same feeling."
For that reason, he has a difficult time "being content in simple situations because I think there's no super high going on."
COUNTRY STAR RILEY GREEN REVEALS WHY FAN EMOTION AT HIS SHOWS BEATS INDUSTRY AWARDS EVERY TIME
That’s forced him to "get really good" at being quiet, which he says doesn't come naturally to him.
Rhett and Akins married in 2012. (Jeff Kravitz/Getty Images for CMT)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Hearing people singing his songs while he’s performing on stage has always seemed surreal, but the one that "gets" him is witnessing people cry when they meet him "because I don't see myself that way. Period."
TYLER HUBBARD STAYS CALM AS WIFE PULLS FISH HOOK FROM HIS SCALP ON FAMILY CAMPING VACATION
"And I have, you know, definitely five kids that definitely don't see me that way," he joked.
The couple share Willa, 10, Ada, who turns 9 on Aug. 12, Lennon, 6, Lillie, 4, and Brave, who was born in February.
He admitted trying to be "super dad" and taking his kids to school while he’s in the middle of doing late-night concerts can also be exhausting.
Later, in the podcast, when asked what marriage advice he would give, Rhett said, "Don’t forget to continue to date your wife."
Rhett and Akins share five children together. (Getty Images)
JESSIE JAMES DECKER ON WHY HER MARRIAGE TO ERIC DECKER HASN'T LOST ITS SPARK AFTER FOUR KIDS
"It gets so much harder when you have children to make time for each other because there's so many other bodies that need your full-time assistance," he explained.

The singer said he and his wife recently spent two days just the two of them in London before joining friends in the Cotswolds, noting that "you feel sad, and your kids are like ‘Why are you leaving?' And you're like, ‘Because we want to stay married!’" he joked.
Earlier this year, he admitted during his years of early fame he felt like he was "living a double life," adding that it almost ruined his marriage.

"I look through my life and I think about all the things that have kind of twisted me or made me like not the best person to be around, and it has always been either around affirmation or lack of affirmation," the country star told Sadie Robertson Huff on her "WHOA That’s Good" podcast.
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Appearing on the podcast with his wife, Rhett said that at the height of his fame, he experienced "the most affirmation I think I'd ever received in my life. And I really liked it."
But he admitted that he didn’t feel he handled his marriage very well at the time.
Thomas Rhett performs during a show in Nashville. (Getty Images)
"I look back at our life during that time, and I'm not — I don't think I stewarded it very well, to be honest with you," he said.

Rhett, who is Christian, said publicly he kept up a façade of spirituality, "but internally I was dying. Like I genuinely, I just liked what was happening so much that I think so much of me was being sucked into the world so hard that it just kept pushing me and her like this," he said, moving his hands away from each other.
CLINT BLACK AND LISA HARTMAN BLACK'S ONE RULE THAT HAS KEPT THEIR MARRIAGE STRONG FOR NEARLY 35 YEARS
Rhett noted that he and his wife said from "day one, divorce is not an option," but, "the more you actually think about it, anything is actually an option if you let it become that."

It wasn’t until 2020 that he "actually discovered bits and pieces of who I actually was at my core, without a microphone, without a stage with and without affirmation, because it was the first time it had ever been taken away from me, if that makes any sense," Rhett explained, referring to the pandemic.
"I’m not perfect," he continued. "I'll never be perfect, but I would say, like today, us looking at each other and being a married couple, I would say this is… I'm living my most true self now."

He pointed to his wife and added, "She always sort of has been."
