title: Viagra could do more than advertised as study reveals surprising health superpower
summary: Sildenafil, Viagra's active ingredient, may restrict cancer metastasis by limiting cancer cells' cholesterol access, a new study has found.
story: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence and potentially new diagnoses.
Viagra could do more than give men a boost in the bedroom, as new research suggests it may have benefits for cancer patients.
The prescription medication, which is manufactured and distributed by Viatris, is commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction by increasing blood flow during sexual stimulation.

It was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
A new study published by the American Association for Cancer Research found that the pill may have properties that can prevent cancer from spreading.

Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, led by Dr. Yarden Ariav in the lab of professor Ayelet Erez, found that Viagra’s active ingredient — sildenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor — may restrict cancer metastasis, or the formation of new tumors.
Viagra’s active ingredient, sildenafil, may restrict cancer cells from spreading, a new study suggests. (Getty Images)

The team, which included scientists at the U.S. National Cancer Institute, analyzed human and mouse cancer cells, genetic experiments and 20 years of health data from 5 million members of Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest nonprofit healthcare provider and health insurer. They also examined how genes, proteins, fats, cholesterol and cellular energy interact.

The analysis revealed that sildenafil limits the cancer cell’s ability to make use of cholesterol, which is an important mechanism in how the cell breaks away from the primary tumor and migrates throughout the body, according to a press release from the American Committee for the Weizmann Institute of Science.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Sildenafil was found to block an enzyme called phosphodiesterase type 5, or PDE5, and increase the signaling molecule called cGMP, which dilates blood vessels – the feature that has made Viagra a successful treatment for erectile dysfunction.

According to the researchers, cGMP also binds to a protein that transports cholesterol within cells, reducing the cholesterol available for essential cellular functions. Cancer cells are "particularly vulnerable to this reduction in cholesterol supply," they noted.

Viagra was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials. (Alex Segre/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Based on their findings, the researchers suggested that combining Viagra-related drugs with statins, which lower cholesterol, could help slow the spread of cancer by reducing tumor cells' access to both existing and newly produced cholesterol.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We have uncovered a new biological pathway that links a well-known signaling molecule to cholesterol regulation within cells and shown how this pathway can be harnessed to interfere with the ability of cancer cells to form metastases," Erez, senior researcher and dean of Weizmann’s Miriam and Aaron Gutwirth Medical School, commented in a statement.

Combining drugs from the Viagra family with statins – a class of drugs responsible for reducing cholesterol production in the body – may be even more effective in restricting the spread of cancer, the researchers suggested. (iStock)

"Beyond their therapeutic promise, our findings highlight that cancer biology is shaped not only by mutations in tumor cells, but also by the patient’s metabolic state and by medications they are already taking for other conditions."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The researcher added that this study "underscores the importance of treating the whole patient – not just the cancer – when tailoring the most effective therapy."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study’s use of mouse models could pose a limitation to the final implications, as cancer treatment may not always translate similarly to humans, the researchers acknowledged.
The human evidence is also observational, which reveals an association instead of a proven cause and effect.
Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors and the medication's manufacturer for comment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 5 reasons more Americans are cutting off their own parents, according to psychologist
summary: The spotlight on NFL quarterback Aaron Rodgers' family estrangement has sparked renewed interest in why relatives become estranged. A psychologist breaks down five common contributing factors.
story: Dr. Richard L. Blake, a British psychologist and author based in Austin, Texas, shared five factors that he believes commonly contribute to fractured family relationships.
Cutting off family members is becoming more and more common, leading experts to consider the drivers of the division.

NFL quarterback Aaron Rodgers' years-long estrangement from members of his family — which reportedly ended recently after a reconciliation with his parents — has renewed public interest in why some relatives become permanently divided.
A 2025 YouGov survey found that 38% of U.S. adults are estranged from at least one family member, including siblings, parents, children or grandparents.
'DOORMAT MOM' CUT OFF BY DAUGHTER AMID ESTRANGEMENT TREND: ‘COMPLETELY BLINDSIDED’

Based on his research and work in the field of family estrangement, Dr. Richard L. Blake, a British psychologist and author based in Austin, Texas, shared the following five factors that he believes commonly contribute to fractured family relationships.
No. 1: Political and value differences

A longstanding study of more than 2,000 mother-adult child relationships found that "value dissimilarity" was a strong predictor of estrangement, suggesting that differing beliefs may play a large role in family rifts.
Cutting off family members is becoming more and more common, leading experts to consider the drivers of the division. (iStock)
"That could be political values, that could be gender ideology," Blake told Fox News Digital.

"There were people more likely to cut off someone for having a different opinion than for people who have done serious violent crimes," he said. "So certainly, political differences are a big problem."
No. 2: Social media influence

Heavy social media use has been linked to poorer parent-child relationships. A study of nearly 9,800 teens found that spending more than two hours a day on social media was linked to significantly greater odds of negative relationships with one or both parents.
Blake believes social media may also normalize family estrangement by exposing users to viral "no contact" stories and encouraging what he described as "word-of-mouth mimicry."
SECOND LADY USHA VANCE GETS CANDID ABOUT NEW BABY, JUGGLING FOUR CHILDREN AND MOTHERHOOD

"Someone might see a video on TikTok — 'I cut off my parents, and I'm much happier now. They were toxic narcissistic boundary crossers. And now I'm great,'" he said. "And people mimic that. Or they think, 'Oh, this person's getting a lot of attention.'"
Although he acknowledged that there are no long-term studies that have definitively documented an increase, "that doesn't mean absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence."

A long-standing study of more than 2,000 mother-adult child relationships found that "value dissimilarity" was a strong predictor of estrangement, suggesting that differing beliefs may play a large role in family rifts. (iStock)
According to Blake, society has shifted away from what he described as a "dignity culture" toward one that places greater value on "victim culture."

"So now it's a race to the bottom," he said. "If you don't have enough victim status because of the way you were born, you can create a victim status by suggesting your parents abused you or neglected you … and therefore you have value, a reason to cut them off."
No. 3: ‘Therapy culture'
The expert also pointed to what he described as "therapy culture," claiming that changing attitudes toward trauma and abuse have influenced how some people view relationships with their parents.

"Another justification is, ‘I cut off my parents to protect my mental health’ — and this is a sort of false belief," he told Fox News Digital. "There is this huge bias that if you're struggling in your adult life, it must be because your parents did something they shouldn't or didn't do something."
An expert argued that family relationships remain one of the strongest protective factors for mental health. (iStock)
Blake argued that family relationships remain one of the strongest protective factors for mental health.
"Families are one of the most evidence-based buffers against mental illness," he said. "There’s this myth that families are not important."
The psychologist pointed to a well-known Minnesota study of adopted twins, which found that twins often resembled their biological parents more than the adoptive parents who raised them.
BECKHAM FAMILY FEUD: WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT BROOKLYN'S WIFE, BILLIONAIRE HEIRESS NICOLA PELTZ

He also cited a 2024 study led by German sociologist Karsten Hank, which found that adults estranged from parents or siblings reported lower life satisfaction and more depressive symptoms than those who maintained family relationships.

"So it seems like it's certainly a health event for parents who get cut off, and it's probably a negative health event for the kids or the adult children who are doing the cutoff," he said. "It's this lie they're getting sold on social media: ‘Cut off your parents and your mental health will be better.’"
No. 4: Communication breakdowns
The way families communicate during conflict can determine whether disagreements escalate into long-term estrangement, according to Blake.
It’s important to listen first, he said, noting that "hostage negotiation" can be useful in these scenarios.
"Perhaps we should be learning from our grandparents more than the therapists."

"[That means] listening to the other person and then repeating back what they said as you understood it and validating that … and then waiting until that person's really finished before you give your side of it."
Blake also raised the issue of "moralized language," or "therapy words" that get thrown at parents — "such as abuse, toxic, boundaries, narcissists, gaslighting."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"When you use moralized language like that, compromise becomes far more difficult," he said.

"So I tell parents to pause before they really react ... and then say back, ‘Okay, you've used the word toxic. Can you describe the behavior or behaviors that you consider to be toxic?’ Then you're dealing with facts and events, rather than who’s a better person or who's the worst person."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The psychologist also recommends starting with "I" statements rather than using the word "you," and also avoid using the words "always" and "never."
No. 5: Outside influences
Finally, Blake said that outside influences — including romantic partners and evolving parenting philosophies — can also contribute to family estrangement.
Heavy social media use has been linked to poorer parent-child relationships. (iStock)
Those outside influences may differ by gender, he noted, with romantic partners often playing a larger role for men.

As an example, Blake pointed to public figures such as Brooklyn Beckham and Prince Harry, suggesting that romantic partners can sometimes influence how people view their relationships with family members.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Conflicting parenting philosophies may also strain family relationships, as adult children and grandparents sometimes disagree over how children should be raised, according to Blake.
"Parenting styles are obviously different, and they've changed a lot over the last few years," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If you look at the outcomes of the gentle parenting or the permissive parenting that we've slipped into, we have the most mentally ill generation in history, the least fit for adulthood," Blake suggested. "Perhaps we should be learning from our grandparents more than the therapists."

title: Tick-borne 'rabbit fever' spreads with cases reported near major metro area
summary: Three probable tularemia cases on Long Island have officials warning residents about the tick-borne illness after a 9-year-old developed severe symptoms.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the surge in Powassan tick-borne virus cases, prevention methods and treatments. The rare virus, often carried by deer and mice, has seen a record number of reported cases this year.
Health officials on Long Island are warning residents about a rare but potentially serious tick-borne illness.
Three probable cases of tularemia — also known as "rabbit fever" — have been confirmed by the Suffolk County Department of Health Services (SCDHS).

"SCDHS currently has three probable cases of tularemia this year," the agency said in a statement provided to local outlets. "Confirmation of a tularemia diagnosis requires a combination of laboratory testing and fulfillment of specific clinical or epidemiologic criteria. The laboratory testing to confirm a tularemia diagnosis may take several weeks."
NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE

One case involved a 9-year-old patient who was bitten by a tick while playing outside, according to NBC4 New York. After the tick was removed, he later developed high fever, severe head and neck pain, swollen lymph nodes/glands, body aches and extreme fatigue.
After multiple doctor visits and nearly a month of illness, an infectious disease specialist diagnosed the boy with tularemia.
Health officials on Long Island are warning residents about a rare but potentially serious tick-borne illness. (iStock)

Although the family's yard is home to wild rabbits, the patient's mother said he never handled the animals. Doctors believe infected ticks likely fed on the rabbits before biting the boy, transmitting the bacteria, according to reports.
What to know about rabbit fever
Caused by the bacteria Francisella tularensis, the disease commonly infects rabbits, hares and rodents. However, it is zoonotic, which means it can spread from animals to humans.

The bacteria is a "tier-1 select agent," a classification given to agents and toxins that "present the greatest risk of deliberate misuse with significant potential for mass casualties or devastating effects to the economy, critical infrastructure or public confidence, and pose a severe threat to public health and safety," per the CDC.
TICK BITE ER VISITS HIT HIGHEST SEASONAL LEVEL IN YEARS AS DOCTORS WARN OF DISEASE SURGE

Although tularemia remains rare, with 196 U.S. cases reported in 2023, the disease has become more common in recent years. CDC surveillance found 2,462 cases between 2011 and 2022 — a 56% increase in incidence compared with the previous decade (2001–2010).

Daniel Ruderfer, M.D., chief of the Division of Pediatric Infectious Diseases at Hackensack Meridian K. Hovnanian Children's Hospital in New Jersey, believes that the increase in cases is mostly due to improved microbiology detection methods.
Caused by the bacteria Francisella tularensis, the disease commonly infects rabbits, hares and rodents. However, it is zoonotic, which means it can spread from animals to humans. (iStock)
"The traditional method of confirming cases has historically been via growth in culture and antibody testing," he previously told Fox News Digital.
"However, newer detection methods, such as PCR testing, are likely a major contributor to the increase in reported cases."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Humans can contract the disease through bites from deer flies or ticks, contact with infected animals, or exposure to contaminated water or aerosols, the same source stated.

Symptoms of tularemia can vary depending on the type of disease. General symptoms include chills, headache, malaise, fatigue, anorexia, myalgia, chest discomfort, cough, severe sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, according to Ruderfer.
Humans can contract the disease through bites from deer flies or ticks, contact with infected animals, or exposure to contaminated water or aerosols. (iStock)
"Depending on the location of the infected bit or scratch, people can develop localized lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes) and a cutaneous ulcer at the infection site," he said.
"Other manifestations include conjunctivitis, pneumonia and potentially even bloodstream infections."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The death rate from the disease is typically low, less than 2%, but the CDC noted that it can be as high as 24% in rare, severe cases.
Tularemia can be treated with antibiotics, but no vaccine is currently available.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The infection is absolutely dangerous and potentially life-threatening if not treated with appropriate antibiotics," said Ruderfer.
Those most at risk include children between 5 and 9 years of age, older men, American Indian and Alaskan Native people, and those living in central U.S. states, according to the report.
"The infection is absolutely dangerous and potentially life-threatening if not treated with appropriate antibiotics."
The general population is not at an "obvious" risk for infection unless they come into physical contact with an infected rabbit, tick or deer fly, the expert noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Those who hunt or interact routinely with rabbits should see a doctor if they develop any concerning symptoms, he advised.

"Many factors might contribute to the higher risk for tularemia in this population, including the concentration of Native American reservations in central states and sociocultural or occupational activities that might increase contact with infected wildlife or arthropods," the CDC wrote.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may help protect against a deadly disease, doctor says
summary: A breast cancer surgeon explains how GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer recurrence risk by reducing BMI, estrogen and inflammation.
story: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications may be associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence.

GLP-1 medications have transformed diabetes and obesity treatment, but emerging research suggests their benefits could extend far beyond those purposes — potentially even aiding in cancer prevention and survival.

Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, said growing research suggests glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer diagnoses and recurrence.

She pointed to findings presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting in Chicago, where researchers reported an association between GLP-1 use and lower breast cancer recurrence rates, as well as a potential role in preventing the disease.
MILLIONS COULD GAIN EASIER ACCESS TO POPULAR PEPTIDES AFTER FDA PANEL VOTE
However, she noted that the evidence remains observational and can’t prove that the drugs reduce cancer risk.
Emerging research suggests that GLP-1 medications could aid in cancer prevention and survival. (iStock)

"So these aren’t studies that, unfortunately, patients can latch onto, call their doctor and say, ‘I want to get on a GLP-1 right now to reduce my risk of breast cancer or make my breast cancer better,’" Rourke told Fox News Digital. "However, what it did do was shine the light on GLP-1s and that relationship."
The cancer connection
The main reason that GLP-1s may aid in cancer prevention, according to Rourke, is that the drugs promote weight loss and reduce chronic inflammation.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"GLP-1s cause a decrease in your BMI. They cause weight reduction," she told Fox News Digital. "We know that a lower BMI equals a better prognosis with breast cancer."
In particular, post-menopausal women who are struggling with weight gain could get an extra benefit, the doctor said. (iStock)
"So if the secondary effect of taking a GLP-1 means you’re going to lose weight, then that’s a benefit, because we know you’re going to do better with breast cancer."
Diabetes and obesity medications can also lower estrogen production associated with excess body fat, the surgeon noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The more fat you have, the higher your estrogen production," Rourke said. "You’re kind of bathing your body in estrogen, so to speak. So it intuitively makes sense that we are seeing this correlation or association."
GLP-1s also decrease the inflammatory state in which cancer thrives, the surgeon noted.
"The more fat we have, the higher your estrogen production."
"So if it’s fixing the overall chronic inflammation of the body, that’s going to help for a lot of reasons," she said.
"I think this is going to extend beyond breast cancer, but we need to get that scientific proof of a direct cause — is this just an association or a correlation?"
More research needed
Rourke emphasized that researchers have not yet proven that GLP-1 medications directly affect breast cancer cells.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"But this study has now garnered enough attention, interest and scientific hypotheses that the work is getting started for the randomized controlled trials that we’re all waiting for — and then we can act upon those."
The main reason that GLP-1s may aid in cancer prevention is that the drugs promote weight loss and reduce chronic inflammation, according to a doctor. (iStock)
To patients who are considering starting GLP-1s, Rourke offered the following advice.

"My bottom-line message on this one is, if you have an elevated BMI, you’re trying to lose weight, you’ve tried a healthy diet, you’ve tried to exercise, and you’re not winning that fight, consider GLP-1s, and you’re going to get a secondary benefit."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In particular, post-menopausal women who are struggling with weight gain could get an extra benefit, Rourke added, but she urges them to "call their doctor and have that one-on-one conversation."

title: Living longer could hinge on one surprising dietary change, study review suggests
summary: A review of 350+ studies finds protein restriction triggers the hormone FGF21, delivering longevity benefits similar to calorie restriction.
story: Food safety experts outline the benefits and risks of eating shark, advising vulnerable groups to avoid it altogether while encouraging healthier seafood alternatives for routine meals.
Eating less protein, not cutting calories, may be an easier path to a longer, healthier life for sedentary adults, according to a new scientific review.

While previous research has long tied calorie restriction to improved lifespan and lower rates of age-related disease, studies have found that many people have difficulty maintaining strict low-calorie diets.
A review of more than 350 studies published in the journal Cell Press Blue suggests that targeted protein restriction can deliver similar metabolic benefits without the need to cut calories.
LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS

Across the reviewed studies, lower protein intake was associated with better metabolism, altered nutrient signaling, reduced cellular damage and improved cellular maintenance, according to the published review.
While research has shown the benefits of high protein intake for active people, new research says the opposite may be true for sedentary individuals. (iStock)

Much of the benefit stems from a metabolic hormone known as fibroblast growth factor 21, or FGF21. Restricting protein triggers a surge in FGF21, which animal studies have shown can boost energy expenditure, reduce inflammation, improve blood sugar control and extend lifespan.

Researchers highlighted three essential amino acids that are building blocks of protein — methionine, isoleucine and valine. Under certain conditions, they may contribute to biological pathways associated with aging under certain conditions.
FORGET THE GYM: A 30-SECOND TEST MAY BE ONE OF THE BEST INDICATORS OF LONGEVITY

For people who don't exercise regularly, high levels of these amino acids may keep certain growth-related processes constantly active. Over time, that stimulation can create cellular damage, systemic inflammation and weight gain.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's absolutely crystal-clear that there are benefits of protein for muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," said Dudley Lamming, the paper’s corresponding author and a researcher at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
Since most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, the researchers said. (iStock)

"But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences," he added in the press release.

There were some limitations to the study findings. Because the paper is a scientific review rather than a new clinical trial, it identifies patterns across existing research but cannot establish cause and effect in humans, the researchers acknowledged.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Longer-term human studies are still needed to determine whether these metabolic benefits ultimately translate into increased lifespan, they noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The review emphasizes that protein needs are not one-size-fits-all, and that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation to consume inadequate amounts.
For active individuals, the dietary amino acids associated with protein intake are crucial for building muscle tissue. (iStock)

Physically active people and athletes process protein differently. Exercise helps to direct dietary amino acids toward building and repairing muscle instead of leaving excess amino acids to be processed by the body, the researchers noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
High protein intake is also crucial for pregnant women and older adults who may face age-related muscle loss.

For the broader, largely inactive population, the findings suggest that public health guidelines should move away from sweeping recommendations and instead tailor protein targets to a person's age and activity level.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Michigan reports 2 deaths in rare parasite outbreak that has sickened more than 11,000
summary: Two deaths linked to Michigan's cyclosporiasis outbreak had significant underlying health conditions impacted by the intestinal parasite and dehydration, health officials said.
story: Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming cyclosporiasis outbreak, with over 4,000 cases in 41 states linked to contaminated produce. He emphasizes the need for caution as the parasitic infection isn't fully controlled, despite FDA tracing efforts. Siegel also critiques the FDA panel's recommendation to ease peptide restrictions, highlighting insufficient human studies on their long-term health impacts.
Two people in Michigan have died in connection with the state's sprawling cyclosporiasis outbreak, marking a rare fatal outcome from the intestinal parasite, health officials said Monday.

The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) said the deaths were identified as part of the ongoing outbreak, which has so far sickened 11,234 people statewide. As of Thursday, 193 people with reported infections said they had been hospitalized.

According to the agency, medical records showed both people who died "had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration." Officials said no additional information about the cases will be released.
CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW
A massive surge in Cyclospora cases means people may be mistaking this parasitic foodborne infection for a standard summer stomach bug. (iStock)

State health officials are continuing to investigate the source of the outbreak and said available evidence points to lettuce or salad greens as a potential culprit. However, investigators cautioned that other food items have not been ruled out, and no specific type of produce, grower or supplier has been identified.
Since the cyclospora outbreak was linked to shredded lettuce at some Taco Bell locations, the chain has been offering deals on lettuce-free menu items. (iStock)
MDHHS said it is working with local health departments and other partners as the investigation continues and will provide updates as more information becomes available.
WHITE HOUSE ADDRESSES GROWING PARASITE OUTBREAK AFTER MORE THAN 400 AMERICANS SICKENED

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis. The hallmark symptom of a cyclospora infection is watery, often "explosive" diarrhea that can last for weeks or even months if left untreated, the CDC says. Other symptoms include severe abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea, fatigue and significant weight loss.
Man sits on a bed and holds his stomach while home alone. Abdominal pain can be caused by digestive problems, infections, intestinal inflammation or more serious diseases. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Health officials emphasized that cyclosporiasis is generally not considered a life-threatening illness and that deaths associated with the infection are uncommon in the United States.
Fox News Digital's Angelica Stabile contributed to this report.

title: Forget the gym: A 30-second test may be one of the best indicators of longevity
summary: A certified personal trainer reveals the benchmarks for the 30-second chair stand test and exercises that can improve lower body strength and fall risk.
story: Nick Schofield, a tactical athlete physical coach in the U.K., demonstrates how to perform the sit-to-stand exercise, which can be an indicator of lower-body strength and is closely linked to mobility, functional fitness and healthy aging.
As more Americans prioritize staying mobile and independent as they age, experts are pointing to a surprisingly simple measure of health.
The number of times a person can rise from a chair in 30 seconds can be an indicator of lower-body strength, which is closely linked to mobility, functional fitness and healthy aging.
Interest in the test appears to be growing, with online searches for "sit to stand exercise" up 287% over the past three months, according to Google Trends analysis.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'

The CDC's Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths & Injuries (STEADI) program states that the purpose of the 30-second chair stand test is to assess leg strength and endurance, with below-average scores indicating increased fall risk.

Bruno Pontes, an ACSM- and AFAA-certified personal trainer at Muscle Booster in California, shared what the sit-to-stand test actually measures and why experts consider it a strong indicator of fitness.
Nick Schofield, a tactical athlete physical coach in the U.K., also provided a video demonstration of the exercise for Muscle Booster. (Muscle Booster)
Nick Schofield, a tactical athlete physical coach in the U.K., also provided a video demonstration of the exercise for Muscle Booster.

"What makes this test a great measure of fitness is that it simulates the everyday movement of getting up and down from a chair, compared to machine-based strength tests, which instead isolate muscle groups," Pontes told Fox News Digital.
'FIT MOM' DID 'EVERYTHING RIGHT' — THEN A COLON CANCER DIAGNOSIS CHANGED HER LIFE

"The sit-to-stand test is an excellent indicator of lower-body strength, muscular endurance, balance and mobility," Pontes said. It is also commonly used by healthcare professionals to help assess fall risk in older adults.
While there are several iterations of the sit-to-stand test, the 30-second chair stand test is the go-to exercise endorsed by public health organizations like the CDC, the expert noted.
How to perform the test at home
The sit-to-stand test is easy to perform at home, Pontes said, as the only thing needed is a sturdy chair. He outlined the following steps.
The sit-to-stand test is easy to perform at home, as the only thing needed is a sturdy chair. (iStock)
Position a sturdy chair against a wall to prevent it from moving.
Start by sitting upright in the chair with the feet flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart, with arms crossed over the chest.
Once the timer starts, rise to a full standing position with straight knees and hips before sitting back down again.
Repeat as many full stands as possible in 30 seconds and record your total.
LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW

"As an important note, anyone with significant balance problems, recent surgery, severe joint pain or cardiovascular concerns should consult a healthcare professional before performing the test," Pontes advised.
What counts as a ‘good’ score?
What is seen as a "good" score varies from person to person and is dependent on a number of factors, including age and gender, Pontes said.

"However, the following benchmarks are good to aim for to measure your lower-body strength," he added. These benchmarks are based on how many full stands can be completed in 30 seconds from a standard-height chair.

"It is important not to obsess over the number you achieve — the focus should be on the ease of movement and making daily functions easier," Pontes said.

"If rising from a chair becomes easier over time, that's a great indicator that lower-body strength and functional fitness are improving," he went on. "If you fall below the target number, don’t worry — there are many different exercises you can implement into your daily routine to help strengthen your lower body."
Top exercises to help build strength, balance and endurance
The following exercises can be executed at home to help improve your sit-to-stand performance, according to Pontes. These moves help to build strength in the quads, hamstrings, glutes and calves.
Squats

"Squats help to build strength primarily in the quadriceps and glutes, while also engaging the hamstrings and core," Pontes told Fox News Digital. "They are also a great exercise for seniors, as they place limited amounts of stress on your hips and spine."
"Squats help to build strength primarily in the quadriceps and glutes, while also engaging the hamstrings and core," an expert said. (iStock)
Squats can be performed by standing with the feet shoulder-width apart and lowering the hips back and down into a seated position. Be sure to keep the back straight and chest up.
Lunges
"These low-impact exercises can help identify any strength imbalances that may be affecting mobility and stability, as each leg works independently," Pontes said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

To perform a lunge, stand with the feet shoulder-width apart and step forward with one leg, creating a right angle at the knee. The front knee should sit directly over the ankle/heel and should not extend past the toes.
Hold this position briefly before pushing through the heel on the front foot to engage the glutes and return to the starting position, then repeat for the other leg.
Calf raises
"Calf raises help keep the calf muscles strong and functional as we age, to support everyday, functional movements," Pontes said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Stand with the feet hip-width apart, keeping an upright posture and engaging the core. Slowly push through the balls of the feet to raise the heels off the floor as high as possible. Pause briefly at the top, then lower the heels back down to the ground with control.
Importance of leg strength for longevity

As people age, they become more susceptible to sarcopenia, the gradual loss of muscle mass and strength over time, according to Pontes. This can make routine activities more difficult and increases the risk of injury.

To perform a lunge, stand with the feet shoulder-width apart and step forward with one leg, creating a right angle at the knee. The front knee should sit directly over the ankle/heel and should not extend past the toes. (iStock)

"Lower-body strength plays a vital role in maintaining independence because it supports many of the movements we rely on every day, such as climbing stairs, getting up from chairs, carrying groceries and walking confidently," the fitness expert noted.

Maintaining strength in the legs and hips helps to preserve mobility and lower the risk of falls and injury, Pontes said.
"This mobility helps enable people to remain active and keep moving freely through their later years."

title: Early eating habits could have lasting effects on dementia risk, study suggests
summary: A study of about 64,000 people found that lower sugar intake during pregnancy and early life was linked to up to 23% lower dementia risk decades later.
story: Fox News medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel breaks down a groundbreaking study from the American Academy of Neurology showing that limiting sugar intake before age two can lower the risk of developing dementia by 23 percent. Siegel also warns parents about the alarming rise in daily caffeine consumption among children and teenagers, highlighting common caffeine sources like sweet baked goods and soda.
Consuming less sugar during pregnancy and the first years of life may lower the risk of developing dementia decades later, according to new research.

A study published in Neurology found that people who were exposed to less sugar before birth and during their first one to two years of life had up to a 23% lower risk of developing dementia compared with those born after sugar became widely available again.
Researchers examined the health records of more than 64,000 people in the United Kingdom who were born before and after World War II sugar rationing ended in 1953.

People who experienced lower sugar intake before birth and through their first year of life had a 21% lower risk of dementia, while those whose sugar intake remained limited through age two had a 23% lower risk, researchers found.
DAILY EATING HABIT LINKED TO BETTER BRAIN HEALTH IN OLDER ADULTS, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Consuming less sugar during pregnancy and the first years of life may lower the risk of developing dementia decades later. (iStock)
The study also found that people with lower sugar exposure early in life developed dementia an average of 2.6 years later than those who consumed more sugar.

"Our findings suggest that limiting sugar during the earliest stages of life may have lasting benefits for brain health," study author Jiazhen Zheng of The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology said in the press release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Dariush Mozaffarian, director of the Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts University, who was not involved in the study, said the research raises an interesting question but cautioned against drawing firm conclusions.
"I'm impressed with the researchers' creativity, pulling together information across decades to look at this question, but the findings are not convincing," Mozaffarian told Fox News Digital.
People who experienced lower sugar intake before birth and through their first year of life had a 21% lower risk of dementia. (iStock)

He said many other factors likely differed between people born during and after wartime, including overall nutrition and calorie intake, making it difficult to know whether sugar alone explains the difference.
Still, Mozaffarian said the broader guidance for pregnant women remains the same.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Ultimately, we know from other research that women who are pregnant should consume the healthiest foods possible for both their own health and that of their baby," he told Fox News Digital.
Health experts emphasize that pregnant women should eat as healthfully as possible to support both their own well-being and their baby's development. (iStock)

He recommended focusing on minimally processed foods such as fruits, vegetables, beans, nuts, seeds, whole grains, fermented dairy products and fish while limiting ultra-processed foods high in sugar, starch and salt.
Researchers stressed that the study found only an association between early-life sugar intake and dementia risk and does not prove that reducing sugar directly prevents the disease.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Researchers also noted several limitations, including that the study used exposure to a historical rationing policy as a proxy for individual sugar intake and could not eliminate the influence of other differences between the groups.
As a result, the findings cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship between lower sugar intake early in life and a reduced risk of dementia.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: America hits major marijuana milestone as daily weed use surpasses daily drinking
summary: Daily marijuana use among American adults jumped 21% between 2022 and 2025, with adults aged 26 and older driving the dramatic surge in cannabis use.
story: New research raises concerns about high-potency cannabis, as Fox News senior medical contributor Dr. Marc Siegel explains. Siegel highlights how increased THC levels contribute to addiction and adverse mental health effects, particularly in developing brains. He emphasizes that claims of cannabis helping with anxiety and depression are often bogus, leading to increased ER visits.
Marijuana is officially leading the pack for the most-used daily drug among Americans.

New data from the 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), reveals that there are 21.4 million daily or near-daily marijuana users in the U.S.
This surpasses the 19.9 million people who smoke cigarettes and the 17.2 million who consume alcohol.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE

The annual federal survey of Americans age 12 and older defines daily or near-daily use as consuming marijuana on 300 or more days in the past year. Daily cigarette smokers were characterized as those who smoked on all 30 days of the past month.
The number of Americans using marijuana daily or almost daily rose about 21% between 2022 and 2025. (iStock)

The number of Americans using marijuana daily or almost daily rose about 21% between 2022 and 2025 — from 17.7 million to approximately 21.4 million. This amounts to an increase of about 3.7 million frequent users.
The biggest jump occurred between 2021 and 2022 with an increase of roughly 2.8 million users, according to SAMSHA.
This pattern in higher marijuana use is driven mostly by adults, particularly those age 26 and older, rather than teenagers.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Between 2021 and 2025, the number of adults 18 and older using marijuana daily or almost daily increased about 22%, from 17.2 million to 20.9 million.

Although marijuana is now the most commonly used substance on a daily or near-daily basis, alcohol remains the most widely used substance overall. During the previous month, about 129 million people drank alcohol while 43.8 million used marijuana.
General marijuana use rose from 13.2% to 15.1% from 2021 to 2025. (iStock)

Cigarette and broader tobacco product use has been on a decline, decreasing from 20.1% of Americans in 2021 to 15.9% in 2025. Meanwhile, general marijuana use rose from 13.2% to 15.1% during that same period.

A recent report by San Francisco-based workplace mental health platform Modern Health found a concerning increase in the number of workers turning to substances to manage stress, especially THC and marijuana products.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The survey of 1,000 full-time employees in April 2026 found that 63% of the workforce engages in at least one form of self-medication after the workday, while 52% have self-medicated during the workday.

Gen Z is the only generation of workers where THC use exceeded alcohol use after work – 59% report using marijuana products compared to 50% who drink alcohol. In that group, 51% reported using THC during the workday.
A survey of 1,000 full-time employees in April 2026 found that 63% of the workforce engages in at least one form of self-medication after the workday. (iStock)
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel said the SAMHSA data reflects a "very disturbing trend."

"Too much attention has been put on the bogus or exaggerated uses of marijuana for pain, insomnia and anxiety, when in fact it increases anxiety exponentially, especially in those with underlying mental health issues," he told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Too little attention has been paid to the growing THC content in all cannabis products, which makes it far more dangerous in terms of mental performance, judgement, memory and all forms of impairment."
THC has been associated with a growing share of fatal motor vehicle crashes, Siegel said, arguing that increased acceptance of marijuana use is "feeding a dangerous trend."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"So I firmly believe that the rising use – coupled with decreasing alcohol and cigarettes – is directly due to lack of awareness of all the dangers of marijuana versus an increased awareness of all the dangers of cigarettes and alcohol," he added.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: How often are married people having sex? What to know about the intimacy standard in America
summary: Research reveals once a week may be the sweet spot for marital satisfaction, with no added happiness boost from more frequent sexual intimacy.
story: Fox News Senior Medical Analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming decline in the U.S. fertility rate to a record low of 1.56 children per couple, highlighting impacts on population size. Dr. Siegel then explains the surge in seasonal allergies nationwide due to a cold winter and wet spring, emphasizing the "hygiene hypothesis" in immune system development.
New survey data offers a snapshot of how often married Americans are having sex, while researchers say the findings challenge common assumptions about relationship health.

National demographic studies suggest that lower sexual frequency is often a normal part of aging and long-term relationships, and that there may be a "sweet spot" associated with marital satisfaction.
Data from the General Social Survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, found that married Americans report a wide range of sexual frequency.
WEIGHT-LOSS MEDICATIONS COULD IMPACT SEXUAL HEALTH IN UNEXPECTED WAYS
The survey asked how often couples have had sex during the last 12 months. Among the 1,893 married respondents surveyed in 2024, the responses were as follows.
New survey data offers a snapshot of how often married Americans are having sex, while researchers say the findings challenge common assumptions about relationship health. (iStock)

The average American adult has sex 53 times a year — or a little more than once per week, according to research by the telehealth platform Hims.
The average American adult has sex 53 times a year — or a little more than once per week, according to research by the telehealth platform Hims. (iStock)

While marriage is often associated with less frequent sex, research has found the difference to be relatively small. A 2014 study found that married people had sex about 55 times a year, compared with 59 times a year among their unmarried peers.
"There’s no ‘perfect statistic’ or ideal amount of sex."

"Experts aren’t sure precisely why this difference exists or why what used to be an advantage has become a disadvantage, but some believe it may be related to the increasing age at which most people get married," Hims wrote in a medically reviewed article.
"There’s no ‘perfect statistic’ or ideal amount of sex. In other words: You like what you like, and that’s perfectly OK."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Clinical data suggests that aiming for a daily or high-volume sexual quota does not actually improve relationship quality.
A study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science in 2015 evaluated more than 30,000 individuals over four decades and discovered a drop-off in additional benefits.
Roughly 17% of adults aged 70 and older engage in sexual activity on a weekly basis, according to AARP data. (iStock)

While overall happiness increased as physical intimacy moved from monthly to weekly, couples who had sex two, three or four times a week experienced no additional statistical boost in marital satisfaction compared to those hitting the weekly threshold.
Experts emphasize that sexual desire naturally fluctuates as couples navigate career demands, parenthood and biological aging.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Despite some research suggesting a slowdown with age, intimacy remains an important factor in healthy aging, linked to improved physical and emotional well-being.
AARP survey data indicates that physical connection remains routine for many older Americans, with roughly 17% of adults aged 70 and older engaging in sexual activity on a weekly basis.
Reasons for declining intimacy
When a couple experiences an intimacy dry spell, medical professionals recommend evaluating physiological factors rather than jumping to conclusions about incompatibility.
Healthcare providers encourage couples dealing with mismatched sexual desire to discuss the issue openly and consult a doctor. (iStock)
Educational resources from the International Society for Sexual Medicine note that the following physical conditions can influence libido.

title: No cure, no vaccine: Experts warn of rare Bourbon virus after first NY case
summary: A Long Island patient was hospitalized after researchers confirmed the first Bourbon virus case in New York transmitted by the common lone star tick.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming rise of Powassan virus, a rare tick-borne disease, with 15 cases reported this year, following a record 76 in 2025.

A rarely diagnosed tick-borne virus with no vaccine or specific treatment has been confirmed in New York for the first time, prompting researchers to warn that additional infections may be going undiagnosed.

The Bourbon virus, "transmitted through the common lone star tick, could soon begin to complicate diagnoses if it becomes more prevalent this summer and in coming years," Stony Brook Medicine warned in a news release reporting on a study of the virus.
Only six human cases have been reported since Bourbon virus was first identified in Bourbon County, Kansas, where the first known patient was diagnosed in 2014. That patient later died.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The virus has been linked to at least two deaths, including the original 2014 case and another reported in 2026. Researchers believe, however, that additional infections have likely gone undiagnosed.
Symptoms of Bourbon virus include fever, fatigue, rash, headache, body aches and nausea. Because there is no commercially available diagnostic test, doctors have a difficult time identifying it.
Adult female lone star ticks are identifiable by a white dot, or lone star, on their backs. (iStock)
Many healthcare providers are also unfamiliar with the virus, "thus increasing the possibility of misdiagnosis," the release said.

A team of researchers led by Stony Brook Medicine confirmed the first case of Bourbon virus in New York in a patient from Long Island who developed severe symptoms and an eight-fold rise in antibody titers of the Bourbon virus. The patient was hospitalized.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There are a lot of lone star ticks in New York and in the Northeast, we have dense populations and when someone is infected with Bourbon virus symptoms they are similar to other tick-borne infections," Luis Marcos, Stony Brook Medicine professor and director of the Tick-borne Disease Clinic, said in the news release.
"For these reasons, the Bourbon virus is likely more prevalent than we think in our region, and other cases are likely not being diagnosed."
Marcos and his co-authors said their findings show the need for expanded surveillance and better testing to improve diagnosis and track the spread of Bourbon virus.
People bitten by ticks should remove them as soon as possible. (iStock)

"Without identifying the cause of an infection, the chances of developing accurate diagnostic tests or effective treatments are minimal," he said. "That is why it is so important to first understand the true impact of the virus in high-risk areas."
According to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), "The lone star tick is widely distributed in the Northeast, South and Midwest United States."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The tiny, blood-feeding, parasitic arachnid has established populations in Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia, according to the CDC.
Lone star ticks are an "aggressive tick," according to the agency.
To avoid tick bites, experts advise wearing long pants and sleeves, using insect repellent and avoiding overgrown areas. (iStock)
"The adult female is distinguished by a white dot or ‘lone star’ on her back. The nymph and adult females most frequently bite humans and spread disease," the CDC reports.
Despite the Bourbon virus’ severity, "only a select few [ticks] bite and transmit bacteria, viruses and parasites (pathogens) that cause diseases in people," according to the CDC.
To avoid tick bites, people should wear protective clothing, such as pants they can tuck into boots and long-sleeve shirts.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Experts also recommend applying insect repellent, such as permethrin, to clothing and outdoor gear, not directly on the skin.
Stay out of tall grass and on well-beaten trails whenever possible because ticks thrive in overgrown and heavily wooded areas.

Check for ticks after spending time outdoors and remove them as soon as you find them. Seek medical attention if you develop fever, rash, fatigue or other flu-like symptoms in the days or weeks following a tick bite.
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Skin condition under the eyes goes viral, and doctors warn it could signal hidden health issue
summary: Doctors reveal how low ferritin levels in the body can cause dark under-eye circles, pale skin and fatigue even as they warn against self-treating an iron deficiency.
story: Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name ‘ferritin face.’
Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."
Experts say there's some truth behind the trend with important caveats.

Ferritin can be thought of as the body's "iron storage vault," according to Dr. Josef Hadeed, a double board-certified plastic surgeon at Hadeed Plastic Surgery in Beverly Hills, California. It is a protein that stores iron inside the body's cells and releases it when needed.
LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW
"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," Hadeed told Fox News Digital.
Low iron levels can compromise skin elasticity, which can make the tissue appear thinner and less resilient, the doctor said.
Dark under-eye circles can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media with the name "ferritin face." (iStock)
When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable, Hadeed noted.
Symptoms of low ferritin
Besides pale skin and dark under-eye circles, other symptoms may signal that someone is lacking iron.
CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"The severity of these symptoms generally increases as ferritin decreases," Dane Thomas, a Texas-based hematology/oncology physician associate who specializes in the care of patients with hematologic disorders and cancer, told Fox News Digital.
Low energy, fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches, fainting, brittle or thin nails, hair loss, cravings to chew ice and restless legs syndrome are a few signs, according to Thomas.

"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," an expert told Fox News Digital. (iStock)
"Some patients also experience decreased exercise tolerance, difficulty concentrating or shortness of breath with exertion," he said.
Other symptoms can include pounding or "whooshing" in the ears, a sore or smooth tongue, rapid heartbeat, intolerance to cold and poor sleep, according to the American Society of Hematology.
Underlying conditions

Beyond cosmetic concerns, ferritin face may signal an underlying medical condition, including chronic bleeding, gastrointestinal disorders or cancers or malabsorption, according to hematological experts.

With the rise in bariatric surgery, more patients are developing iron deficiency due to impaired iron absorption, Thomas said. Certain over-the-counter acid-suppressing medications, including proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2-receptor blockers, may also contribute to low iron.
"This is not something that someone should self-treat."
While treating iron deficiency is important, identifying and addressing its underlying cause is equally critical, he said.

"Whenever possible, I work with my patients to determine why their iron deficiency developed so we can reduce the likelihood that it will recur," Thomas told Fox News Digital. "This often involves collaboration with gastroenterologists, gynecologists or other specialists to evaluate for sources of blood loss or malabsorption."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Pregnancy, heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent blood donation can also contribute to lower iron levels. Vegetarians, vegans and those who follow diets that do not include iron-rich foods may also be at risk, according to the American Society of Hematologists.
Diagnosis and treatment
If a person thinks they may have low ferritin, it is important to see a physician.

"This is not something that someone should self-treat, and I always advise them to seek professional help," Hadeed advised. "Unlike water-soluble vitamins, the body has no easy mechanism to excrete excess iron, and over-supplementation can lead to increased levels of iron in the body, which can affect the liver and heart."
When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable. (iStock)

A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. Further evaluation may include stool and urine tests to look for blood, along with endoscopy to examine the esophagus, stomach and colon. Women may also undergo a gynecological evaluation, according to experts.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Treatment for iron deficiency may include oral supplementation and, in cases of severe anemia, intravenous (IV) iron or blood transfusions.
"The biggest drawback of oral iron is gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and stomach upset," Thomas noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"These side effects can often be minimized by taking iron every other day rather than daily, a strategy that also maintains excellent absorption for many patients."
He also recommends spacing them apart from calcium supplements, dairy products and antacids, which can affect absorption.
A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. (iStock)
Following a diet that includes iron-rich foods can also help, according to the American Society of Hematology website.

Some examples include beef, pork, or lamb; organ meats like liver, chicken, turkey, duck and fish (especially shellfish, sardines and anchovies); leafy greens, such as broccoli, kale, turnip greens and collard greens; legumes, including lima beans, peas, pinto beans and black-eyed peas; and iron-enriched pastas, grains, rice and cereals.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ferritin face is reversible, Hadeed emphasized.
Once iron stores are safely restored and hemoglobin levels rebound, the skin recovers its healthy capillary flush, and dark under-eye circles tend to fade over several months.
Amy McGorry is a contributing health writer for Fox News Digital. Follow her on Twitter @amymcgorry.

title: Maryland's lone congressional Republican blasts Moore's redistricting push as alleged 2028 White House play
summary: Rep. Andy Harris claims Gov. Wes Moore is pushing a Maryland ballot amendment to eliminate his district in furtherance of presidential ambitions.
story: U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., told Fox News Digital in an interview that Gov. Wes Moore is not "paying attention to Maryland issues" and is more concerned with the "national political scene."

U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., the only Republican in Maryland's congressional delegation, is accusing Gov. Wes Moore of backing an amendment to the state constitution that could eliminate his district through redistricting, arguing that the push is driven by the governor's alleged presidential ambitions.
The amendment, if approved by voters in November, would give the Democratic-controlled General Assembly far greater latitude to redraw the state's congressional districts ahead of the 2028 election.

"The governor certainly led the charge in trying to eliminate the only Republican in the Maryland delegation in furtherance of his presidential aspirations," Harris told Fox News Digital in an interview. "It's obvious that this is not being done for Maryland, it is being done for a national agenda."
Moore has repeatedly said he is not running for president in 2028. but speculation around his potential White House bid remains.
TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT OUSTED IN HOUSE PRIMARY AS GOP REDISTRICTING PUSH SET TO RESHAPE TENNESSEE
Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., arrives for a news conference following a Maryland delegation meeting at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on June 25, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Harris also called out Moore for engaging in a "photo-op" on Wednesday by publicly signing the bill that will put the amendment on the ballot this fall.

The bill passed Tuesday with three-fifths majorities in both chambers, which is the only requirement for an amendment to become a ballot question, according to Article XIV of the Maryland Constitution.

"Gov. Moore, never missing a photo op for his presidential aspirations, convened a signing ceremony, which is a little unusual considering there's really nothing to sign for the governor," Harris said. "But again, this is all for show. This is to make sure that he can look Gavin Newsom in the eye and say, 'Yeah I did something too for mid-cycle redistricting.'"
Fox News Digital reached out to Moore's office for comment.

Harris, who worked as an anesthesiologist before getting into politics, has represented Maryland's first congressional district since 2011. The district contains the entire Eastern Shore, a relatively rural part of the state, as well as parts of Baltimore County.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore sits between Senate President Bill Ferguson and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk during a signing ceremony for HB2100 on August 5, 2026. The bill Moore signed puts a question on the November ballot to amend the state's redistricting practices. (Maryland Governor's Office)
VIRGINIA VOTERS CEMENT SWING DISTRICT REMATCH AFTER DEMS’ REDISTRICTING FAIL
The proposed amendment Harris is fighting against could allow state lawmakers to carve up his district and make it untenable for a Republican to win.
As it stands, the Maryland Constitution requires General Assembly districts and U.S. House districts to respect natural boundaries and existing county and municipal lines.
The amendment would remove those requirements for congressional districts while leaving them in place for state legislative districts.
"It absolutely sets up a double standard for redistricting in the state of Maryland. And again, the blatant attempt is to eliminate the Republican representation," Harris said.

The Maryland State House, which houses the General Assembly, in Annapolis on April 22, 2025. If the amendment Moore supports is approved by voters, state legislators would be granted far greater leeway to redraw congressional maps. (Jonathan Newton/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)
MARYLAND BALLOT BLUNDER SPARKS HOUSE GOP PROBE AHEAD OF PRIMARY

The amendment is already facing a court challenge from the Oversight Project, a conservative watchdog group that filed a complaint Thursday night in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court seeking to keep it off the November ballot.
The Oversight Project, along with Harris, accused state legislators of bypassing the established July 1 deadline to introduce statewide ballot questions.
The ballot question for the amendment was introduced by Maryland House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk and Senate President Bill Ferguson on Aug. 3, more than a month after the deadline.
Fox News Digital reached out to Peña-Melnyk and Ferguson for comment.
The move by Peña-Melnyk and Ferguson at the tail end of the legislative session is a response to a 2022 court ruling that struck down Democratic lawmakers’ proposed congressional map at the time.

Judge Lynne Battaglia found that the map — which added more Democratic voters to Harris' district — failed to give sufficient regard to the natural boundaries and political subdivisions throughout the state.

An aerial view of Chesapeake City, a city in Maryland's mostly-rural Eastern Shore that has been represented by Harris in Congress since 2011. (Visions of America/Joseph Sohm/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
TWIN COURT RULINGS RESHAPE HOUSE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS FIGHT UPHILL REDISTRICTING BATTLE

Amending the state constitution could be a way to get around this, but Harris said that even if voters approve the amendment, it would not guarantee that the courts would approve subsequently drawn maps that have "hyper-partisan gerrymandering."
If the state legislature tried to eliminate or substantially dilute Republican voting power his district, Harris said he would sue based on the precedent set by Battaglia's 2022 ruling.
Meanwhile, Moore has framed his support of the amendment as a necessary response to GOP redistricting around the country, which he called "political redlining."

"For over a year, I have warned that Donald Trump and Republicans across the country are working to rig the system, weaken voting rights, and make this pain permanent. I am proud that today we united and took action," Moore said. "I continue to believe that our country needs national redistricting reform. But until that happens, inaction is not an option."
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore speaks during a press conference at the Maryland State House on August 5, 2025 in Annapolis, Maryland. (Jamie Sabau/Getty Images)
DEMOCRATS TARGETING 12 ADDITIONAL RED DISTRICTS IN MIDTERMS PUSH TO RETAKE HOUSE
Harris pushed back on Moore's assertion that Republicans are responsible for the current redistricting battle playing out in dozens of states.

He pointed out that the redistricting organization founded by Eric Holder, who served as attorney general under President Obama from 2009 to 2015, aggressively pursued litigation to change legislative and congressional maps in North Carolina and Alabama.

However, a mid-decade congressional redraw was successfully enacted by Texas Republicans in 2003. The Supreme Court largely upheld the redraw in 2006 but said one district violated the Voting Rights Act because it diluted Latino voting strength.

Former Attorney General Eric Holder attends Lambda Legal Hosts 2024 National Liberty Awards at The Glasshouse on May 30, 2024 in New York City. Harris pointed out that Holder, a Democrat, has also pursued redistricting. (Arturo Holmes/Getty Images)

Although courts have upheld the legality of redrawing congressional maps between the decennial censuses, Harris said he would like to move away from the practice in the future.

"I don't think it is good for anyone," Harris said. "It's not good for democracy. You get to know your constituents, your constituents get to know their representative. That's important in a representative government like we have."

title: Ex-Obama, Biden diplomat blasts former boss’ border failures: 'They woke up too late'
summary: Ken Salazar says the Biden administration "woke up too late" on the border crisis, creating a vacuum that handed Trump his strongest political issue.
story: Former Interior Secretary and ex-Ambassador to Mexico Ken Salazar said the Biden White House made Mexico and the Americas a low priority, lacked urgency, planning and a comms strategy. He said Trump made the border

Former Cabinet secretary and U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ken Salazar says the Biden administration "woke up too late" to address the border crisis, arguing its failure to prioritize Mexico and effectively communicate its strategy helped hand President Donald Trump one of his strongest political issues.

Salazar, whose family has lived in the southwest since it was part of Mexico, laid out in his new book "Borderlands" how America’s foreign policy is too often on an "east-west paradigm" looking to Asia and Europe and neglecting Mexico and the Americas. He also argued that same mindset plagued the Biden administration, leaving it overly focused on Europe and Asia while neglecting Mexico and the Western Hemisphere.

"From day one, there should have been a great sense of urgency in addressing the crisis of a broken border and the migration crisis that we are seeing," Salazar said, arguing the Biden White House lacked both a comprehensive strategy and a coherent communications operation, creating what he described as a communications vacuum that Republicans filled.
BOMBSHELL MEMO SHOWS BIDEN PLANNED TO LEAVE TRUMP WITH EVEN MORE MASSIVE IMMIGRATION CRISIS
President Biden, left; Ken Salazar, right. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
"I think that's what trapped the administration into this sense that they woke up too late by the time they did the right things to get control of the border," he said.

In the book, he recounts nearly resigning from his ambassadorship during a visit to Mexico with Biden and several inner-circle officials after being left out of an important meeting where he wanted to make the case for appointing a border-and-migration czar.

After one meeting at the Palacio Nacional in Mexico City, Salazar wrote that he decided to present his plan the next day but found out that he and former Sen. Christopher Dodd, D-Conn., weren’t going to be in the key meeting the next day.
Ultimately, he was able to meet privately with Biden at the last minute, where he expressed his concerns:

"We need someone in the White House to oversee the border, migration, Mexico, and the Americas. No one is in charge now. We need a border and migration czar," he said, reminding Biden that adviser Jeffrey Zients served as a "czar" for the COVID-19 response.

"[We need] someone focused exclusively on this crisis, with the authority to coordinate and direct action across agencies in Washington and communicate the message with one voice on these issues. With all due respect, Mr. President, if we are to succeed, it is urgent that we have someone like this in charge."
Salazar wrote that even after Biden's June 2024 executive order sharply reduced crossings, the administration failed to communicate the policy's success before Biden exited the race.
He said that gave President Donald Trump an opportunity to campaign on the "low-hanging fruit" of the border crisis.
TANVI RATNA: LATIN AMERICA'S RIGHT TURN IS REDRAWING THE UNITED STATES' BACKYARD

A split screen of former U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ken Salazar and President Joe Biden. Salazar criticized Biden and his administration's handling of the border crisis and revealed he almost ran for president in 2024. (Matt Kelley/AP Photo)
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Biden for comment.
Both Biden and Trump, however, displayed what Salazar called "foreign policy malpractice" in terms of the Americas — something administrations have struggled with for 100 years, according to Salazar.
"That’s where everybody gets trapped," he said.
"Republicans, like Donald Trump, use it as a political advantage because that's how they win elections. And they realized that way back 20-some years ago."

"Democrats, on the other hand, have a sense that it is very important. And they do focus, but only on the border and on domestic migration issues [like] immigration reform. They don't focus at all or enough on Mexico [or] the border between Mexico and Guatemala — And that's what I believe we have to do. And that is what 'Borderlands' proposes that we do," he said, referring to his book.
HARRIS CALLS FOR ICE PROBE AFTER MAINE SHOOTING AMID RENEWED 'BORDER CZAR' CRITICISM

WASHINGTON - FEBRUARY 12: U.S. Interior Secretary Ken Salazar speaks during an Abraham Lincoln birthday celebration event at the Lincoln Memorial February 12, 2009, in Washington, DC. It marked the 200th birthday of the 16th President of the United States Abraham Lincoln.  (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
TRUMP BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN WANTS POPE LEO XIV TO RIDE ALONG WITH ICE AGENTS: 'THEY DON'T UNDERSTAND'

Instead of demonizing migrants or focusing only on social aspects of the crisis, Salazar said his "Borderlands Platform" is a new vision that is grounded in realizing economic and national security prosperity for all three North American countries.

Salazar's proposed "Borderlands Platform" calls for a "New American Alliance" among the United States, Mexico and Canada, including deeper security cooperation, expanded labor mobility and renewed investment in North American trade. He argued immigration policy should be treated as both a national security and economic issue rather than solely a domestic political fight — and wrote supportively about renewing Trump’s USMCA, which had supplanted Bill Clinton’s NAFTA.
Salazar said Trump is correct that the border is "broken," but said he disagreed with Trump's approach, calling it divisive and pointing to ICE-involved shootings.

"It's not the American way where people have rights, where you have a sense of security, understand the importance of our security within our own country and the importance for supporting law enforcement."
Salazar pointed to his tenure as Colorado attorney general, where he led "thousands of cops," as evidence of his longstanding support for law enforcement.
KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

"What is being neglected here is the bigger picture. And that's this foreign policy paradigm that is so required for the United States and Mexico and the Americas. And I don't see this administration moving in that direction to create the kind of legal frameworks that are essential that will give us our national security and ensure that we have a border that works and ensure we have an immigration system that is reformed and does the right thing," he said.
Salazar confirmed he has met with several Democrats viewed as potential 2028 presidential contenders, strongly advising them to make border and migration policy a top issue.

"Not that I have a lot of sway, but at least I will do everything I can to make sure that this is at the heart of every Democrat running for president," he said, noting that Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., was one lawmaker who met with him and endorsed his "Borderlands" book.
Asked if he would entertain Republican invitations, Salazar said if Trump reached out he would meet with him, but underlined that he would not become "political fodder for anybody."
TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

"I do think that the Trump administration has an opportunity here because they, at the end of the day, recognize that the big questions of our time are affordability for the American people. The cost of strawberries, blueberries, and avocados, food, fuel, all those things are very much impacted by what's happening with tariffs and the uncertainty with Mexico right now," he said.

"I spent a lot of time on our ranch, I pumped the diesel into our [machinery], and I can tell you that across rural America, people are hurting because of what's happening with trade and we are losing a lot of our advantage here. Agriculture is in for a very hard time in the years ahead."

He said he hopes Trump would consider a "Borderlands"-type plan for a "new era" in Intracontinental relations.

"I don’t think that’s going to happen, but I certainly would give him that advice."
