title: Pentagon plots new nuclear options for Trump as America’s biggest adversaries raise stakes: report
summary: President Donald Trump could gain new tactical nuclear weapons options under a classified Pentagon strategy led by Elbridge Colby, NBC reports.
story: US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker discusses escalating U.S.-Iran tensions amid reports of Chinese missile transfers to Tehran. He also addresses Russia's missile attack on Kyiv after Zelenskyy's warning and Ukraine's urgent need for air defense.

The Pentagon is drafting a new nuclear strategy aimed at giving President Donald Trump more options for using shorter-range nuclear weapons in a potential regional conflict with China or Russia, according to a report.

The classified effort, led by Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, would put greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons — systems intended for use against military targets in a regional conflict — rather than relying primarily on long-range strategic forces, NBC News reported, citing five people familiar with the plans.

The strategy is designed for scenarios in which China or Russia attacks a U.S. ally and Washington must determine how to respond without immediately escalating to a large-scale strategic nuclear exchange, according to the report.
TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING FOR HIGH-STAKES XI TALKS AS TAIWAN TENSIONS, TRADE DISPUTES TEST US STRENGTH

FILE - This photo taken from video provided by the Russian Defense Ministry Press Service on Feb. 19, 2022, shows a Yars intercontinental ballistic missile being launched from an air field during military drills in Russia. The Russian Defense Ministry said that the military will hold drills involving tactical nuclear weapons – the first time such exercise was publicly announced by Moscow. (Russian Defense Ministry Press Service via AP, File) (Russian Defense Ministry Press Service via AP)

"Our view is that we need credible nuclear options," a senior War Department official told NBC. The official said the strategy would "expand the President’s option space by providing him with realistic and credible options and therefore strengthen deterrence."
The reported shift comes as the United States confronts two nuclear-armed adversaries with increasingly capable arsenals.

Russia retains a large stockpile of theater nuclear weapons and has repeatedly invoked its nuclear capabilities during the war in Ukraine. China, meanwhile, is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear forces, creating what U.S. military officials increasingly describe as a two-peer nuclear challenge.

Tactical, or non-strategic, nuclear weapons are generally designed for theater or regional use rather than long-range strategic missions. They often have shorter-range delivery systems and may be intended for military targets.
But the label does not mean they are limited in consequence: a nuclear detonation could kill large numbers of people, spread radioactive fallout and trigger nuclear retaliation.
US FALLS BEHIND IN HYPERSONIC RACE AS CHINA, RUSSIA GAIN EDGE
China may be conducting low-yield nuclear tests, a State Department official says. (Tingshu Wang/File Photo/Reuters)
The War Department has not publicly announced a change in nuclear employment policy or a new tactical nuclear weapons program. Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

The review also comes six months after New START, the last treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals, expired without a replacement, leaving Washington and Moscow without binding limits or inspections for the first time in decades.

The treaty did not cover tactical nuclear weapons, an area in which Russia holds a substantial numerical advantage. U.S. Strategic Command estimated this year that Moscow possesses up to 2,000 theater nuclear warheads.
An unarmed LGM-30G Minuteman III sits inside the silo of U-01 at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming, July 9, 2025. (Staff Sgt. Michael A. Richmond/U.S. Air Force)

Russia has long relied on its non-strategic nuclear arsenal in part to offset NATO’s conventional military strength. China’s growing arsenal is adding a separate challenge for Pentagon planners preparing for the possibility of confronting two nuclear-armed competitors.

Supporters of the Pentagon’s reported shift argue that giving Trump more credible limited-response options could strengthen deterrence by convincing an adversary that Washington has ways to respond short of an all-out strategic exchange.

Critics argue that putting greater emphasis on weapons intended for regional use could lower the threshold for nuclear employment and increase the risk that a limited conflict spirals into a broader nuclear war.

title: READ THE DOCUMENTS: Secret ‘Oxferd Comma’ probe cast Trump as potential Russian asset after Comey firing
summary: The FBI opened a counterintelligence probe codenamed "Oxferd Comma" after Trump fired James Comey, seeking direct ties to the Russian Federation.
story: Article III Project president Mike Davis discusses the DOJ subpoena of former FBI Director James Comey in an investigation into a ‘grand conspiracy’ to undermine Trump’s presidency on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

The White House released a trove of documents showing that the FBI opened a 2017 investigation into whether President Donald Trump was acting on behalf of or under the influence of Russia when he fired FBI Director James Comey.
The investigation, codenamed "Oxferd Comma," opened after Trump fired Comey in May 2017, according to the White House’s release.

Investigators sought to determine whether Trump was "directed by, controlled by, and/or coordinated activities with, the Russian Federation in a manner constituting a threat to the national security of the United States and/or a violation of federal criminal statutes," according to an FBI memo dated May 16, 2017. The memo also said investigators would examine whether Trump or others had obstructed or conspired to obstruct an associated FBI investigation.
TRUMP ALLY DIGENOVA TAPPED TO LEAD DOJ PROBE INTO BRENNAN OVER RUSSIA PROBE ORIGINS
US President Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. (Photo by Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images) (Aaron Schwartz / AFP Getty Images)

The opening memo cited information developed during Crossfire Hurricane, the FBI’s counterintelligence investigation into whether individuals associated with Trump’s 2016 campaign were coordinating with the Russian government to interfere in the 2016 election.
READ THE DOCUMENTS:

It also identified later events and information, including Trump’s interactions with Comey, the administration’s shifting explanations for Comey’s firing, Trump campaign discussions concerning the Republican platform’s language on Ukraine aid and Trump’s business ties and real estate interests involving Russia.
SECRET FBI PROBE CAST TRUMP AS POSSIBLE RUSSIAN ASSET AFTER COMEY FIRING, MEMOS SHOW

Former FBI Director James Comey testifies before the Senate Intelligence Committee about his interactions with President Donald Trump and the Russia investigation on June 8, 2017, in Washington, D.C. (Cheriss May/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Trump initially cited Comey’s handling of the FBI investigation into Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server while she was secretary of state as the reason for his ouster, though he later said the Russia investigation was also on his mind when he made the decision.
The FBI memo said the circumstances surrounding Comey’s dismissal could support an inference that the bureau’s counterintelligence investigation was a factor in Trump’s decision to fire Comey.
READ THE DOCUMENTS:
However, the decision to open the investigation did not mean those suspicions had been substantiated.

Special counsel Robert Mueller, appointed in 2017 to investigate Russian election interference, reported in 2019 that his team did not establish coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia and did not make a prosecutorial decision on obstruction. Attorney General William Barr appointed John Durham to review the origins and handling of the FBI’s Russia investigation in 2019. Durham’s 2023 report concluded that the FBI opened the full Crossfire Hurricane investigation without sufficient evidentiary support and did not apply the same rigor it had used in other sensitive investigations.
READ THE DOCUMENTS:

A separate 2019 Justice Department inspector general review found the FBI had enough information under its rules to open Crossfire Hurricane, though it later identified serious errors and omissions in surveillance applications involving former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page.

A review of the White House’s original release shows the code name rendered as "Oxferd Comma," with the letter "o." Former acting Assistant Attorney General Jeff Clark, who served in Trump’s first administration, said a document expert he consulted concluded the "o" in "Comma" found within the FBI documents was a zero. Clark speculated the unusual spelling was intended to make the records harder to find through FOIA searches.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The documents were published by the White House Wednesday, which said they had been declassified and released through its Government Transparency Task Force.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Senate Republicans push Election Day deadline for California's marathon ballot counts
summary: Sens. James Lankford and Mike Lee cite a Supreme Court ruling as they push legislation requiring all mail-in ballots be received by the time polls close.
story: Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, are taking advantage of an opening left by the Supreme Court to halt blue states like California from accepting and counting ballots after polls close on Election Day.

FIRST ON FOX: A pair of Senate Republicans are bursting through a crack in the door left by the Supreme Court to force blue states like California to vastly cut down on how long it takes to count ballots.

Sens. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, are introducing legislation that would create a federal deadline for states to accept ballots received by the time polls close on Election Day across the country.
Lankford pitched the bill, called the Ballots by Election Day Act, as a bid to build more trust in the country’s elections.
TRUMP UNLOADS AFTER SUPREME COURT UPHOLDS LATE MAIL-IN BALLOTS IN MISSISSIPPI
A voter casts a ballot at a polling location. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I have made fun of other states for years because there's quite a few states around the country that can't seem to figure out how to be able to count," Lankford told Fox News Digital in an interview. "In Oklahoma, our election ends at 7 p.m. on a Tuesday night."

"Usually by 9 p.m., all of our thousands of precincts are all in and counted," he continued. "We start the verification process. We do an audit after that. We have great trust in our elections because we know. We all vote. But we get them all in on that."

Lankford and Lee’s bill would create a nationwide deadline for counting absentee and mail-in ballots, meaning that if those ballots aren’t in by the time polls close across the expanse of time zones in the nation, they won’t be counted.
CALIFORNIA’S SLUGGISH VOTE COUNTING RIPPED ACROSS THE POLITICAL SPECTRUM: 'EXTREMELY EMBARRASSING'
It targets states, like California and Washington state, where ballot counting can take days, sometimes weeks, beyond when polls close.

"States counting late ballots are inviting fraud and sowing doubt in their own election results," Lee told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Our bill will clarify protocol and restore trust by counting only ballots received before the polls close on Election Day."
Lankford contended that those states, "like California and others, New York," breed distrust in the system.
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES
Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, spoke during a news conference about the SAVE America Act at the U.S. Capitol on March 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"When you vote you may not know for weeks to months what the final election count is," he said. "That shouldn't be in the United States of America."
Their push comes after the Supreme Court’s decision to allow mail-in ballots post-marked before Election Day to still be counted if they came in later.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While the court contended that mail-in balloting could continue, it didn’t explicitly address that there could be no deadline for when the ballots could be counted.

"Once the court made their ruling, as that came out, they left a clear door open to say this could be defined by the United States Congress," Lankford said. "So I said, let's step in and actually do that. Let us provide some real clarity for that. This shouldn't be controversial. This should just be something to build trust in our elections."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Resurfaced Mamdani interview ignites internet frenzy over alleged 'fake' Ugandan accent

story: A 2016 radio interview promoting his mother's Disney film, Queen of Katwe, resurfaced recently, prompting a wave of criticism on social media. (Credit: YouTube/Kaya 959 - Oct.14, 2016)

title: Trump's pick for top law enforcement official gets crucial last-minute lifeline for confirmation
summary: As Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation appeared headed for defeat, one on-the-fence Senate Republican threw him and President Donald Trump a vital lifeline.
story: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on the Senate impasse over President Donald Trump's nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general as Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis remain noncommittal.
As Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation appeared headed for sure defeat, one on-the-fence Senate Republican gave him, and President Donald Trump, a vital lifeline.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., has remained quiet throughout this and last week on how he would vote on Blanche, who barely survived his confirmation vote from the Senate Judiciary Committee. Now, after conversations with Trump's pick to lead the Department of Justice (DOJ), the pieces are in place to confirm Blanche.

"I will vote for Mr. Blanche," an emotional Cassidy said on the Senate floor. "I'll be criticized for this vote. What's new? But the people of Louisiana can be assured that I worked hard to understand the issue and to make the right decision."
COLLINS DROPS THE HAMMER ON TRUMP'S PICK TO LEAD DOJ, JEOPARDIZING PATH TO CONFIRMATION
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation went from doomed to possible after Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., announced that he would support him.  (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

With Cassidy's green light, Blanche has a chance, even with Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., missing in action. But to be confirmed, Senate Republicans will need an assist from Vice President JD Vance. Still, it’s unclear whether the Senate will actually vote on Blanche on Friday, which could be the upper chamber’s grand finale of the summer before it exits Washington, D.C., for the remainder of August.

Cassidy explained that after a series of conversations with Blanche and former DOJ officials, including former Attorney General Bill Barr, he reached the conclusion to support Trump's pick, even after having sparred with the president since being ousted from office by him earlier this year.

He contended that Blanche has been "criticized for things over which he has no control," like Trump's pardons of Jan. 6, 2021, rioters who stormed Capitol Hill, but was still leery of his role in the nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund, which the president has signaled he wants to revive.
But he argued it would be better to have an attorney general confirmed by the Senate that could, if needed, stare down Trump on issues.

"I am realistic that President Trump can be unrelenting on this, but this will be true no matter who the attorney general is," Cassidy said. "And this is the rationale for having a Senate-confirmed attorney general with more leverage to push back."
TRUMP'S AG PICK SURVIVES — FOR NOW — AS REPUBLICANS QUESTION IF WHITE HOUSE DEAL WILL HOLD

It comes after Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, announced that she would not support Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s top prosecutor and law enforcement official, dealing another blow to his rocky confirmation process.

Her defection, despite a heavy lobbying effort by Blanche that saw him make the trek to Alaska, means that Senate Republican leadership can’t afford to lose any more votes to get him across the finish line, given that Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., though now back home, has still not returned to the Senate.

Murkowski acknowledged Blanche’s visit to Alaska and heavy lobbying effort throughout the last few weeks, but it’s his connection to President Donald Trump’s nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund, and broader concerns of a weaponized Justice Department, that proved the nail in the coffin for her.

"The politicization — even weaponization — of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it," Murkowski said in a statement. "I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators."

"I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage," she continued. "Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds."
TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS
Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, speaks to members of the media following a vote outside the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, Oct. 3, 2025.  (Graeme Sloan/Getty Images)

To Murkowski’s latter issue, several lawmakers on both sides of the aisle acknowledge that though Blanche and the DOJ agreed to permanently rescind the fund in writing to Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, there’s nothing stopping Trump from reviving it.
And on several occasions, he’s made clear he wants to see it come back.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration," Murkowski said. "I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case."
Before making her decision, Trump already took a swipe at her during an interview with Punch Bowl News published Friday morning.
"I’m against Murkowski," Trump said. "I do more for Alaska than any president in history. No president’s done for Alaska what I’ve done. She’s not good."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Smithsonian's taxpayer funds face chopping block as GOP demands accountability for 'woke' history
summary: Rep. Andrew Clyde says tying Smithsonian funding to requirements highlighting American exceptionalism is the best way to reform the museum system.
story: Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., a member of the House Appropriations Committee, suggested that one way to make the Smithsonian change its history teachings was through Congress' power of the purse.
FIRST ON FOX: House Republicans are threatening the Smithsonian's federal funding amid GOP outrage over the museum system's presentation of American history.

"The Smithsonian is accountable to the taxpayers. So defunding them in certain ways, or tying their funds to requirements, I think is probably the best way to ensure that we bring the Smithsonian back to its required mandate," Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., told Fox News Digital. "And that is to tell the truth about the American story, and to tell about the exceptionalism of this country and its people."
Congress allocates roughly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to the Smithsonian Institution every year, which oversees 21 museums and the National Zoo. It also receives private funding.

But Republicans have heaped scrutiny in recent weeks on the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, accusing its curators of long painting an overly critical and "woke" picture of the country's past while ignoring its triumphs.
TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED
The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History is accused of perpetuating a "woke" version of U.S. history. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Clyde, who is on the House Appropriations Committee — which is one of two panels on Capitol Hill tasked with mapping out how Congress spends part of the yearly budget — suggested that using the legislative branch's power of the purse could compel museum curators to change that.

"We can tie funding to specific requirements, and I think that might be the most effective way to go — saying that... 'You have to highlight the exceptionalism. You have highlighted the good things that [the Founding Fathers have] done. You know, there's no perfect country because there's not a perfect person. But we are the best there is on the planet Earth," Clyde said.

Another House Appropriations Committee member, Rep. Ben Cline, R-Va., told Fox News Digital, "The Smithsonian’s role is to teach historic facts, not to put our country under a political kaleidoscope of woke ideology."
WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING

"As Congressional Appropriators, it is our duty to ensure that taxpayer dollars are being used responsibly. If the Smithsonian is unable and unwilling to have an objective view of our Nation’s history, House Republicans will have to act," Cline said.

A video playing at the entrance of the National Museum of American History’s Entertainment Nation exhibit features scantily clad women and a clip from the feminist thriller "The Handmaid’s Tale." (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)
Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, a third House appropriator, told Fox News Digital that stricter guardrails on Smithsonian funding are "justified."
"Congress has the responsibility to ensure those funds are used to celebrate and preserve Amrican history, not distort it," Cloud said.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order late last month directing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to utilize existing avenues "to restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution," including installing "temporary exhibits or signage on [federally owned] sidewalks, walkways, and land used by the public that corrects inaccurate information presented in the Museum."

The issue came before Congress in July when Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, led a hearing where Republicans accused the National Museum of American History of promoting a politicized agenda on issues of race, class, gender and sexuality, at the expense of accurate teachings.
The Committee on House Administration, led by Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., led a similar hearing scrutinizing the Smithsonian's teachings.
TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY
Democrats, on the other hand, have accused Republicans of trying to "whitewash" controversial moments in history while erasing the struggles and contributions of the country's minority populations.

"They want to rewrite the history of this country and take away the resources and leadership of people who have fought, marched and served this country for generations," Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said during Gill's hearing. "We refuse to let historians, artists, scholars, and people who love these institutions with their entire hearts to be punished by an administration that is trying to exercise...political control, and rewrite American history."
The "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

The House and Senate are both working through proposals to fund the government for fiscal year (FY) 2027, which begins on Oct. 1. The House proposal would allocate roughly $961 million to the Smithsonian Institution, an 11% reduction from the current level.
But there's still a long way to go before both chambers strike a deal, with time for House conservatives to push for new guardrails or even less funding.

title: Church protesters could face tougher penalties under rare bipartisan crackdown
summary: A bipartisan House bill would impose civil fines up to $10,000 for protests that disrupt worship within 100 feet of a house of worship entrance.
story: Pastor Jonathan Parnell and attorney Doug Wardlow join 'Saturday in America' to discuss the controversial decision by the St. Paul city attorney to not prosecute anti-ICE protesters who stormed Cities Church in January, calling their actions a "peaceful protest."

There's a rare show of bipartisan unity in the House of Representatives this week, as lawmakers from opposite sides of the aisle come together to crack down on destructive protests targeting houses of worship.
Reps. Brad Knott, R-N.C., and Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y., are introducing a bill to make it a crime to knowingly disrupt or impede people from attending a religious service.

That includes demonstrations taking place within 100 feet "from any pedestrian or vehicular entryway of any house of worship, during the period beginning 1 hour before the start of and ending 1 hour after the conclusion of a scheduled religious service," according to legislative text obtained by Fox News Digital.
VIDEO SHOWS MOB OF TEENS INVADING NYC CHURCH OF SCIENTOLOGY IN SOCIAL MEDIA STUNT
Federal law enforcement with anti-ICE agitator William Kelly, one of three people accused of leading a protest inside a church in St. Paul. (X/@Sec_Noem)
A violation of those guidelines would carry a $2,500 civil fine on the first offense, a $5,000 penalty on the second offense, and $10,000 for a third.
The bill does carve out limitations, however, such as demonstrations that are taking place with a federal, state, or local government-issued permit.
The text's language also specifically classifies disruptions based on things like volume, duration, and impact, rather than the content of speech — meaning the First Amendment is still protected.

"Today, many Americans are unable to worship without fear of harassment, assault, or other forms of intimidation. The right to worship freely is foundational to our nation and was one of the motivations for its founding. No American should ever feel that their choice is between worshiping in fear and not worshiping at all," Knott said.
FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP DOJ REACHES SETTLEMENT WITH PRO-LIFE PROTESTER TARGETED BY BIDEN ADMIN
Suozzi said he supports people's right to peacefully protest but "attendees of religious services should not be harassed, threatened, intimidated, or targeted for practicing their faith."
Anti-ICE protesters shouting in a church on Sunday. (Facebook/DawokeFarmer2)

At least four states adopted laws banning the disruption of religious services earlier this year, the Associated Press reported.
It followed an incident in which Minnesota demonstrators upended service at a church where a federal immigration official was reportedly a pastor.

title: Fatal air ambulance crash exposes growing GPS danger facing US flights
summary: A National Transportation Safety Board report reveals a New Mexico air ambulance crew lost GPS navigation during a military jamming exercise before striking the Capitan Mountains.
story: University of Texas GPS expert Todd Humphreys says a fatal New Mexico medevac crash raises broader questions about aviation safety, outdated cockpit GPS technology and the growing threat of GPS jamming.

Federal investigators say a fatal New Mexico air ambulance crash unfolded after the crew lost GPS navigation while the U.S. military was conducting a scheduled jamming exercise — a chain of events that is raising new questions about whether civilian aviation is prepared for an era of electronic warfare.

The National Transportation Safety Board's preliminary report found the Beech King Air crew reported losing GPS capability minutes after departing Roswell, New Mexico, May 14 as the military conducted a planned GPS-denial exercise. Air traffic controllers twice asked officials to halt the jamming while assisting the flight, though investigators have not determined whether the interference caused or contributed to the crash.

The crew took off from Roswell, New Mexico, shortly before midnight on an air ambulance flight to Ruidoso, New Mexico, according to the preliminary report. Before the flight, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had issued a notice to airmen warning that a scheduled military GPS jamming exercise could disrupt satellite navigation across a radius of hundreds of miles around White Sands Missile Range.Minutes after departure, the pilots reported losing GPS capability and requested assistance from air traffic controllers, who twice asked the military to suspend the jamming exercise. Three other aircraft in the area also reported GPS outages.
Federal investigators are examining the causes of recent close calls between airliners and other safety issues. (Michael Dwyer, File/The Associated Press )

The crew later reported the airport in sight and requested a visual approach. After the military resumed the exercise, the aircraft descended toward the runway but struck the Capitan Mountains, killing both pilots and two flight nurses. The National Transportation Safety Board has not determined whether the GPS interference contributed to the crash.

The crash comes as aviation authorities worldwide warn that GPS interference is becoming a growing operational hazard. The FAA now advises pilots to be prepared to fly without GPS because intentional jamming is "of greater and growing concern," while the U.N.'s aviation agency has warned that interference can affect aircraft far beyond conflict zones.

In its 2026 guidance, the agency said the hazards associated with GPS jamming and spoofing have "rapidly spread" in recent years and cited industry data showing reports of GPS loss increased 65% in the first half of 2024 compared with the previous year. The agency warned that interference can cause pilots to deviate from assigned flight paths, misreport their position, lose situational awareness and struggle to transition safely to backup navigation.

Todd Humphreys, director of the University of Texas' Radionavigation Laboratory, said the crash also raises questions about whether the navigation technology used in many civilian aircraft has kept pace with evolving GPS jamming threats.
Humphreys said many FAA-certified cockpit GPS receivers rely on older technology that is more susceptible to jamming than newer commercially available systems.
"The iPhone that the pilot carried was almost certainly a better GPS receiver inside than the FAA-certified receiver providing navigation guidance to the aircraft," Humphreys told Fox News Digital.

Unlike illegal consumer GPS jammers, military electronic warfare systems are designed to deny satellite navigation across large operational areas so troops can train in conditions resembling combat. In the New Mexico exercise, the FAA warned GPS disruptions could extend hundreds of miles from White Sands Missile Range.
INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH

Humphreys argued that while newer GPS technology has become more resilient to interference, aviation certification has moved too slowly to keep pace with the evolving threat from jamming and spoofing.

Humphreys' concerns echo warnings from international aviation regulators. In March 2025, the International Civil Aviation Organization, along with the International Telecommunication Union and International Maritime Organization, warned of increasing GPS jamming and spoofing incidents that can affect aircraft "far beyond the immediate affected area," creating safety risks across multiple flight regions.

Paul Deres, vice president of operations at the Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association Air Safety Institute, said the focus should remain on pilot preparation and proficiency, noting that today's general aviation fleet includes a wide range of older and newer avionics designed to improve situational awareness.
"Technology can always fail, and it does," Deres said.

European regulators have repeatedly updated guidance for pilots and air traffic controllers in response to growing GPS interference, most recently in July after analyzing additional jamming and spoofing incidents.

The FAA declined to comment on the ongoing investigation, but said it issues notices alerting pilots to planned GPS disruptions and maintains backup navigation systems to help aircraft navigate during satellite outages.
Asked about Humphreys' criticism that FAA-certified GPS receivers have not kept pace with newer technology, the agency did not directly address the claim.
GPS interference has become a growing challenge for commercial aviation in parts of Europe and the Middle East, where airlines routinely encounter jamming and spoofing linked to regional conflicts.

"There are some in the community who believe that we have passed the point of peak safety in aviation, maybe four years ago," Humphreys said, pointing to the rise of GPS jamming, spoofing and other forms of hybrid warfare that can disrupt aircraft navigation.
But it remains relatively uncommon in U.S. airspace outside of military testing.

In March 2025, multiple commercial airliners approaching Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport near the nation's capital received false collision alerts that forced several crews to perform go-arounds. Congressional testimony later revealed the alerts were triggered by Secret Service and U.S. Navy counter-drone testing.

Regardless of whether investigators ultimately link the GPS outage to the crash, the report documents how quickly a routine medical flight became a complex navigation emergency after the crew reported losing satellite guidance. The National Transportation Safety Board preliminary report describes a chain of events in which the crew lost GPS shortly after departure, requested assistance from air traffic control, and later opted to continue visually toward the airport before striking terrain.
As drones become more prevalent, GPS jamming as a form of counter-drone operations only will become more common.

"Nation states have woken up to the fact that this is one of the ways they can protect themselves from drones," he said. "We've got to move more quickly on the aviation side to build better systems, better receivers, better antennas to deal with this so that flights can be safer again."
A photograph hangs on a fence at the Trinity Site during an open house in 2022 in White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico.  (Matt McClain/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
JASON CHAFFETZ: AMERICA NEEDS A DRONE DEFENSE PLAN BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

Humphreys said the United States has so far avoided the level of disruption seen in Europe, but argued regulators need to modernize aviation technology before GPS interference becomes a more routine operational challenge.

"The FAA, I think they've just got to move faster. They've got to wake up and recognize that sticking to their old rules about you know, certification that takes years and millions and millions of dollars to get through is not at the service of safety anymore, because the environment has changed. "

title: Trump-backed incumbent ousted in House primary as GOP redistricting push set to reshape Tennessee
summary: Trump-backed incumbent Andy Ogles falls despite a late push from the president, while Republicans’ new congressional map set up a Trump-vs.-AOC proxy fight that could prove pivotal come November.
story: Fox News contributor Joe Concha joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze new polling in the Michigan, Wisconsin and Texas races. Concha also discusses the rally supporting WNBA player Sophie Cunningham for defending women's sports.

President Donald Trump’s clout with Republican voters was put to the test in Tennessee Thursday, as voters headed to the polls for the state’s first primaries under a newly redrawn congressional map designed to bolster Republicans’ chances of expanding their thin majority in the U.S. House this fall.

The night delivered a split verdict for Trump in two of the state’s closely watched Republican House primaries. Trump-backed state Sen. Brent Taylor captured the GOP nomination in the newly redrawn 9th Congressional District, while former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher toppled Trump-endorsed incumbent Rep. Andy Ogles in the 5th District.

Taylor’s victory sets up a November showdown against AOC-backed progressive state Rep. Justin Pearson, one of the so-called "Tennessee Three" lawmakers who gained national attention after he was expelled following a gun control protest in 2023.

Elsewhere, Sen. Marsha Blackburn captured the Republican gubernatorial nomination, putting her on course to potentially become Tennessee’s first female governor and eventually create an opening for another U.S. Senate appointment.
SQUAD-BACKED ‘TENNESSEE THREE’ LAWMAKER WINS HOUSE PRIMARY IN NEWLY REDRAWN DISTRICT
Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., on Capitol Hill. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"From the bottom of my heart, thank you, Tennessee! One year ago, we set out on this journey with one goal: to make Tennessee America's conservative leader and show the nation what strong, bold, conservative leadership looks like," Blackburn said following her win Thursday night. "I am humbled and honored that you've chosen me as your Republican nominee for Governor. Together, we've taken a major step toward that goal. I won't let you down. On to November."

Ogles’ defeat was a glaring setback for Trump on the night. The president threw his support behind the conservative House Freedom Caucus member and stepped in as the race tightened, praising Ogles as a strong businessman and America First lawmaker during a virtual tele-rally last month. Hatcher, endorsed by term-limited Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, handed the two-term incumbent an upset defeat despite Trump’s intervention.

Ogles, backed by Speaker Mike Johnson in addition to Trump, faced a high-dollar outside effort to knock him out of the race. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a clean-energy super PAC largely bankrolled by California crypto billionaire and major Democratic donor Chris Larsen, spent roughly $1 million opposing Ogles and supporting Hatcher before purchasing another $700,000 in advertising ahead of the primary, according to a Fox News Digital review of federal filings.
Ogles accused the group of trying to punish him for opposing Biden-era clean-energy subsidies and suggested his close ties to Trump had also put a target on his back.

The Trump-backed incumbent was also running on unfamiliar terrain after Tennessee Republicans dramatically redrew his 5th District. While the change made the district significantly more Republican for November, it left Ogles to face a significantly new GOP electorate than what had elected him in the past.
TENNESSEE PASSES NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP LIKELY TO FLIP FINAL DEM SEAT AS PROTESTS ERUPT INSIDE CAPITOL
Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., walks through the U.S. Capitol on February 03, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Ogles’ district was not the only one transformed. Tennessee Republicans redrew the state’s congressional lines this spring, breaking apart the Democratic-controlled 9th District and giving Republicans a chance to turn Tennessee’s current 8-1 GOP delegation into a 9-0 sweep.

The effort prompted longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen to abandon his reelection bid in that Memphis-area district, which was transformed from a district that previously favored Democrats into one that now tilts Republican.
Thursday's primaries now set up a particularly nationalized fight for that seat.
DARLINE GRAHAM CONSIDERING RUNNING FOR FULL A SENATE TERM AS MEMORIAL SERVICES SET FOR LINDSEY GRAHAM: REPORT

Taylor, who won the GOP 9th district primary Thursday, carries Trump’s endorsement, while Pearson, the winner of the 9th district's Democratic primary, has been embraced by members of the far-left "Squad" on Capitol Hill, including, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, D-Memphis, raises his fist after visiting with supporters in the gallery of the House chamber Thursday, April 6, 2023, in Nashville, Tenn. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)

Taylor will try to deliver Republicans the final seat needed for a clean sweep of Tennessee’s congressional delegation, while Pearson will attempt to preserve a Democratic foothold in the Memphis-area district despite a less favorable map.

Blackburn, meanwhile, defeated Rep. John Rose in the Republican gubernatorial primary to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Lee, clearing a major hurdle between her and the governor’s mansion in the heavily Republican state. If elected in November, Blackburn would become Tennessee’s first female governor.

Her victory could also produce consequences in Washington. Blackburn was reelected to a six-year Senate term in 2024, meaning she did not have to surrender her seat to run for governor, as Rose had to. But, she would have to give up her seat if elected governor, which would create a Senate vacancy and another round of political jockeying over who could succeed her.

title: Trump’s Smithsonian clash exposes striking pattern among museum curators
summary: Every curator on the Smithsonian exhibit's seven-person team has incorporated themes of racial injustice or social justice into their academic work.
story: Dr. Jody Edward Ginn, historian and museum professional, told Fox News Digital the Smithsonian has shifted from education to activism after his recent visit.

The scholars behind a Smithsonian exhibition targeted by the Trump administration have built their careers around the same race, gender, sexuality and social-justice themes now fueling accusations of ideological bias at the museum, a Fox News Digital review found.

Entertainment Nation, which opened in December 2022, is an ongoing exhibition at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that uses artifacts from music, film, television, theater and sports to examine how popular culture has shaped American life.

Every member of the exhibit’s seven-person curatorial team has incorporated themes involving racial injustice, gender inequality, sexuality or other progressive social causes into their academic work, public commentary or prior museum projects. Fox News Digital’s review found praise for communist-linked figures, alignment with progressive activist movements and explicit statements connecting museum work to social justice.
TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

A video playing at the entrance of the National Museum of American History’s Entertainment Nation exhibit features scantily clad women and a clip from the feminist thriller The Handmaid’s Tale. (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)
Speaking to Fox News Digital previously, a senior White House official accused Entertainment Nation of promoting "fringe or activist ideologies masquerading as history."

John Troutman, the exhibit’s lead curator, told The Washington Post in 2023 that the project was meant to do more than present a conventional history of entertainment, saying it was not intended to serve as "a gallery that provides a history of entertainment," but instead to examine broader social movements reflected in popular culture.
Troutman’s colleagues have similarly examined entertainment through themes of racial exclusion, gender stereotypes, homophobia and other social conflicts commonly emphasized by the political left.

Curator Kenneth Cohen, for example, published "They Will Have Their Game" in 2017, a book examining how the development of sports in the United States "produced a sense of democracy while also reinforcing racial, gender, and class divisions," according to a description from his publisher. The book, per the description, examines how sports contributed to the "creation of the white male republic" in the United States.

"Although competition and risk were central to understandings of ‘sport’ in early Anglo-America, the formation of a sporting culture based on those elements was not inevitable," Cohen's book reads. "It was a purposeful choice, made largely by empowered white men, to construct sporting culture around traits that encouraged engagement within their ranks and helped to define them as a group despite internal class and ethnic divides."
WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING
A placard in the "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. honors Dr. Anthony Fauci. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)
Cohen’s colleague on the exhibit, curator Krystal Klingenberg, has similarly focused much of her scholarship on music, race, social justice and the Black Lives Matter movement.

For another Smithsonian project she worked on in 2022, Klingenberg stated that her goal was to "connect history with the ongoing fight for civil rights and social justice in American society." Klingenberg lists "social justice" as one of her scholarly interests on her CV, alongside a number of scholarly projects related to it.

Klingenberg also co-hosted the Collected podcast where she examined "why Black feminist critique remains crucial to understanding the times we are living in."

All seven curators have, to varying degrees, examined race, gender, sexuality, inequality or identity in their academic or museum work.
Fox News Digital reached all seven curators for comment, but did not receive replies.

"As always, our work is driven by rigorous scholarship, evidence, and nonpartisanship to help the American people better understand our nation's history, culture, challenges, and triumphs," a Smithsonian representative told Fox News Digital on Friday.

The current conservative crusade against the Smithsonian launched in March 2025 when President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing his administration to review the Smithsonian's exhibits and programs.

Allegations of bias in Entertainment Nation drew renewed national attention in July amid a congressional hearing scrutinizing the National Museum of American History and the release of a 162-page White House report documenting what the administration described as evidence of ideological bias across the Smithsonian.

"American taxpayers should not be funding institutions that undermine our country or promote one-sided, divisive political narratives," a White House official previously told Fox News Digital. "The Smithsonian Institution should present history in a way that is accurate, balanced and consistent with the values that make the United States of America exceptional."
The White House official’s criticism followed reports in 2025 of displays within Entertainment Nation that allegedly used left-of-center language to portray America negatively.
SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES

(From left to right) Krystal Klingenberg, John Troutman, Ashley Mayor and Theodore Gonzalves speak during an Entertainment Nation event in 2024. (YouTube/National Museum of American History) (YouTube/National Museum of American History)

These displays included a section that claimed circuses "expressed the colonial impulse to claim dominion over the world," a placard arguing that Mickey Mouse’s "outsized facial features, white gloves and trickster temperament were vestiges of longstanding traditions of blackface minstrelsy," and a placard describing Alexander Hamilton as an "influential and flawed founding father," language the White House report criticized as unfairly diminishing him.
Some of the curators have publicly commented on their rationale behind procuring specific items for the exhibit.

Ryan Lintelman, another of Entertainment Nation’s curators, was instrumental in acquiring one of the iconic red costumes from the Hulu adaptation of "The Handmaid’s Tale," according to an interview he gave to Variety. The dystopian novel written by feminist author Margaret Atwood depicts a world where America has become a totalitarian theocracy that strips females of their rights and forces fertile women, known as "Handmaids," into reproductive servitude.
Lintelman stated that the costume’s importance to liberal protest movements motivated his work to acquire one for the Smithsonian.
FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Demonstrators dressed as handmaidens from "The Handmaid's Tale" take part in an anti-Trump protest marking one year since the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump, in Washington, D.C., U.S., November 5, 2025. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

"I believe that popular culture is a unique and accessible lens to introduce the museum’s audiences to complex narratives involving race, sexuality, gender, identity, representation, economics, migration, social change, and power," he wrote for his Smithsonian biography.

The 2017 Women’s March, where the Handmaid’s costume featured prominently, was seen as one of the most important early expressions of resistance to the first Trump administration. Theodore Gonzalves, another Entertainment Nation curator, also cited the march approvingly in a 2018 essay praising Barbara Dane, a lifelong socialist and former Communist Party USA member.

Dane was an acclaimed folk musician who spent much of her career involved in left-wing politics, most notably defying the United States government by visiting Cuba while it was under the rule of dictator Fidel Castro. She went on to found a record label that produced songs praising communist figures such as Mao Zedong, calling him China’s "savior," and Ho Chi Minh, actively supporting America’s enemy in the Vietnam War.

Gonzalves described Dane as "singing truth to power" and creating music that "reflected the stakes and the hopeful dreams of millions trying to make sense of a world dominated by superpowers with world-ending weaponry."

Gonzalves, whose scholarship has examined historical abuses against Asian Americans, also uses the term "Filipinx" in his work – which is a gender-neutral term for Filipinos similar to the term "Latinx."

Ashley Mayor, another Entertainment Nation curator who specializes in "Latinx and Afro-Latinx music and culture," regularly shares posts from left-wing organizations on social media. Eric Jentsch, the seventh curator, has also written about race and racism in American sports history, Fox News Digital found.

In its July report, the White House charged that the Smithsonian "no longer treats the American story as a shared national inheritance to be taught or celebrated, but as a political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens."

title: Communist, socialist network helped fuel Madison protests after Corey Ruiz shooting, investigation finds
summary: Communist and socialist groups including the Party for Socialism and Liberation and Freedom Inc. drove Madison protests after the Corey Ruiz shooting.
story: Police in Madison, Wisconsin, cleared an encampment site that grew after homeless man Corey Ruiz was fatally shot by police, Fox 6 News Milwaukee reports. The cleanup ended a nearly two-week occupation that later gave way to renewed protests and overnight unrest.

A coalition of communist, socialist and left-wing activist organizations helped drive nearly two weeks of protests and a sprawling encampment in Madison, Wis., following the fatal police shooting of homeless man Corey Ruiz, with the demonstrations later escalating into clashes with police, street fires and blocked intersections, a Fox News Digital investigation has found.

Among the most prominent groups backing the protests are the Madison chapter of the openly communist Party for Socialism and Liberation, Freedom Inc., a Madison-based "social justice" nonprofit, and the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, a Marxist-Leninist political organization, all of which have publicly backed the protests.

Together, the groups have organized demonstrations, maintained a sprawling protest encampment, demanding the officer's arrest and repeatedly referring to him as a "killer cop." Freedom Inc. also publicly said it bailed out dozens of protesters following recent arrests.
Footage of protesters marching through Madison with scenes of overnight unrest that followed demonstrations over the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. (REUTERS/Jim Vondruska)
600 GROUPS WITH $2B IN REVENUE MOBILIZE 3,000 MAY DAY PROTESTS IN A 'RED-BLUE' ALLIANCE, PROBE FINDS

The mobilization reflects a broader pattern in which communist and socialist organizations have used local confrontations with law enforcement to build protest movements and advance broader political agendas, national security experts say.

Before city crews dismantled the encampment Tuesday morning, it had expanded to include dozens of tents, four portable toilets, food distribution areas and memorial displays. Organizers also brought a raised-fist sculpture from Minneapolis' George Floyd Square to the encampment.

The initial demonstrations erupted after Ruiz was fatally shot on July 22 after police said officers responded to reports of theft before Ruiz fled on a bicycle. After several officers caught up with him, authorities said Ruiz pulled a knife, injured one officer during a struggle and was fatally shot by another officer.

Protesters have accused law enforcement of using excessive force and, during several demonstrations, drawing parallels to the 2020 death of Floyd by while he was being restrained by Minneapolis police.

The Madison unrest culminated late Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday when protesters allegedly threw projectiles at city workers, set five street fires and clashed with officers, according to the Madison Police Department. Police said the unrest resulted in at least 22 arrests, while officers also recovered a handgun from a juvenile protester arrested on unrelated charges.
WISCONSIN PROTESTER BRANDS MADISON AS 'CORRUPT CITY' DURING ANTI-POLICE TIRADE FOLLOWING DEADLY SHOOTING

A raised-fist sculpture from George Floyd Square in Minneapolis stands at the protest encampment established after the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wis., on July 25, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
The Party for Socialism and Liberation

Among the organizations helping drive the demonstrations was the Party for Socialism and Liberation, which Fox News Digital has previously identified as a key organizer of nationwide protest movements within the broader activist ecosystem surrounding organizations funded by Marxist tech entrepreneur Neville Roy Singham, who lives in Shanghai.
Earlier this year, a Fox News Digital investigation documented roughly $285 million flowing from Singham into a global network of nonprofits, activist organizations and media operations.

Since the shooting, the Madison chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation has used its social media accounts to mobilize supporters with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly referring to the officer involved as a "killer cop," The group has helped organize demonstrations, urged followers to "take the streets" and pressured elected officials through coordinated phone and email campaigns demanding the officer's arrest.

After city crews dismantled the protest encampment Tuesday morning, the Party for Socialism and Liberation posted an Instagram video showing officers clearing flowers, candles and memorial items from the intersection where Ruiz was shot before urging supporters to attend another evening demonstration outside Madison City Hall.
WATCH: Protests over police shooting lead to fiery night after Madison encampment cleared
HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM

The accompanying caption accused city officials of protecting the officer, stating: "Killer cop … is still walking free. Still on the streets. Still getting paid," the post read, while identifying the officer by name.
The group concluded the post by writing: "You can destroy a memorial, but you cannot destroy a movement."

Hours after the Party for Socialism and Liberation promoted the evening demonstration, protesters returned to the streets, where officers reported multiple arrests, street fires and blocked intersections.

While the activist group has repeatedly identified the officer involved and demanded his arrest, Madison police have declined to publicly identify any of the four officers involved in the encounter. All four remain on administrative leave while the Wisconsin Department of Justice investigates the shooting, according to local reports.
Freedom Inc.
Another prominent organizer is Freedom Inc., a Madison-based activist nonprofit that advocates abolishing police, defunding law enforcement and broad criminal justice reforms.

In an Instagram post on Wednesday, Freedom Inc. claimed it had "bailed out 50 people" from the Dane County Public Safety Building following the previous night's arrests and had "shut down Doty Street directly in front of the jail while working to get people released."

Fox News Digital was unable to independently verify Freedom Inc.'s claim that it bailed out 50 protesters and has reached out to the organization for comment. Fox News Digital also sought comment from the Party for Socialism and Liberation.
Protesters block access to bars in downtown Madison, Wis., on July 25, 2026, during demonstrations following the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. (Chris Juhn / Anadolu via Getty Images)

IRS filings reviewed by Fox News Digital show Freedom Inc. reported roughly $4.9 million in revenue in 2024, including about $1.24 million in government grants, after reporting roughly $4.2 million in revenue in 2023, including about $1.13 million in government grants.

The overlap between Freedom Inc. and the Madison chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation was evident Wednesday morning, when they jointly published an Instagram post calling supporters to another protest outside the Dane County Courthouse.

The poster declared, "All out for Freedom, Inc.! Don't arrest me, arrest the cops!" while the caption urged supporters to attend, declaring: "Jail killer cops! Justice for Corey Ruiz! Dare to struggle, Dare to win!"

On social media, Freedom Inc. identified itself as the organizer of Monday night's "mass mobilization" that saw protesters climb onto Madison City Hall and hang a giant banner reading "Arrest the Killer Cop" across the front of the building. They also threw balloons filled with red liquid at the building, according to local media outlet WKOW.
Following the encampment's removal, Freedom Inc. accused Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway of "sending armed militia to raid the memorial site."

The rhetoric reflected Freedom Inc.'s broader platform. In a February Instagram post pinned to its page, the group called to "Abolish Police," defund police and ICE, end deportations and close jails, prisons and ICE detention centers.

The organization wrote that "Police and ICE are tearing families apart, racially profiling our people, criminalizing poverty, and inflicting violence on Black, Brown, immigrant, and working-class communities," adding that communities deserve "safety without surveillance" and "care without criminalization."
DEM SOCIALIST RUNNING FOR WISCONSIN GOVERNOR PUSHED 'ABOLISHING THE POLICE'

People gather at the memorial and protest encampment following the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wis., on July 24, 2026. The encampment included a raised-fist sculpture from George Floyd Square in Minneapolis and signs reading "Defund the Police" and "Arrest the Killer Cop." (Christopher Juhn / Anadolu via Getty Images)
The wider network

Freedom Inc.'s organizing also drew support from Fight Back! News, which jointly published an Instagram post with the group highlighting its organizing at the protest encampment. The post described individuals and organizations traveling to Madison from "around the country" to "help organize on the ground" and highlighted a four-day educational series and postcard-writing campaign by Freedom Inc. demanding the officer's arrest, defunding the police, strengthening civilian oversight and expanding community control of policing.

Fight Back! News openly states on its website that some of its writers and staff are members of the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, another far-left organization that has appeared alongside the Party for Socialism and Liberation in previous Fox News Digital reporting on protest movements from Minneapolis to Los Angeles.

Freedom Inc.'s organizing also extended nationally. On July 22, the group jointly published an Instagram post with the National Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression and the Milwaukee Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression calling for "Justice for Corey Ruiz" and "Community Control of the Police Now!"

Meanwhile, the Freedom Road Socialist Organization also publicly promoted the demonstrations. Its Wisconsin chapter collaborated with Freedom Inc. and Madison Students for a Democratic Society on protest posters, while the organization's national social media accounts repeatedly shared footage and updates from the Madison protests.

Meanwhile, state Rep. Francesca Hong, who is running for governor and has previously called for "abolishing the police," appeared at the memorial site shortly after Ruiz's death. Hong does not appear to be affiliated with any of the groups.

Madison police arrest a protester near the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets in Madison, Wis., on Aug. 4, 2026, after city officials dismantled the protest encampment established following the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Madison resident Tom Beck, a retiree who has lived in the city for about 12 years, said city officials allowed the encampment to become entrenched before finally dismantling it.
"They should have given them maybe 48 hours and then go in there and just push it out of the way. Instead, they let it grow," Beck told Fox News Digital.
"It's just become an embarrassment."

Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway defended the city's response, saying officials first offered shelter and hotel accommodations before clearing the encampment, citing public safety concerns and its detrimental impact on nearby businesses and the surrounding neighborhood.
A protester holds a memorial poster for Corey Ruiz during a demonstration in Madison, Wis., on July 23, 2026, one day after Ruiz was fatally shot by a police officer. (Scott Olson / Getty Images)
Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.

title: Autism providers cheer Trump crackdown after millions allegedly stolen from children through Medicaid fraud
summary: Autism care providers back the Trump administration's Medicaid fraud crackdown but warn policymakers not to create barriers for families of autistic children.
story: Former federal prosecutor Andrew Cherkasky joins host Harris Faulkner on 'The Faulkner Focus' to react to DOJ takedowns of massive Medicaid healthcare fraud schemes. Cherkasky warns that these brazen operations mirror organized crime syndicates, actively looting millions in critical state funds and putting the lives of vulnerable Americans at serious risk when essential healthcare resources dry up.

FIRST ON FOX: American autism care providers are backing the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud, arguing that the alleged theft of millions of federal funds has hurt both taxpayers and children with autism who rely on those services.

A coalition of autism clinicians, behavioral therapists and families of children with autism are speaking out in favor of the administration's efforts to hold people accountable for the suspected exploitation of the Medicaid system.

The group — the Autism Families Alliance — describes itself as a national advocacy organization dedicated to supporting Applied Behavior Analysis providers and the families who rely on their services. It aims to ensure that every child and family has access to high-quality care without unnecessary barriers, reduced access or funding cuts.

"We do this work because we believe every child deserves the chance to communicate, gain independence, and live the fullest life possible," Taylor Sanders, a family advocate at the Autism Families Alliance, told Fox News Digital. "I’ve worked with children who found their voice after being nonverbal. I’ve watched families go from fear and uncertainty to hope because their child was finally making progress. Those are the moments that keep us going. That’s why we’re here."
WATCH: DR. OZ SAYS NEWSOM, OTHER BLUE STATES HAVE TURNED MEDICAID FRAUD INTO A 'FEATURE'
American autism care providers are backing the Trump Administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
"President Trump and the administration are right: fraud is unacceptable and those responsible should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," Sanders added.
The group argues that every dollar allegedly stolen by fraudsters should have been used to help a child with autism learn to communicate, gain independence and receive the care they need.

The members strongly support eliminating fraud and prosecuting suspected criminals, but they also fear that broad federal and state efforts to root out fraud could unintentionally make it more difficult for legitimate providers to care for children with autism.
Some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Indiana, have taken steps to enhance oversight of autism services.

But the coalition is calling on policymakers to ensure fraudsters are removed from the system without creating what they describe as unnecessary barriers for families of vulnerable children seeking care.

"There’s real concern among the families I work with that their children’s care could be interrupted because of the government’s response to these criminals," Sanders said. "Access to these programs aren’t a political talking point to these families, it’s their lifeline. Losing this lifeline is a real fear that parents worry about every day. As some states move to crack down on fraud, we have to make sure we’re targeting fraudsters, not putting new barriers in front of families trying to get their children the care they need."
The coalition's stance on the administration's fraud crackdown echoes comments made recently by Dr. Mehmet Oz, who serves as administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
READ: DR. OZ PUTS ALL 50 GOVERNORS ON NOTICE OVER BILLIONS LOST TO MEDICAID FRAUD

A coalition of autism clinicians, behavioral therapists and families of children with autism are speaking out in favor of the administration's efforts to hold people accountable for the suspected exploitation of the Medicaid system. (REUTERS/Kylie Cooper)

"The good news is, our biggest allies are the folks who are doing it right," Oz said at a press briefing earlier this year as part of an announcement of a sweeping national anti-fraud initiative targeting multi-billion dollar Medicaid and Medicare leakage across various states.

"They are the people who are doing hospice right, home healthcare right, who are doing all the things that we need for autism in this country. Those people come to us actually frustrated, angry that we’re allowing, tolerating fraudsters who not only hurt people they care about but are stealing their business inappropriately," he said at the time.
Rocio Berni, the mother of an autistic child, Manny, in Charlotte, North Carolina, spoke about how her child has benefited from ABA providers.

"Working alongside ABA therapy providers has been immensely beneficial for my son," she told Fox News Digital. "Manny struggled with tantrums, and while he loved being around other children, he was frustrated by his inability to communicate with them."

"Today, through the work of dedicated therapists, we have learned to better regulate his behavior," she continued. "My son is now able to approach other children, and we hope he will be able to carry on basic, fulfilling conversations. I simply can’t imagine what his life would be like without this care. I pray that policymakers will ensure that Manny and children like him maintain access to this essential care."
Kelsey Bennett, also a family advocate at the Autism Families Alliance, said fraud has "no place" in healthcare, emphasizing that ABA is "no exception."

"As a practicing clinician, it is disheartening to see the actions of a small number of bad actors cast a shadow over the thousands of ethical clinicians who have dedicated their careers to improving the lives of children with autism and their families," she told Fox News Digital.
The coalition's stance on the administration's fraud crackdown echoes comments made by Dr. Mehmet Oz. (Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Bennett said she backs moves to hold fraudsters accountable, but warned that those targets must be carefully pursued.

"We fully support efforts to identify and hold accountable those who engage in fraudulent billing, improper claims, or substandard care," Bennett said. "Fraud harms taxpayers, undermines trust in the healthcare system, damages the reputation of legitimate providers, and, most importantly, puts vulnerable children at risk."

"At the same time, efforts to combat fraud must be carefully targeted," she continued. "Policies designed to stop abuse should focus on those responsible without creating unnecessary barriers for families seeking medically necessary services. For children with autism, consistency and continuity of care are critical to long-term progress, and significantly limiting telehealth for supervision and assessments can further restrict access for families in rural and underserved areas. Families should not have to worry that broad policy changes or administrative burdens will interrupt the treatment their children rely on."

"The overwhelming majority of ABA providers are committed to providing high-quality, evidence-based care with integrity," she added. "Effective policy should protect public resources by eliminating fraud while preserving timely access to medically necessary treatment for the children and families these programs were created to serve. Children with autism should never bear the consequences of the unethical actions of a small minority of providers."

title: Democratic group launches $15M war on DSA after socialist primary wins: 'Mortal danger'
summary: Third Way launches $15 million campaign against Democratic Socialists of America, calling the DSA a "mortal danger" after Michigan's primary.
story: Asked about El-Sayed's race, Melat Kiros argued a victory would reflect growing voter frustration with the Democratic establishment and support for candidates focused on working families over corporate interests.
A leading centrist Democratic group is launching a new $15 million effort between now and 2028 to discredit democratic socialism, Fox News Digital confirms.
The group, Third Way, says it plans to target the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which they believe poses a "mortal danger" for Democrats.

The move comes in the wake of left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s victory this week over more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in the high-profile and high-stakes Senate primary in battleground Michigan.

El-Sayed's razor-thin win over Stevens, along with DSA-aligned and progressive candidates winning in two congressional primaries in Michigan, come amid earlier victories this spring and earlier this summer, and are emboldening the left in its ideological battle for the future of the Democratic Party.
MEET THE FAR LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed holds a news conference two days ahead of his primary victory, in Detroit, Michigan on Sunday August 2, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

"We believe the DSA poses a serious threat to Democrats. Their ideas are dangerous and their politics are toxic. If we are to beat MAGA Republicans, we cannot allow our party to be defined by radicals," Third Way co-founder Matt Bennett told Fox News Digital.

The group says their effort will include opposition research into the DSA, polling, social media programs and educating Democratic activists and leaders, but that their push is not directed at individual candidates, some of whom are now the party's nominees in a growing number of congressional races in this year's midterm elections.

Responding, DSA co-chair Megan Romer told Fox News Digital, "$15 million to tell working class people that a better world isn’t possible? We believe in people power, and our vision for a better future is winning. We will keep building our movement, and they will waste their money."

The centrist group Third Way is launching a major push to target the Democratic Socialists of America, which it views a a threat to the Democratic Party. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
