"I don't think this would ever happen, but, you know, there's people that, you give that technology, they can someday turn on you," Trump told reporters at Camp David on July 31.
"So we have to be very careful," he warned.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: At least 72 dead amid mass migrant rush to storm Spanish enclave of Ceuta sparking border crisis
summary: At least 72 migrants are dead as Spain searches for more victims and a deadly border crossing sparks renewed political tensions across Europe.
story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett reports on the political repercussions of migrants storming the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on ‘Fox Report.’

At least 72 migrants are dead after a chaotic rush to storm the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, turning one of Europe's latest border crises into a humanitarian disaster that is reigniting debate over immigration across the continent.

Spanish authorities continued searching the waters off Ceuta over the weekend for additional victims after an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 migrants — most of them young men — poured into the tiny Spanish territory in North Africa. Officials said many of the victims drowned while attempting the crossing, while others were killed in a stampede near a breakwater barrier.

The mass crossing unfolded over several days, temporarily increasing Ceuta's population of roughly 84,000 by more than half. By Sunday, many migrants had returned to neighboring Morocco, while others remained in the city or tried to avoid authorities.
SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD
Migrants who crossed into Spain return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Bernat Armangue)

The deaths have intensified the political fight over immigration in Spain and across Europe. Far-right leaders called for tighter border security and the removal of migrants who remained in the enclave.

Santiago Abascal, leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, visited Ceuta on Sunday and blasted the country's government, calling the migrant influx "an invasion" and accusing officials of failing to protect Spain's borders.
Guardia Civil officers recover the body of a migrant from the water in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Antonio Sempere)

Tensions were also on display Saturday when European Parliament member Alvise Pérez faced angry counterprotesters during a rally in Ceuta. Pérez eventually took shelter inside a nearby bar before police escorted him away.
MIGRANT CRISIS PUSHES ITALY TO RESTORE BORDER CHECKS WITH SPAIN, TESTING EUROPE'S OPEN-BORDER SYSTEM
Many local residents expressed sorrow over the loss of life, even as the political debate intensified.

"It pains me deeply that young people are dying at sea. It's not right that, in the year 2026, women with children as young as two months old should be crossing the sea only to die," Karima Abenaz, a French national in Ceuta with family in Morocco, told Reuters.

"In Morocco, there's food, there's everything we need," she said. "If we don't have a decent job, we should go on strike and demand our rights from the government. We shouldn't be dying at sea. It's not right."
Escorted by the Spanish army, migrants who crossed into Spain return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Antonio Sempere)
WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED
Other local residents said the migrants themselves should not be blamed.
Mohamad Abdelkader Driss, a waiter in Ceuta, told The Associated Press that responsibility lies with the authorities.
"If you open the border, of course everyone comes in, but the young men aren't to blame. The authorities are responsible," he said.

Others said the events had tested Ceuta's reputation as a city where Christian, Muslim, Jewish and Hindu communities have long lived side by side. Some also voiced concerns about security and questioned whether another mass crossing could happen again.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The U.S. State Department on Saturday raised its Travel Advisory for Ceuta to Level 3: Reconsider Travel in response to the surge, warning that the "massive and uncontrolled arrival of migrants from Morocco to Ceuta may lead to unpredictable and dangerous security situations."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Mayor calls upscale restaurant bombing a 'brutal terrorist act' after 3 killed, 21 injured
summary: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin vowed to hunt down those responsible after a body-worn bomb detonated at an upscale restaurant on Saturday killing three.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A bombing at an upscale restaurant in Moscow that killed three people and wounded at least 21 others on Saturday was a "brutal terrorist act," according to the city’s mayor, who vowed to hunt down those responsible for the attack.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin made the declaration Sunday, a day after the explosion tore through the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant in the Russian capital.

"Yesterday, a brutal terrorist act was committed in Moscow that claimed human lives. The victims are currently in the city’s hospitals, where they are receiving all necessary care," Sobyanin wrote on social media Sunday.
EXPLOSION AT RESTAURANT IN CENTRAL MOSCOW LEAVES THREE DEAD, MORE THAN A DOZEN INJURED
Police block an area near a deadly explosion at a restaurant in Moscow, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency via AP)
He added investigators are working to identify those behind the attack and vowed they "will certainly be found and will face the punishment they deserve."
Russian authorities have not identified any suspects, and no group had claimed responsibility as of Sunday.
Emergency vehicles are parked in an area near a deadly explosion at a restaurant in Moscow, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency via AP)

Russia's National Anti-Terrorism Committee said the blast was caused by a homemade explosive device. Russian state news agency RIA Novosti, citing local officials, reported that a woman carrying the bomb tried to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard before it exploded.

The blast killed the woman, the security guard and a restaurant patron, RIA Novosti reported. At least 21 other people were injured in the explosion, which happened around 8 p.m. local time at the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square.
UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS
The restaurant was closed to the public Saturday night for a private event, according to its website and Russian state media.
Police block an area near a deadly explosion at a restaurant in Moscow, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency via AP)
Video released by Russian state media showed heavily armed police officers, ambulances and other emergency vehicles outside the damaged restaurant as investigators examined the scene.

Earlier this year, Russia's Federal Security Service, or FSB, said it would tighten security for senior military and government officials following a series of assassination attempts in Russian cities since the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Russian authorities have not linked the restaurant bombing to those earlier attacks or to the war in Ukraine.
Fox News Digital’s Brie Stimson and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Satellite images show evidence of oil leak spreading from sanctioned vessel near Oman
summary: The Caroline Bezengi, reportedly carrying over 800,000 barrels of Russian crude, is leaking oil into a marine reserve home to endangered wildlife off Oman's coast.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A sanctioned tanker loaded with crude is leaving a growing trail of oil in protected waters off the coast of Oman, according to newly reviewed satellite images, as experts warn the stranded vessel could break apart during the region's rough monsoon season.

Satellite images reviewed by The Associated Press show an oil sheen covering roughly 20 square kilometers, or about 8 square miles, around Dhofar's Qibliyah Island, part of Oman's protected Hallaniyat Islands. Dark patches of crude have also reached the shoreline. Experts say the leak has worsened in recent days, fueling fears that rough weather could trigger a much larger spill.

"The last few days, the imagery indicates an increase in oil coming out, as the size of the sheen is growing," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental expert with the Dutch peace organization PAX, told the AP.
REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

This satellite image from Planet Labs PBC shows crude oil leaking and spreading from the sanctioned Suezmax tanker Caroline Bezengi grounded off the coast of Oman, on Friday, July 31, 2026. (Planet Labs PBC via AP)
He said the biggest risk is that the vessel could break apart as strong winds and rough seas during the annual monsoon season continue to pound the ship's hull.

The 899-foot, Cameroon-flagged Caroline Bezengi has been stranded off Oman's southern coast since June after its crew reported an onboard explosion, according to maritime news outlets. Reuters, citing maritime security sources, reported the vessel first ran into trouble on June 8 near the Yemeni port of Mukalla, where initial assessments suggested a blast may have occurred. The cause has not been confirmed.

This satellite image from Planet Labs PBC shows crude oil leaking and spreading from the sanctioned Suezmax tanker Caroline Bezengi grounded at Qibliyah Island, off the coast of Oman, on Friday, July 31, 2026. (Planet Labs PBC via AP)

Ship-tracking data reviewed by Reuters showed the tanker had loaded Russian crude at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk before its latest voyage. The vessel has been sanctioned by the United Kingdom, the European Union, Canada and Switzerland for allegedly transporting Russian oil as part of Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" — a network of aging tankers used to bypass Western sanctions imposed after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
HUNDREDS OF RUSSIAN SHADOW TANKERS TRIGGER MILITARY ALARM TRANSITING NATO WATERS: REPORT

Zwijnenburg estimated the tanker is carrying more than 800,000 barrels of crude oil and said recent imagery suggests at least one section of the hull has been breached. Other maritime specialists who reviewed the images told Reuters the vessel also appears to be listing, adding to concerns that it could eventually break apart.
A satellite image shows an oil slick next to the Caroline Bezengi, a sanctioned vessel off the coast of the Dhofar Governorate, Oman, July 28, 2026. (Planet Labs PBC/Handout via REUTERS)

The spill threatens a protected marine reserve in the Arabian Sea that is home to endangered petrels and other rare wildlife. Greenpeace Germany warned that oil has already polluted stretches of coastline and damaged the area's fragile ecosystem.

"With oil apparently continuing to leak and the tanker stranded in a difficult location, there is a serious risk of a much larger oil disaster, with even more devastating consequences for the region's coastlines and marine ecosystems," Greenpeace Germany's Nina Noelle told the AP.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The U.N.'s International Maritime Organization said earlier this week it is monitoring the situation, adding that while the vessel has not broken apart, authorities are continuing to assess the safety and environmental risks.

Oman's Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology ordered the vessel's owners to remove the ship and its cargo by July 23. It is unclear whether that deadline was met or whether the owners have responded.

title: Iran's war on Americans began decades ago. These families still carry the scars
summary: Robert Bartlett says he died three times after an Iranian-supplied EFP tore through his Humvee in Baghdad, launching a decades-long fight for justice.
story: The sister of Maj. Stuart Wolfer and widow of Capt. Shawn English say Iranian-backed attacks in Iraq left wounds that remain raw nearly 20 years later.

Nearly two decades before the latest war with Iran, an explosively formed penetrator tore through a U.S. Army vehicle on a Baghdad road, killing Staff Sgt. William Brooks and leaving retired Sgt. Robert Bartlett with injuries so severe that he says he "died three times."

The weapon was part of a broader Iranian campaign that armed and trained proxy forces to target American troops in Iraq, according to federal court findings. In cases involving hundreds of U.S. victims, judges found that Iran manufactured or supplied the weapons used in the attacks and that the assailants were trained or directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

"It cut me in half from my temple down through my jaw, and then took my gunner’s legs off, and then took the top of my truck commander’s head off," Bartlett told Fox News Digital. "I would end up dying three times and spent four years at the old Walter Reed receiving surgeries, reconstruction and rebuilding."
ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER'

The vehicle driven by Sgt. Robert Bartlett after it was struck by an explosive device on Route Pluto in Baghdad on May 3, 2005. Staff Sgt. William Brooks was killed, while Bartlett and two other soldiers were wounded. (Fox News)

Bartlett was driving an armored Humvee on Route Pluto in Baghdad, May 3, 2005, when an explosively formed penetrator tore through the vehicle. Staff Sgt. William Brooks was killed, while Bartlett and two other soldiers were wounded. Bartlett suffered massive facial trauma.

The Army casualty report described Bartlett as "very seriously injured," with massive facial and dental trauma. He was the vehicle’s driver during the route-security mission when an explosive detonated from its right side.
Bartlett said the weapon was an Iranian-supplied explosively formed penetrator linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ campaign to arm militias attacking American forces in Iraq.
"When you’re blown up, you don’t know what’s hit you," he said. "You get the information after, when the intelligence reports come down and command lets you know what you got hit by."

Bartlett’s survival places him alongside two Gold Star families who say Iran’s long-running campaign against Americans did not begin with the latest fighting — and cannot be understood solely through the current headlines.

Capt. Shawn English was killed by an explosively formed penetrator in Baghdad on Dec. 3, 2006. Maj. Stuart Wolfer was killed when a rocket struck a gym inside a U.S. base in Baghdad’s International Zone on April 6, 2008.

In the federal cases involving Bartlett, English and Wolfer, the courts found both that Iran manufactured or supplied the weapons used in the attacks and that the assailants were trained or directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
I'VE STUDIED MILITARY STRATEGY. TRUMP NOW FACES IRAN'S OLDEST BATTLEFIELD TRICK
Capt. Shawn English with his three sons. English was killed in Baghdad on Dec. 3, 2006, when an Iranian explosive device struck his vehicle. (Courtesy of the English family)
Federal courts later held Iran liable for providing weapons, training, financing and other material support to the proxy forces responsible for attacks on U.S. personnel in Iraq.
For their loved ones, those findings offered formal acknowledgment of Iran’s role. They did not end the grief.
‘It’s really hard to only have memories’
"He really was my best friend," Wolfer’s sister, Beverly Wolfer Nerenberg, said in tears before her voice broke. "Sorry, even 18 years later, it doesn’t get easier to talk about."
At her wedding, she chose not to have bridesmaids. Instead, her brother stood beside her as her "man of honor."
"I couldn’t think of anybody else who I was closer to, who really understood me and knew me," she said.
Wolfer was 36 and the father of three young daughters when he was killed.

His sister said he had gone to exercise with a friend when an incoming-fire warning sounded. Those inside the gym had only seconds to react and dropped to the floor because there was no time to reach a protected space.

A military investigation found that a rocket struck the gym’s roof at approximately 3:28 p.m., sending shrapnel into the building. Wolfer and Col. Stephen Scott were almost directly beneath the point of impact and suffered severe injuries. Wolfer was transported to a combat support hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Wolfer’s daughters were approximately ages 5, 3 and 18 months old when their father died, according to his sister.
"I’m beyond grateful and proud of my nieces and how they’ve grown up," Wolfer Nerenberg said. "But it’s really hard to only have memories."
MILITARY FAMILIES WANT DOJ TO DISTRIBUTE NEARLY $800M FROM FRENCH CEMENT COMPANY FOUND GUILTY OF BRIBING ISIS
Maj. Stuart Wolfer, who was killed in Baghdad on April 6, 2008, when an Iranian rocket struck a gym on a U.S. base. (Courtesy of the Wolfer family)
She described the family as the keepers of Wolfer’s memory, preserving it for children who had little time to know him.
Her family was told soon after the attack that the rocket had come from the direction of Sadr City, Iraq, and was Iranian, she said.
"This war began a long time ago," Wolfer Nerenberg said. "For many of us, the past 18 years has been one long continuous war."
The weapon he feared killed him

Tricia English said her husband understood the threat posed by explosively formed penetrators, or EFPs — sophisticated roadside bombs designed to punch through armored military vehicles — before one killed him.
During a period of leave shortly before his death, Capt. English appeared distracted and remained awake late into the night working on his computer, she recalled.
"He told me that there were these weapons — specifically called them EFPs — that they had discovered," she said. "They knew where they were coming from, and it was really bad."
"He knew it was Iranian," she added.
English was serving on a military transition team working with Iraqi forces when the EFP struck his vehicle during a convoy operation.

An Army investigation said his mixed American-Iraqi patrol was traveling north when an explosively formed projectile struck the right side of his vehicle. English was evacuated to a combat support hospital and died from his wounds.
A billboard depicting Iran's supreme leaders since 1979 is displayed above a highway in Tehran on March 10, 2026. (AFP/Via Getty Images)
His widow said he remained conscious during part of the evacuation and that she was told his last conscious message was: "Tell Trish and the boys that I love them."
"You think after 20 years it wouldn’t be this hard," she said, struggling to continue.

English said the military initially described the weapon simply as a roadside bomb or improvised explosive device. The legal proceedings later exposed her to evidence about the weapon, the people who supplied it and the broader network behind the attack.

"Sitting in the courtroom, I then got so much more information about what really happened and what this really looked like," she said. "That was traumatizing. But he deserved it. I needed to stand up for him."
‘Doing right by them’
Bartlett said he joined the litigation not only for himself, but for those who never returned.
"My buddy died, and plenty of my guys — plenty of people — died over there at the hands of the IRGC," he said.

"If I was sent back, if I died and saw the other side and came back, and I’m not doing right by them and their families who didn’t get to have their child come home, then I’m not doing justice," he said. "I’m not living my faith, and I’m not living what I fought to protect, which is the truth."
The legal cases were brought under the terrorism exception to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, which allows certain American victims to sue designated state sponsors of terrorism.

Iran generally did not appear to defend the cases, resulting in default proceedings. However, the judges still required the plaintiffs to produce evidence demonstrating that Iran’s material support was a substantial factor in the attacks.

The resulting judgments found that Iran, acting through the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its Quds Force, supplied Shiite militia groups with funding, training, weapons and technical assistance used to target Americans. Iran has not voluntarily paid the judgments, and the plaintiffs continue to face significant obstacles collecting the money they were awarded.
Iranians burn a U.S. flag during a rally at Azadi (Freedom) Square celebrating the 41st anniversary of the Islamic Revolution, in Tehran, Iran, Tuesday, Feb. 11, 2020. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)
‘We weren’t at war with Iran’
Iran saw the fall of Saddam Hussein as both an opportunity and a threat.

With its longtime enemy removed and U.S. troops stationed next door, Tehran sought to shape Iraq’s political and security system, expand its regional influence and pressure Washington without confronting the U.S. military directly. The Quds Force cultivated Iraqi militias as proxies, providing weapons, funding and training that allowed Iran to attack American forces while maintaining a degree of deniability.
The Treasury Department has described the Quds Force as Iran’s main instrument for supporting militant groups to advance the regime’s national interests.
Tricia English said the distinction matters because American troops in Iraq were being targeted by a country against which the United States had not formally gone to war.
"We weren’t at war with Iran," she said.
The EFP attacks required Iran’s expertise, money, intelligence, manufacturing and organized networks to transport and deploy the weapons, she said.
"To have such a sophisticated, targeted, supported, funded (operation) — it was so sophisticated," she said. "I think it’s important for Americans to see that."

For Bartlett and the English and Wolfer families, the latest war is not the beginning of America’s confrontation with Iran. It is another chapter in a conflict they have carried in their bodies and families for nearly two decades.
Protesters gather in Najaf, Iraq, on March 1, 2026, to denounce the killing of Iranian leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in U.S. and Israeli airstrikes. (Karar Essa/Anadolu/Getty Images)
"This war began a long time ago," Wolfer Nerenberg said. "For many of us, the past 18 years has been one long continuous war."

For those who buried their loved ones or carried the effects of Iranian-supplied weapons home in their bodies, Iran’s war against Americans did not begin with the latest fighting — and it has never truly ended.

The court cases presented evidence that the IRGC’s Quds Force built, funded, armed and directed Shiite militia networks, supplying them with sophisticated anti-armor weapons designed to penetrate American military vehicles. The litigation also examined Iranian support for Sunni terrorist organizations operating in Iraq.

The cases challenge the perception that the attacks were solely the work of an organic Iraqi insurgency. Instead, the court findings described a broader Iranian system of proxy warfare that allowed Tehran to target American personnel through militia groups operating on the ground.
She said successive administrations have invoked Iran’s record of killing Americans when convenient, while the families have continued waiting for meaningful accountability.

"Shawn did his job every single time his country asked him to do it, regardless of who was in power," she said. "It’s been a little disheartening to watch our country — various administrations, people in power—not do theirs when it comes to this."
Bartlett said Americans exhausted by decades of war must still confront the history behind the current conflict.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

An armed member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) monitors the area while mourners participate in the funeral for the late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and his family in Tehran, Iran, on July 6, 2026. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
"You can’t add to truth and you can’t take away from it," he said. "It just is what it is."

For the families, that truth is measured not only in court judgments or military reports, but in missing fathers, brothers and friends — and in wounds that still hurt as sharply as they did when the telephone first rang.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Israeli orphans of fallen heroes find pride, connection on US journey
summary: A young Oct. 7 hostage survivor shared his story with fellow bereaved children during the IDF Widows & Orphans Organization's Bar/Bat Mitzvah trip.
story: Aviva and Keith Siegel, freed hostages from Hamas, recount their harrowing experiences in Gaza and thank first lady Melania Trump for her efforts to secure their release.

Twenty-eight children from across Israel who lost a parent killed while serving in the country's security forces participated in a three-week delegation to North America as part of the IDF Widows & Orphans Organization's annual Bar/Bat Mitzvah program.

The journey began last month in Chicago, where the children spent a weekend with host families before traveling to Camp Chi in Wisconsin for nearly a week of activities with American kids. They then continued to New York City, where they visited Times Square and saw "The Lion King" on Broadway, before heading to New Jersey. For many, it was their first visit to the United States.
FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY
The IDF Widows & Orphans Organization's annual Bar/Bat Mitzvah program delegation in NYC at Times Square. (Yiftach Moran)

"Everything is planned very carefully. ‘The Lion King,’ for instance, is more than a Broadway show for them. It’s the story of an orphan who is able to honor his father’s memory and move forward because of the support of his friends. Nothing about this trip is accidental. It is deliberately designed to give them as powerful and meaningful an experience as possible," Daniel Elbaum, executive director of the IDF Widows & Orphans USA Organization, told Fox News Digital.

With the United States home to the world’s largest Jewish population outside Israel, the trip gave the children an opportunity to meet people from diverse backgrounds and levels of religious observance while, for many, experiencing international travel independently for the first time — which Elbaum said reflects their entry into the covenant with the Jewish people in a tangible and meaningful way.

Although the trip was not designed as an initiative to combat antisemitism, Elbaum said fostering a strong Jewish identity, pride in Israel and solidarity with its people are among the most important ways to help American Jews confront the world's oldest hatred.
Memorials at the site of the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attack on the Supernova music festival near Kibbutz Re'im, Israel, on May 27, 2024. (Kobi Wolf/Bloomberg via Getty Images )

"As much as I think we are doing something important for these Israeli children, whose families have paid the highest price for Israel, what we are doing for the American children is almost as important in giving them a sense of pride and connection they might not otherwise experience," he added.
INSIDE ISRAEL'S MISSION TO TRAIN CIVILIANS TO STOP THE NEXT OCT 7-LIKE TERROR ATTACK

Founded in 1991, the IDF Widows & Orphans Organization supports more than 18,000 widows, widowers and orphans through assistance programs, rehabilitation, advocacy and legislative efforts. Since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre and the ensuing war, 359 widows and widowers — including 48 pregnant widows — and 910 new orphans have joined Israel’s circle of bereavement.

Among this year’s participants was 11½-year-old Tal Goldstein-Almog from Kibbutz Kfar Aza, who was taken hostage to Gaza with his mother and two siblings on Oct. 7 and held for 51 days. His father, Nadav, and sister Yam, an IDF soldier, were murdered during the attack.
Tal did not tell the other children he had been held captive until one evening, when he felt ready to share his experience.
The IDF Widows & Orphans Organization's annual Bar/Bat Mitzvah program delegation in NYC after seeing "The Lion King" on Broadway. (Yiftach Moran)

"It’s not hard to tell people, but it’s not easy either. Once you’ve said it, you don’t know how others will react or treat you. That night, it felt safe to open up, and nothing has changed in the way they treat me since," he told Fox News Digital.
The trip was Tal's first extended journey without his family. He learned about the program from a friend from the kibbutz who also participated.
ISRAEL'S NEW EXHIBIT EXPOSES YEARS OF HAMAS TERRORIST PLANNING BEFORE OCT 7 MASSACRE
"Now that I came, I think I will continue taking part in these things after meeting new kids, feeling comfortable around them and understanding that we experienced the same things," he said.
Tal said that since Oct. 7, the connections in his life have helped him maintain a sense of normalcy.
"My motto is that life is always going to continue," he added. "It feels refreshing to come to a new country and experience fun things here."

Shadan Khnefiss first participated in the program as an IDF orphan and has since returned as a counselor, supporting the next generation of bereaved children. A member of Israel’s Druze community, she also joined the delegation to help translate for participants whose first language is Arabic.

"I met a lot of people here who don’t know about the Druze. We serve the country, we love our country, and we even die for it. We pay the same price as everyone else. Most terrorists in Israel are Arab, but because we speak Arabic and serve our country, it’s a bit of a twist," she told Fox News Digital.
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER
Shadan Khnefiss, left, enjoying New York pizza with other participants in the IDFWO delegation.  (Yiftach Moran)

Shadan became an orphan at the age of 3. Her father, a Border Police officer stationed in Jerusalem, transferred to northern Israel after her brother was born with a serious skin condition so he could be closer to the family. He was killed in a car accident during his first shift there.

"This program helped me in so many ways throughout my life. The people around me have not all lost their father, so sometimes I can’t relate to them. Sometimes I want to share how I feel, but they don’t understand. This program made me feel comfortable talking about things I can’t discuss with people in my everyday life," she said.

Noor, 13, was one of three participants whom Shadan helped during the trip. His father, Yosef Saleh, served in the IDF before joining the Israel Police, where he was killed in the line of duty in 2013.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Noor told Fox News Digital that it was his first trip to the United States. "My message to other children like us is to go on trips, meet new kids and make new friends," Noor said.
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Rep. Andy Ogles loses his Republican primary in Tennessee
summary: Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee has lost his Republican primary, NBC News projects, falling to a former state official in a primary season that has seen an unusually high number of incumbents lose renomination.
story: Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee has lost his Republican primary, NBC News projects, falling to a former state official in a primary season that has seen an unusually high number of incumbents lose renomination.
See live results

Charlie Hatcher, the former state agricultural commissioner, rode support from prominent establishment Republicans to a victory over Ogles, a controversial congressman backed by President Donald Trump. He is a heavy favorite in the general election in the deep-red district.
Ogles was outraised and outspent on the airwaves, largely because of a massive ad effort from a pro-clean energy group — a last-minute campaign Ogles criticized in an interview with Fox News.

While Ogles had arguably the most important endorsement in a GOP primary in Trump’s, Hatcher had backing from Gov. Bill Lee, former Gov. Bill Haslam and other prominent Republicans, like former Trump Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue.

Ogles has faced various controversies over the years. He said this year that Muslims don’t belong in American society, deleted a homophobic social media post after having blamed a staffer and argued last year that the federal government should revoke future New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s citizenship and deport him.

He was also investigated on suspicion of campaign finance violations; he has not been charged with any crimes. Ogles told The Associated Press that the Justice Department returned his cellphone, which it had seized during the investigation.

But while Ogles had fended off a well-funded primary opponent before, he couldn’t do it this time. Hatcher didn’t run away from Trump, either, despite Trump’s support for Ogles. Hatcher aligned himself with Trump and his policies and sought to contrast himself with Ogles.
“Think what President Trump could do if our congressman spent less time talking and more time doing,” reads a quote on Hatcher’s website.

Ogles is the ninth House member — six Democrats and three Republicans — to lose a primary this year. That’s the most in a nondecennial redistricting year since 1970, according to Vital Statistics on Congress.

Two senators, Republicans Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and John Cornyn of Texas, also lost their primaries, and an additional House member — Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas — finished second in his primary and then decided to drop out of the race and resign before a GOP runoff.

title: Sen. Marsha Blackburn wins the Republican primary for governor of Tennessee
summary: Blackburn, a longtime Trump ally, defeated Rep. John Rose for the nomination, NBC News projects, after the president decided not to endorse in the race.
story: Sen. Marsha Blackburn has won the Republican nomination for governor of Tennessee, NBC News projects, defeating Rep. John Rose in a race in which President Donald Trump declined to endorse.

Blackburn, 74, became the first woman to represent Tennessee in the Senate after she won her current seat in 2018; she had served in the House since 2003. If she wins the governor’s race, she would be the first female governor.

She will be a heavy favorite in the general election in the red state to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Bill Lee. Jerri Green, a member of the Memphis City Council, won the Democratic nomination.
Blackburn is considered one of the most conservative members of the Senate, known for her stances on abortion and transgender rights and her criticism of China’s influence.
While Trump stayed out of the race, Blackburn and Rose both leaned on his name.

The Tennessee Freedom Fund, a pro-Blackburn outside group, has spent heavily to tie her to Trump, airing advertisements featuring clips of Trump referring to her as “an incredible person” and saying: “Fantastic job you did. We’re proud of you.”

At a rally in Washington in January, Trump praised Blackburn, saying, “Unfortunately, she’s running for governor,” and adding: “I’d love her not to. I begged her: ‘I said, ‘Marsha, don’t. We don’t want to lose you in the Senate.’”

But the Nashville Banner reported that Trump told members of Tennessee’s congressional delegation on a flight to Memphis on Air Force One that he would not endorse Blackburn because of his relationship with Rose, according to two members of Congress who were present for the conversation. Rose, who represents Tennessee’s 6th District, is a former state agriculture commissioner who also positioned himself as a loyal Trump ally.

It makes the race a rare Republican contest in which Trump has stayed on the sidelines. Trump has even double-endorsed GOP candidates in past races, like in South Carolina, where he added an endorsement of state Attorney General Alan Wilson to his backing of Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette ahead of a runoff Wilson won.
Rose spent almost $13 million self-funding his gubernatorial bid.
Blackburn is part of an unusually large group of senators running for governor in this election cycle.

GOP Sen. Tommy Tuberville won his party’s gubernatorial nomination in Alabama this year, while Democratic Sen. Michael Bennet lost his primary in Colorado. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar will be on the ballot for governor in Minnesota next week.

title: How three health factors can help delay dementia for up to 13 years
summary: New research from NYU Langone Health found that people who avoid three vascular risk factors in middle age had about 13 more dementia-free years.
story: It may be possible to ward off or prevent one of the most common types of dementia, a new long-term study suggests.
The risk of cognitive decline increases as we get older, with about 42% of Americans over the age of 55 expected to develop dementia during their lives.

The research, published Wednesday in the journal Neurology Open Access, found that people who avoid three vascular risk factors in middle age — high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking — had about 13 more dementia-free years.

For the study, NYU Langone Health researchers tracked about 12,400 middle-aged participants in the U.S. for about 26 years. At the start, their average age was 56. Just over half of participants were women and about 25% were Black. None of the participants had signs of vascular cognitive impairment, a condition linked to strokes and small-vessel disease.

The researchers compared people who were diagnosed with the risk factors of diabetes, hypertension (blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher) and who used tobacco to those with none. Diabetes, hypertension and smoking cause damage to blood vessels, including those that supply the brain.
For people with the three risk factors, dementia risk rose from 23% at age 55 to 37% at 75. By 85, only 7% of people with all three risk factors were dementia-free.
People with the three risk factors had an about 18 dementia-free years of their lives, compared to an estimated 30 years for those with no risk factors.

Dr. Josef Coresh, the director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone Health and an author of the study, said the researchers wanted to summarize the effects of midlife health habits on dementia and to give a simplified, “bottom-line” message for the population.
“We found if you had more risk factors, you had an elevated risk of both dementia and mortality,” Coresh said.

The findings reinforce evidence that healthy blood vessels not only protect against heart disease, but also protect brain health, said Dr. Cynthia Carlsson, a geriatrician at University of Wisconsin Health, who was not involved in the study.

Dr. Anna S. Nordvig, an assistant professor of neurology at Weill Cornell Medicine, not involved in this study, said that if brain tissue is no longer receiving proper nutrition and blood flow, then that can lead to cognitive decline.

“Those three risk factors are all known to contribute to both small and large blood vessel disease in the brain,” Nordvig said. “Controlling anything that improves cardiovascular health will also improve brain health.”

Prevention is crucial since there’s no cure for vascular dementia or Alzheimer’s, Coresh said. The NYU research focused on vascular health, although many of the same risk factors also contribute to Alzheimer’s, Coresh said. “Vascular health in midlife influences Alzheimer’s pathology,” he later said via email. “Treating vascular risk works on both fronts.”
About half of dementia is preventable through lifestyle changes, Coresh said. “There’s a lot you can do.”
Experts agree that it is never too late to start addressing vascular health.
“I encourage people to start with something tangible,” Carlsson said. “It’ll be different for each person based on what their risk profile looks like.”
Nordvig said that in addition to the three factors included in the research, she recommends focusing on other critical risk factors for dementia, such as high cholesterol, sleep apnea and obesity.
“Fifty-five [years old] is a great time to drastically improve your future of vascular health, both in your body and in your brain, and that also means slowing down dementia,” Nordvig said.

title: Appeals court blocks Trump’s White House ballroom construction
summary: A federal appeals court affirmed a federal judge’s ruling to block construction of the White House ballroom while allowing below-ground construction to move forward.
story: A federal appeals court on Friday affirmed a U.S. judge’s ruling to block construction of the White House ballroom while allowing below-ground work to move forward.

In a 2-1 decision, the court affirmed the modified preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Richard Leon. But they stayed their own ruling for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal the case to the Supreme Court.
The White House did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.
“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” the appeals court’s ruling said.

That’s because the “Constitution assigns Congress — not the Executive — the responsibility to decide whether proposed changes to the physical design of the White House may proceed, even where those changes are said to serve security interests.”

“Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence,” the Ruling said. “The President has no — and claims no — constitutionally assigned authority over that property.”
The ruling paints the current administration as completely ignoring those restrictions.

“Over just three days in October 2025, without undertaking promised consultations or obtaining Congress’s permission, President Trump bulldozed the entire East Wing in order to construct a massive, 90,000 square-foot ballroom paid for by private funds with no congressional oversight,” it said.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now.”

The ruling by U.S. Circuit Judges Patricia Millett, an Obama appointee, and Brad Garcia, a Biden appointee, says it “has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom.

“What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require,” they wrote.

The dissenting judge was Trump appointee Neomi Rao, who said the lower court had “abused its discretion in seizing control of construction at the President’s home and office” through the underlying order that her colleagues were upholding.

That judge had previously let some aspects of the construction to move forward, but then said the Trump administration was taking advantage of a safety and security exception to encompass the entire ballroom construction effort.

“Defendants argue that the entire ballroom construction project, from tip to tail, falls within the safety-and-security exception and therefore may proceed unabated. That is neither a reasonable nor a correct reading of my Order!”Leon, a noted fan of exclamation marks, wrote in his prior April order.
“It is, to say the least, incredible, if not disingenuous, that Defendants now argue that my Order does not stop ballroom construction because of the safety-and-security exception!” he added.

title: Woman who killed husband over two decades ago admits to fatally stabbing firefighter wife
summary: A woman in California admitted on Tuesday that she stabbed her wife to death last year, more than two decades after facing prison time for killing her ex-husband in a similar manner.
story: A woman in California admitted on Tuesday that she stabbed her wife to death last year, more than two decades after facing prison time for killing her ex-husband in a similar manner.

Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in connection with the the death of her wife, Rebecca “Becky” Marodi, 49, a respected California firefighter. She was arrested in connection with the crime last year after fleeing to Mexico.

Rebecca Marodi was found dead in her San Diego County home on Feb. 17, 2025, with several injuries to her neck, chest and back “consistent with a stabbing,” the San Diego County Sheriff’s Office said at the time.
Her wife “was seen on surveillance video earlier in the evening arguing with Rebecca and physically assaulting her,” according to the sheriff’s office.

Rebecca Marodi’s mother, Lorena Marodi, found her daughter with multiple stab wounds and called for help, according to the sheriff’s office. Life saving measures were performed on site, but Rebecca Marodi succumbed to her injuries.

Yolanda Marodi was captured by Mexican officials in the country more than a month later before being brought back the United States. She was found at a hotel roughly 2.3 miles south of the U.S. border in the city of Mexicali, the Baja California Citizen Security Secretariat (SSCBC) said at the time.

An affidavit for Yolanda Marodi’s arrest describes Ring security video captured outside the couple’s home in Ramona, California — about 45 miles northeast of San Diego — on the day that the firefighter was slain.

The document said Rebecca Marodi could be seen with blood on her back and was heard on the video saying, “Yolanda! Please … (I) don’t want to die.” Yolanda Marodi, seen in the video holding a knife, responded, “You should have thought about that before.”
Later, she can be seen wearing different clothes and packing  her silver Chevrolet Equinox SUV before driving away, according to the document.

In 2003, Yolanda Marodi pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter in the stabbing death of husband Jim Olejniczak in 2000, according to NBC San Diego. She was released from custody a decade later, according to the station.
Lorena Marodi told authorities that her daughter informed Yolanda Marodi about a week before the killing that she was ending the marriage, according to the affidavit.

“Becky came home and told me she was leaving, she met someone else, all the messages were lies,” Yolanda Marodi wrote to an unnamed associate the day after the killing, according to the affidavit. “We had a big fight and I hurt her…I’m sorry.”

Rebecca Marodi worked in firefighting for more than 30 years, starting as a volunteer in Moreno Valley, according to a joint statement from the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection, known as Cal Fire, and the Riverside County Fire Department.

The 49-year-old was on the frontlines of the Eaton Fire — one of the state’s deadliest blazes in recent years — last year, according to an Instagram post from Cal Fire’s battalion in Temecula, California, a community about 65 miles north of San Diego.
“Becky was a beloved member of our community and Department, and we miss her greatly,” Cal Fire/Riverside County Fire Department said in a statement after Rebecca Marodi’s killing last year.

title: Sen. Bill Cassidy, a critical Republican holdout, backs Todd Blanche for attorney general
summary: GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski says she will vote against Todd Blanche for AG, putting confirmation in jeopardy
story: WASHINGTON — Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., announced Friday he will vote for President Donald Trump’s pick of Todd Blanche for attorney general, likely assuring his confirmation.
“All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche. I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?” Cassidy said in a floor speech after outlining concerns he said he weighed.
Cassidy’s decision is likely to be decisive in helping Blanche get confirmed to the powerful job.
While he’s “concerned about episodes of apparent lawfare,” Cassidy said, “even critics admit that Mr. Blanche knows the law and is a hands-on administrator.”
Republicans need support from 50 of their 53 senators to confirm Blanche.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, came out Friday against Blanche, joining fellow centrist Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, to oppose the president’s choice. With Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., out indefinitely, and Democrats expected to vote no, a third GOP opponent would have blocked the nomination.
Despite the “numerous constructive meetings” she’s had with Blanche, Murkowski said in a statement, “I will oppose his nomination.”

“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she said.
Murkowski also warned of the “politicization” and “even weaponization” of the Justice Department, which she said has accelerated under the Trump administration.

The senator cited the Justice Department’s handling of the release of files in the case of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and questioned whether the Trump administration’s proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund, which she called a “slush fund” in her announcement, would remain off the table.
A McConnell spokesperson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment Friday about how he would vote if he were able to be present and cast a vote.

The retiring Kentucky senator is not a guaranteed proponent on Blanche; he has voted against some high-profile Trump nominees, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.
In an interview with Punchbowl News on Thursday, before Murkowski’s announcement, Trump lashed out against the moderate GOP senator.

“Murkowski, I was against. I’m against Murkowski,” he said in the interview, released Friday. “I do more for Alaska than any any president in history. No president’s done for Alaska what I’ve done. She’s she’s not good.”

Blanche, the acting attorney general, has already faced a bumpy confirmation process after Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., both withheld their support for the nomination over their concerns about his leadership at the Justice Department.

Cornyn and Tillis had expressed concerns about the fund, which was intended to compensate alleged victims of politically motivated prosecutions. The fund was created as part of Trump’s settlement with the IRS over a leak of his tax records. The settlement also included a guarantee that he and his family business would be sheltered from tax audits.

The senators had sought written assurances that the fund would be rescinded and the scope of the audit immunity clarified, which Blanche ultimately provided. Tillis had also insisted that Blanche meet with Epstein survivors, which he had previously not agreed to do.

After Blanche’s contentious confirmation hearing last month, during which Tillis and other senators aired their concerns about the Justice Department’s handling of the Epstein case, the acting attorney general did meet privately with a group of victims. Epstein survivor Dani Bensky told NBC News, however, that the meeting was “not productive” or “substantive,” while Blanche described it in opposite terms.

Democrats have denounced the Justice Department’s failure to redact personal information about the survivors, but not that of people who may have participated in their abuse. They have also raised concerns the “anti-weaponization” fund is not dead and that loopholes exist to resurrect it.

title: U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July, a sudden reversal for the labor market
summary: The U.S. economy shed 23,000 jobs in July, a sign that the labor market had not stabilized after four months of positive growth.
story: The U.S. economy shed 23,000 jobs in July, a sign that the labor market had not stabilized after four months of positive growth.
The unemployment rate ticked down only slightly to 4.1%.
Economists surveyed by Dow Jones were expecting the release to show 83,000 added roles, more than June’s 57,000.

In yet another troubling sign for the labor market, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said that it revised down the prior two months by a combined 103,000. May’s jobs total was cut by 66,000 to 129,000 total jobs added, while June’s total was lowered by 37,000 to a total gain of 57,000.

The hiring data comes against a complicated economic backdrop. The U.S. war with Iran continues without any kind of agreement to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. As a result, energy prices remain elevated, even if they are off their highest levels of the year.

The change in workers’ average hourly earnings also fell well short of economists’ expectations. Wage growth was 0.1% from June, or 3.2% from one year ago. That’s also below inflation, which was 3.5% in its most recent reading.

“That’s the number that many Americans are focused on right now,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told NBC News. Long pointed out that 3.2% was the lowest wage growth has been in five years. “At the same time, inflation is heating back up again.”
Economists had been expecting wages to continue pacing at 3.5% from a year ago.
“The labor market is stalling again,” Long said, also calling the report “bleak.”

Long also pointed to another troubling data point: The labor force participation rate in July was the lowest since February 2021, a sign that workers are dropping out of the workforce. “It’s pretty shocking,” she said. “Over two million people have left the labor force since November.”
“The magnitude of the payroll miss suggests the labor market may be losing momentum and can no longer be considered the pillar of strength,” said Allianz investment strategist Charlie Ripley.

The average price of regular gasoline also remains high, at $4.04 per gallon as of Friday morning, up 36% since Feb. 28, when the Iran war began. Inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target at 3.5%. Wages are struggling to keep pace.

The BLS said employment contracted the most in “local government education,” which declined by 50,000 roles, likely reflecting teachers during summer break. It also flagged a contraction of 19,000 roles in the retail industry. The financial industry shed 14,000 roles.

The leisure and hospitality industry also contracted by 40,000 jobs. Economists watch this figure closely because a significant loss at hotels and restaurants could be an early warning sign of a shift in consumer spending.

“In July, employment in health care continued its upward trend,” the BLS said, noting a gain of 22,000 jobs. But it said, that was “a slower pace than  the average monthly gain over the prior 12 months.”

The agency’s data also showed a 5,000 payroll gain in the manufacturing sector in July and an additional 22,000 roles in construction. These bright spots come as the AI data center boom has benefited some industries, but deeply divided many communities where the centers are located.
“Employment showed little change” in July in the mining, oil & gas, transportation and professional & business services sectors, according to BLS.

Stocks rose after the report, as investors who were concerned the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates breathed a sigh of relief. The S&P 500 jumped 0.5% and the Nasdaq Composite index increased 1%.
The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium size firms which can be more sensitive to rate changes, rose 0.9%.

Bond yields dropped, with the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield falling to around 4.6%. That Treasury bond specifically drives the direction of consumer lending rates, such as for mortgages, credit cards and personal loans.
Friday’s report likely eases some pressure on the Federal Reserve, which had been widely expected to hike the federal funds rate — potentially as soon as September.
Before the report, the futures market indicated the odds of a September rate hike were over 50%. After Friday’s jobs numbers were released, those odds fell to about 40%.

Avoid misplaced supplies by labeling literally everything: clothes, shoes, notebooks, backpacks, lunchboxes, food storage containers, books — the list goes on. This label maker connects to an app on your phone via Bluetooth, letting you customize labels with words, icons, borders and more so you can keep tabs on all that stuff. How to save while back-to-school shopping

Before the school year starts, focus on buying essentials that students need from day one, experts say. That includes basic supplies like notebooks, folders, pens and pencils, as well as backpacks, lunchboxes and water bottles. Even higher on consumers’ back-to-school shopping lists, however, is clothing and shoes — 48 percent say that’s what they plan on adding to their carts right now, according to a recent survey by RetailMeNot. Apparel tends to get picked over later into the season, so get the color, size or style your student needs before it’s gone, says Stephanie Carls, a retail insights expert at RetailMeNot.

The same advice applies to college students, including as it relates to shopping for dorm rooms: Get what you can’t live without now and save the rest for later. Carls says bedding, towels, shower caddies, kitchen basics, laundry supplies and storage move fast, so if you haven’t bought them yet, grab whatever you can find.

Wait to buy anything you’re not sure students need yet, anything that feels like an “extra” and anything that could be a specific request from the teacher, like certain calculators and computer software, for example. If you hold off on shopping for these items until after the school year starts, you may find better deals than retailers are currently offering, says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, a shopping and savings strategist at Rakuten. They’ll continue hosting sales through September, so don’t feel pressure to buy everything before day one.

As for college students, wait to buy anything that requires coordinating with a roommate or measuring a dorm room, like a mini fridge, rug, furniture or TV, says Carls. Skip decor for now, too — once students are living in the space, they’ll have a better idea of what they actually need to outfit the room.

Hundreds of retailers give undergraduate students, graduate students and teachers exclusive discounts in-store and online, and many of them are year-round, storewide/sitewide offers you can take advantage of every time you shop. To access these discounts, you’ll need to verify your student or educator status by showing a document like a school-issued ID in-person or using a third-party service online like ID.me and SheerID, which connect to brands’ websites to automatically apply the discount at checkout.

Student and teacher discounts aren’t always easy to find — some brands don’t advertise them at all. If you’re shopping in-person, Carls recommends asking a store associate or cashier whether the store has student or teacher discounts available. If you’re shopping online, I recommend browsing sites like Unidays, Student Beans, SheerID and ID.me, which aggregate brands’ student and teacher discounts so you can see them all in one place.

The terms of each brand’s student or teacher discount differ, so make sure you understand what items it applies to, as well as when and how often you can use it. You can often stack these discounts with cashback and sales, saving you even more.

Sales tax holidays are limited periods when a state waives or reduces the sales tax on specific types of products. See the 2026 calendar here. Not all states have them, but those that do often host them around now to help offset the cost of back-to-school shopping — the waived or reduced tax usually applies to products like school supplies, backpacks, clothing, shoes and technology.

If you live in a state that has a sales tax holiday now or in the coming weeks, Gerstley recommends factoring it into your back-to-school shopping savings strategy, but don’t completely rely on it. The holiday will save you money, but to really stretch your budget, you’ll need to stack savings like cashback, stores’ sales and coupons, too.

While the tips I included below are centered around back-to-school shopping, you can use almost all of them throughout the entire academic year. Gerstley says small savings add up over time, and building smart shopping habits now will benefit you long-term.

Make a shopping list: My favorite strategy is to make a shopping list of everything you need, and then step back and categorize the list into “must haves” and “save for laters.” Categorizing items like this forces you to think critically about each one and whether you can survive without it for a few weeks. A list also makes it easier to stick to your budget — if you didn’t write it down, you immediately know it’s not something you absolutely need.Spread out your spending: Back-to-school sales won’t end immediately once the academic year starts, so check items off your list over time rather than doing one big haul. Waiting to buy your “save for laters” also gives you time to look for better deals, especially on pricey products.Buy essentials in bulk while they’re on sale: Retailers tend to discount school supply essentials like pens, pencils, paper and folders, as well as health and wellness basics like hand sanitizer and disinfecting wipes, the most leading up to the academic year. If you see something on sale that you constantly re-buy, throw a bunch of them in your cart, says Carls. You’re guaranteed to use them, so you’ll save money in the long run. Stack your savings: A retailer’s discount price is just a starting point — stacking additional savings opportunities on top of that is what really makes a difference at checkout. Beyond adding deals to your cart, experts recommend shopping through a browser extension or app that lets you earn cashback and find exclusive promo codes; using a credit card that lets you earn cashback or points on purchases; and taking advantage of student and teacher discounts.Comparison shop: Tons of retailers are hosting back-to-school sales right now, so before you buy something, compare retailers’ discount prices, shipping fees and cashback opportunities to make sure you’re getting the overall best deal possible.For teachers: Eligible educators can deduct up to $350 on their federal taxes for school supplies and technology, among other things, so track what you spend, says Gerstley.  For college students: If college students are frequent shoppers at big retailers, they should consider signing up for a loyalty membership if there’s one available at a discounted rate, like Amazon Prime for Young Adults, Target Circle College Student Appreciation and Walmart+ for students. These memberships often come with perks like free, fast shipping, cashback on purchases and exclusive deals on products tailored to students’ needs.

title: Sen. Mitch McConnell discharged from rehab center following hospitalization in mid-June
summary: The Republican senator said he would continue to work from home and didn’t provide a timeline for his Senate return.
story: Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., said Thursday that he has been discharged from a rehabilitation center where he was recovering from a fall he suffered in mid-June.

“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home. Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff,” McConnell said in a statement.
McConnell, 84, said he would continue to work from home, and he did not provide a timeline for his return to the Senate, which is expected to begin a five-week recess in the coming days.

Uncertainty surrounding McConnell’s health has swirled for weeks following his June 14 hospitalization, after which he had not been seen in public. His staff has repeatedly refused to answer questions about his condition, prompting calls for transparency from some critics, including Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear.
Police scanner audio NBC News obtained last month indicated that paramedics conducted CPR on a person experiencing a “cardiac arrest” at McConnell’s address.

In a statement last month, he said he had been hospitalized after he was “briefly unconscious” following a fall. “My doctors have confirmed that I didn’t break any bones or suffer a concussion,” he said July 12. “I didn’t have a heart attack or a stroke. I don’t have any tumors or hemorrhages. But I was briefly unconscious and was taken to the hospital. While receiving excellent care over the past several weeks, I’ve also had to deal with a mild case of pneumonia.”
Since his hospitalization, McConnell has missed 51 Senate floor votes and is expected to miss the vote to confirm Todd Blanche for attorney general if it takes place this week.
McConnell, who has also suffered a number of health issues over the years, is retiring at the end of his term in January.

In February, McConnell was hospitalized for a week with “flu-like symptoms.” In 2023, he was hospitalized for a concussion he sustained when he tripped at a hotel, and the same year, he had several episodes of freezing in the middle of speaking, which were caught on camera and raised concerns about his mental fitness for office. He also fractured a shoulder in 2019 when he fell at his home in Kentucky.
McConnell is one of the oldest members of the Senate after Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, and Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who are 92 and 84, respectively.

title: IRS workers group joins Jan. 6 ‘slush fund’ suit, seeking to block Trump audit carve-out
summary: Career IRS employees joined the weaponization fund lawsuit, challenging a carve-out that would give him and members of his family immunity from certain tax audits.
story: WASHINGTON — An organization representing career Internal Revenue Service employees has joined a lawsuit over the contentious settlement reached in connection with President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS, challenging a carve-out that would give him and members of his family immunity from certain tax audits.

A Jan. 6 prosecutor fired by the Trump administration and others previously sued to block a fund that could have gone to Trump allies who said they were victims of weaponization, potentially including Jan. 6 rioters. A federal judge then temporarily blocked the fund from moving forward in May.

Now, an amended version of the lawsuit filed in the Eastern District of Virginia on Thursday afternoon alleges that the IRS audit immunity that acting Attorney General Todd Blanche agreed to for Trump and his family members in connection with the purported settlement is unlawful and unconstitutional. The National Treasury Employees Union, which represents career IRS auditors, has joined the litigation.
The order would provide the president “and his relatives and affiliates with a lucrative benefit not available to any other Americans,” the lawsuit argued.

The lawsuit describes the purported settlement as “an unprecedented, unlawful, and breathtakingly corrupt attempt by the President and members of his cabinet to manipulate the legal process and laws intended to prevent political interference to achieve benefits that President Trump and his political allies could not have obtained lawfully.”

Both the Trump tax carve-out and the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund grew out of a lawsuit Trump and his family members filed against the government he controls over the disclosure of his tax returns by a former IRS contractor, who was imprisoned over the disclosure.

Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of the group Democracy Forward, which brought the initial case, said Thursday that they were “honored to represent brave IRS employees in this first-of-its-kind case challenging the unlawful scheme, while we continue to pursue the challenge to the $1.776 billion slush fund that will line the pockets of violent criminals, including those who perpetrated the attacks on the Capitol and our elections on January 6.”
Blanche, Perryman said, “cannot tell the public the slush fund is dead while preserving every legal mechanism necessary to resurrect it at a moment’s notice.”

Two key Republican senators — Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas — had raised issues with the “anti-weaponization” fund but then reached a deal with Blanche to memorialize the end of the fund.
Blanche’s nomination to take over the top Justice Department role is now pending before the full Senate, after it was voted out of the Judiciary Committee this week.

The Justice Department could still pay out Jan. 6 rioters even without the fund, although this week, the department told a federal judge in Florida to toss a lawsuit filed on behalf of a number of Jan. 6 participants, saying their claims were barred by the statute of limitations.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the amended lawsuit.

title: Ohio Rep. Max Miller faces a growing number of calls to resign from fellow Republicans
summary: Miller, who is running for re-election, has denied abusing his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who is the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio.
story: A growing number of Republicans are calling on Rep. Max Miller to resign and drop his re-election campaign following abuse allegations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno.

Miller, R-Ohio, has denied the allegations, which exploded onto the national stage after he addressed them on a livestream Sunday, prompting Moreno’s father, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, to denounce him publicly.

Miller has repeatedly vowed to keep running for re-election, even as the senator said in a weekend statement that Miller “is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.”

A spokesperson for the office of Ohio’s secretary of state told NBC News that the deadline to replace a candidate would be Monday. The replacement candidate would be selected by county party chairs in the district.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

Emily Moreno has accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, throwing her against a wall and throwing hot water on her, according to court documents released by her lawyer. Miller has not faced criminal charges related to his ex-wife’s allegations and has repeatedly denied the assertions.
Miller has sued Emily Moreno, alleging defamation following a Daily Mail report regarding the alleged abuse. Lawyers for Emily Moreno have moved to dismiss the suit.
Miller on Tuesday voluntarily requested that the House Ethics Committee investigate the domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife, adding that he has “absolutely nothing to hide.”
In a livestream Sunday, Miller said his ex-wife’s claims that he physically assaulted her were false and released a trove of documents that he said backed up his assertion.

“Ask yourself: If I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?” he said. “Would she have invited me to spend an afternoon at the playground with her and our daughter?”

Emily Moreno’s spokesperson, Stefan Mychajliw, said in a statement that it was “shameful that Max Miller decided to go on a bizarre and lie-filled rant about his ex-wife to desperately try to save his political career.”
“There is a documented trove of evidence that Miller has a history of violent and dangerous behavior and no amount of victim shaming will change that,” Mychajliw added.

The allegations sparked widespread condemnation from Democrats. Now, an expanding group of Republicans has publicly condemned Miller, with some calling for him to bow out of his re-election bid in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District.
A spokesperson for Miller declined to provide a comment. Miller’s congressional office and legal representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., weighed in Thursday after Moreno accused Miller of holding the senator’s 2-year-old granddaughter’s blue bunny toy “hostage,” which Miller denied.

Miller had released screenshots of communications with multiple people trying to coordinate the return of the bunny to his daughter, who is Sen. Moreno’s granddaughter. In his post explaining the screenshots, Miller said that “a man who is not on our approved list” reached out to try to pick up the bunny. Miller said he responded that “it was inappropriate of him to insert himself in family business and that I was waiting for you, @berniemoreno, like we agreed upon.”
Sheehy referred to the bunny situation in a post condemning Miller.

“What kind of person would treat their daughter this way?” Sheehy said on X. “This guy is clearly a degenerate sociopath. Max should step aside and seek help. Staying in this race makes it far more likely we lose this seat and hand Democrats a majority to impeach President Trump.”
Asked if Miller should step down if the allegations of domestic abuse were true, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Nexstar that “any member of Congress who’s involved in domestic abuse should resign.”
Husted said he was “glad” that the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into whether Miller engaged in domestic violence and abuse or used illegal drugs.
Asked whether he should drop out of the race before the committee completes the investigation, Husted did not give a direct answer.
“We’re going to talk more about what potentially can happen there,” he said. “I know that time frame is short, but if he’s guilty of domestic violence, he’s unfit for public office.”
Later, Husted said on X that “anyone who commits domestic violence is not fit to serve in Congress.” He called on the House Ethics Committee to “thoroughly investigate any credible allegations.”

“I believe Max would be making the right decision to step aside as a candidate and resign from Congress to focus on what is in the best interest of his daughter,” Husted said later in the statement. “Years from now, I believe he will look back and know it was the right choice for her.”
On Wednesday, Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., told Semafor that Miller should resign and drop his re-election bid.

“When you watch those [Miller] interviews, if you have ever had anyone in your life that has experienced abuse, they were eerie,” she said, according to the outlet. “But I stand with Bernie and supporting his daughter and his granddaughter, and hope that others will as well.”
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., told the outlet MeidasTouch that he condemns “any type of woman abuse.”
Asked whether Miller should resign, Marshall said, “Based upon what I know, yes.”

“Have I heard his side of the story? No, I have not,” he said, referring to Miller. “But I certainly trust Bernie and his family is such a good family, I’ve met quite a few of them, and they have such high values.”

Other Republicans have expressed support for Moreno, who said in a Sunday statement that the past two years have been “hell” for him and his family. Moreno said that “if there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them.”
“He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Moreno said on Sunday.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., told Politico that she does not know Miller and has not “read a whole lot about him,” but said that if Moreno “thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.”

Similarly, Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., said that “it would surprise me if Bernie were being untruthful.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, also told Politico that allegations of domestic abuse are “not what we want in our lawmakers.”

If you or someone you know is facing domestic violence, call the National Domestic Violence hotline for help at (800) 799-SAFE (7233), or go to thehotline.org for more. States often have domestic violence hotlines as well.

title: Senators vote to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress for invoking the Fifth
summary: Fauci declined to answer senators’ questions over 100 times during last week’s hearing, angering Republican lawmakers who have targeted him for years.
story: Senate Republicans voted to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he declined to answer lawmakers’ questions during a fiery hearing last week.

Fauci, who has been a target of the right since he served as a top health official during the Covid pandemic, repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment right during the hearing, explaining in his opening remarks that he believed Republicans would try to use his testimony to prosecute him.
Now, Republicans on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee have pushed to do just that with the 8-5, party-line vote.

“We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a sweeping federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence,” committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., said in his opening statement at the meeting. Paul was referring to a pardon that then-President Joe Biden gave to Fauci and several others just prior to leaving office, which Biden said was to protect them from potential politically motivated prosecutions.

The committee can refer the contempt of Congress resolution directly to the Justice Department or request that Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hold a full Senate vote. Paul said Wednesday that the “first thing we will do” if the resolution was approved would be to refer the matter to the Justice Department.
Paul said after the vote that the committee would hand-deliver the referral to the Justice Department.
“We will hand-deliver it today to the attorney general, and we will hand-deliver it today to the District of Columbia, to the U.S. attorney there,” Paul told reporters.
